instances.label: Field address listing for a census/survey sample area: the interviewer drives or walks assigned blocks in a residential neighborhood with a tablet map, observes structures, identifies housing units (including hidden units such as converted garages or basement apartments), and adds/corrects/deletes address records in the listing application.

Office-based address frame preparation: the interviewer reviews aerial/street imagery, county parcel and assessor files, postal delivery-sequence files, and prior survey listings on a computer to compile or update a list of addresses and households for an assigned geography.

Locating a specific sampled address or respondent household for an ongoing panel survey: cross-checking directories, USPS records, utility and administrative databases, and contacting neighbors, landlords, or building managers by phone or in person to confirm current occupancy and unit designations.

Listing units in multi-unit buildings, mobile home parks, or gated complexes: obtaining access, reading mailbox banks and unit signage, speaking with a manager, and recording unit designations and household counts in the listing instrument.

Market-research or health-survey household enumeration: building a call/visit list of eligible households in a defined area from purchased sample files, phone lists, and quick verification calls, then recording contact and disposition information in the CATI/CAPI system.

roles.title: Library Assistants, Clerical
roles.description: Compile records, and sort, shelve, issue, and receive library materials such as books, electronic media, pictures, cards, slides and microfilm. Locate library materials for loan and replace material in shelving area, stacks, or files according to identification number and title. Register patrons to permit them to borrow books, periodicals, and other library materials.

tasks.label: Sort books, publications, and other items according to established procedure and return them to shelves, files, or other designated storage areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Public library circulation workroom: emptying the book drop and return bins of a jumbled mix of hardbacks, paperbacks, DVD/audiobook cases and magazines; checking each item in and sorting it onto carts or into bins by established procedure (owning branch, section, format, hold status, damaged/needs-repair).

Public library open stacks: shelving a loaded truck of adult fiction and nonfiction in exact Dewey/alphabetic order — reading spine labels, finding the insertion point on a tightly packed shelf, easing neighbors aside, reaching floor-level and above-head shelves, and working around patrons, strollers and stray items.

Children's/juvenile and media browsing area: filing picture books and board books into alphabetized browsing bins, returning DVDs/CDs/audiobook cases and kits to browser racks and locking-case shelves, and re-sorting items patrons have left out of order or on the floor.

Academic/research or special-collections library: reshelving bound periodicals, oversized volumes, thin pamphlets and theses by long LC call numbers in tall multi-tier or compact movable stacks, plus filing non-print items (microfilm reels into cabinet drawers, pictures/clippings into vertical files).

Holds, transit and closed-stack storage: sorting newly returned and incoming-transit items against the hold queue and placing them on the public holds shelf in patron-code order, or returning items to a closed-stack/high-density storage area by location code.

sources.title: Forsyth County Public Library | Faster Returns With FlexAMH | Bibliotheca
sources.claim: Bibliotheca's flexAMH automated materials handling system, installed at Forsyth County Public Library (Georgia, USA), takes bulk-dropped returns onto a conveyor, reads RFID, checks items in and automatically sorts them into destination bins for reshelving.

sources.title: Library Automation Solutions | Lyngsoe Library Systems
sources.claim: Lyngsoe Systems' Sort Mate 2000 AMH, installed at US public libraries including Santa Barbara Public Library (over 1 million items circulated per year), checks in patron-returned items and routes them to configurable destinations such as bins, trolleys and carts.

sources.title: Stow: Robotic packing of items into fabric pods - Amazon Science
sources.claim: Amazon's robotic Stow system autonomously places individual, highly diverse items into densely packed fabric-pod shelf bins in a production fulfillment center, at human-level packing density and speed, with over 500,000 stows completed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse stowing. Reshelving is the same manipulation problem — inserting individual books/media (a core Amazon item class) into a tightly packed shelf compartment at a machine-designated location, at human speed and without damage — performed where the shelving is brought to the robot.

sources.title: How Amazon's Vulcan robots use touch to plan and execute motions - Amazon Science
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan robot, which picks and stows items to and from fabric pod shelves using force/touch sensing, moved from a six-robot pilot into a 30-robot beta in the Spokane, Washington fulfillment center and is also running in Hamburg.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse pick/stow into shelf bins. Demonstrates the same insert-into-packed-shelf skill on mixed rigid and deformable items comparable to books, DVD cases and magazines, in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: bookBot (Dematic automated storage and retrieval system)
sources.title: bookBot and Collections | James B. Hunt Jr. Library | NC State University Libraries
sources.claim: NC State University's Hunt Library operates the bookBot, an automated storage and retrieval ... up to 2 million library volumes in machine-addressed bins and returns/retrieves them on request instead of open shelving.
sources.transferJustification: Same task, machine-native form: 'returning items to designated storage areas' is executed by the crane placing library items into tracked storage bins in a purpose-built storage module.

sources.title: This Robot Librarian Locates Haphazardly Placed Books | Smithsonian
sources.claim: AuRoSS, an autonomous RFID shelf-scanning robot deployed in Singapore public libraries, navigates library stacks and identifies misplaced books, but it flags them for a human librarian to physically retrieve and reshelve — it performs no manipulation.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound in-library (E2) robot capability: the only robots actually deployed inside library stacks scan inventory; the shelving itself is left to staff.

sources.system: 'From Pixels to Shelf' mobile manipulator stocking system
sources.title: From Pixels to Shelf: An Integrated Robotic System for Autonomous Supermarket Stocking with a Mobile Manipulator
sources.claim: A 2025 mobile-manipulator system for autonomous supermarket shelf stocking achieved over 98% pick-and-place success, but only in laboratory conditions replicating a store, and the authors state performance remains inferior to human workers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shelf stocking in a human-standard retail facility, the closest analogue to shelving in open library stacks; cited to show such work is still lab-stage and below worker quality, supporting the negative E2 judgment.

tasks.label: Open and close library during specified hours and secure library equipment, such as computers and audio-visual equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Morning opening of a public library branch: staff member arrives before posted hours, disarms the intruder alarm, unlocks exterior and vestibule doors, opens security gates, switches on lighting, powers up/logs on the public access computers, printers and self-check kiosks, unlocks study-room and display-case doors, and releases the doors to the public at the posted time.

Nightly closing of a public library branch: closing announcements at 15 and 5 minutes, walk-through of floors and restrooms to move remaining patrons out, shutting down and logging off public computers and kiosks, turning off lights, closing/locking interior doors and windows, locking the exterior doors and setting the intruder alarm.

Securing portable computer and AV equipment at close or between uses: collecting laptops, tablets, hotspots, headphones, cameras, projectors and microphones from meeting rooms, study rooms and desks; returning them to charging carts, locked cabinets or an AV closet; plugging them in; locking the cabinet/cart and logging the items.

Academic or school library shift: opening or closing the library building plus its computer lab, media/AV room and group study rooms at extended hours (early morning, late night, weekend), unlocking/locking room doors and gates, powering lab machines up or down, and handing over keys at shift change.

Non-routine open/close conditions: a patron asleep in the stacks or refusing to leave at closing, an alarm that false-trips or will not set, a jammed or frozen lock, a power outage, an unplanned weather closure, or a contractor/cleaner still in the building who must be signed out before the building can be secured.

sources.claim: bibliotheca's open+ extended-access system physically controls a library building's door locks, security gates, lighting, public-address announcements, public access computers, self-service ... intruder alarms from a central scheduler, running the building while no staff are present.

tasks.label: Locate library materials for patrons, including books, periodicals, tape cassettes, Braille volumes, and pictures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Public or school library open stacks: a patron at the desk asks for a specific title; the assistant checks the catalog, walks to the ranges, reads call numbers on tightly packed spine-out books, pulls the volume (sometimes from a low or top shelf), and hands it to the patron.

Paging/holds run: the assistant works a printed or screen pick list of 20-60 requested items (holds, course reserves, interlibrary loan), walking the open stacks, pulling each item, scanning it, and placing it on the hold-pickup shelf for the patron.

Closed stacks / off-site high-density storage: a request comes in for an item held in a staff-only depository or storage vault; the assistant retrieves it from tray/bin storage and routes it to the circulation desk for patron pickup.

Non-book circulating formats kept on standard shelving or behind the desk: bound and current periodicals, audiobook cassettes/CDs, DVDs, large-print items; assistant locates the requested issue or case, checks it is the right volume/date, and gives it to the patron.

Special/archival media in cabinets and files: microfilm reels in drawers, picture and vertical-file folders, Braille and large-format volumes; assistant opens drawers, reads handwritten or typed folder labels, and pulls the specific flat item or oversized volume.

Item not where the catalog says: patron request is vague or the book is missing from its call number; assistant searches adjacent shelves and shelf-ends, sorting carts, the returns bin, displays and study tables, questions the patron, and offers a substitute copy or edition.

sources.title: bookBot and Collections | James B. Hunt Jr. Library | NC State University Libraries
sources.claim: The bookBot automated storage and retrieval system ... NC State's Hunt Library stores ~2 million items in over 18,000 bins and delivers patron-requested items to the service desk; the crane operates autonomously, though a staff member pulls the individual item from the delivered bin.

sources.title: Vulcan Pick: A robotic system for picking targeted objects from fabric pods - Amazon Science
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan Pick system autonomously picks a targeted individual item out of cluttered, densely packed fabric storage pods and has run in a live warehouse for over six months fulfilling customer orders.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: order picking. Retrieving one specified item (books and media are core Amazon SKUs) from densely packed shelving without dislodging neighbours is the same perception-and-manipulation problem as pulling one requested volume from a packed bin or shelf, at comparable precision and object scale.

sources.title: Amazon robotics: Meet the robots inside fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan robot, deployed at fulfillment centers in Spokane, ..., can pick and stow roughly three-quarters of the item types Amazon stores, at speeds comparable to its human employees.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse item pick/stow. Establishes that item-level retrieval from packed storage now runs at human-comparable throughput on most item types, which is the throughput bar for pulling requested library volumes in a machine-organised store.

sources.claim: AuRoSS, an autonomous RFID shelf-scanning robot deployed in Singapore public libraries and at Temasek Polytechnic, wanders the stacks at night and identifies missing or out-of-sequence books with up to 99% scanning accuracy, but it only flags them for a librarian to retrieve.

tasks.label: Manage reserve materials by placing items on reserve for library patrons, checking items in and out of library, and removing out-of-date items.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Academic library course-reserve setup: instructor submits a reserve list; the assistant pulls the library's copies from the open stacks (or accepts instructor personal copies), changes the item status/loan rule in the ILS, applies a reserve band or label, and shelves the item in the closed reserve area behind the circulation desk.

Reserve desk circulation during the term: a student asks for a specific 2-hour reserve title; the assistant locates it on the closed reserve shelf (or finds it already out), scans it out under the short-loan rule with the student's ID, then on return scans it in, glances for damage/missing inserts, and returns it to the exact reserve shelf slot. Heavy queueing before exams.

Bulk check-in of returned materials at the book drop and desk: emptying the return bin, discharging each item from the patron record, clearing holds/fines flags, and sorting items onto carts (reserve cart, stacks cart, transit bin for other branches) for reshelving.

End-of-term/out-of-date removal: pulling every item for finished courses off the reserve shelves, removing the reserve status and reserve labels, routing books back to the general stacks or back to the instructor, and discarding superseded photocopies, old exams, and expired hold/reserve items.

Technology and equipment reserve at an academic library service desk: laptops, chargers, calculators, headphones and cables checked out on short loan, inspected and recharged on return, and pulled from service when out of date or damaged.

Non-standard reserve material: oversized art folios, anatomical models and lab kits, faculty personal copies with loose inserts, unbarcoded/untagged course packs and multi-part media kits, handled at the desk with item-by-item judgment and ad hoc records.

tasks.label: Lend, reserve, and collect books, periodicals, videotapes, and other materials at circulation desks and process materials for inter-library loans.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Public library circulation desk: patron brings an armful of books, DVDs and magazines selected from the open stacks (plus a holds-shelf pickup), assistant verifies the card, checks items out, deactivates security, prints/stamps due dates and hands them over; includes renewals.

Receiving returns: emptying the exterior book drop and taking items handed over at the desk, checking each in against the patron record, checking for holds/transit status, and sorting onto carts or bins by shelving location, branch or reserve status.

Reserves/holds: working the daily holds pull list, walking the open stacks and shelving ranges to pull the requested titles, checking them in as holds, adding a slip with the patron name, and staging them on the hold shelf or on course-reserve shelving in an academic library.

Interlibrary loan: pulling requested items for lending libraries, checking them out to the borrowing institution, wrapping/banding, labeling and bagging them for the courier or mail; and unpacking incoming courier bags/boxes, checking items in, adding paperwork and routing them to the requesting patron's hold shelf.

Nonstandard desk transactions: items returned damaged, with missing DVD discs or loose parts; untagged, oversized or unbarcoded materials; fine and fee disputes and account problems; lending of equipment and Library-of-Things items (laptops, hotspots, kits) requiring inspection and patron instruction.

instances.label: Public library circulation desk: a patron hands over a stack of 3-10 print books; the assistant scans/RFID-reads each item (the ILS shows due-date status and computes any overdue charge), glances at cover, spine and edges and riffles pages for water damage, tears, writing or items left inside, then puts the item on a return cart and tells the patron of any fine or damage charge.

Bulk returns from the exterior book drop / after-hours chute: staff empty the bin in the workroom and process dozens to hundreds of print books in batches, checking each in (backdating if required), inspecting for weather/water damage, broken spines and torn covers, and routing damaged items to mending or to a billing workflow.

Returned AV and multi-part items: DVD/Blu-ray cases, multi-disc audiobook sets, book+CD language kits, video games. The assistant opens each case, verifies every disc, booklet and piece is present and inspects discs for cracks/deep scratches, then checks the item in and applies overdue or missing-piece/replacement charges.

Academic or school library returns: textbooks, hourly-loan course reserves (which still accrue per-hour fines), and interlibrary-loan/consortium volumes. The assistant checks each in, notes due-date/late status, inspects for highlighting, loose pages and damage, records condition before an ILL item is shipped back, and refers damage to billing.

'Library of things' and technology lending returns: laptops, hotspots, tablets, tools, musical instruments, board games, STEM kits. The assistant verifies every component (charger, cables, pieces) against a checklist, tests or powers up the device, notes physical damage, checks the item in and assesses overdue or damage/replacement fees.

instances.label: Public/school library technical services workroom: a shipment of new hardcover trade books arrives; assistant unpacks, checks titles and counts against the packing slip/invoice, stamps ownership marks, applies barcode and printed call-number spine label plus RFID/security tag, fits and tapes a mylar/polyester protective jacket over each dust jacket, updates the item record, and carts the books to the new-book display.

Books needing labels and tags only (academic library monographs, paperbacks, mass-market and pre-bound juvenile titles, school library sets): stamp ownership, apply barcode, print and apply call-number spine label with clear label protector, apply RFID tag or security strip, verify/complete the item record in the ILS, and shelve-ready the batch. No jacket fitting.

Vendor 'shelf-ready' shipment: assistant opens cartons, matches each item to the invoice/packing list by barcode, spot-checks that vendor-applied labels, covers and MARC/item records match local spec, checks for damage or wrong editions, adds local stickers (genre, 'New', branch), receives the invoice in the ILS, and sorts items onto branch delivery carts.

Audio-visual materials in a public library workroom: new DVDs/Blu-rays, audiobook CD sets and video games; remove shrinkwrap, verify disc count and condition, transfer discs to locking/security library cases or add security case, trim and insert cover art, apply barcode, spine and format labels plus security/RFID tag to case and/or disc, create item records.

Small, school or special library: a single assistant at a shared workroom desk processes a mixed batch — donated and gift books of unknown condition, replacement copies, kits, pamphlets, realia and locally produced items — deciding per item what labels, pockets, reinforcement or repair each needs before creating records.

Serials and non-traditional items: check in periodical issues (stamp, apply security strip and property label, route to display), and prepare 'library of things' items such as device kits, hotspots, tablets and software/media packages — assembling parts, testing/charging, bagging, labeling and inventorying components.

tasks.label: Provide assistance to librarians in the maintenance of collections of books, periodicals, magazines, newspapers, and audio-visual and other materials.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Reshelving returned and used materials into the open stacks of a public or academic library: loaded book trucks of mixed formats (hardbacks, paperbacks, DVDs, oversize), items placed in exact call-number sequence between neighbors on shelves of varying height and tightness, done while patrons browse the aisles.

Shelf-reading and inventory: walking assigned ranges to verify call-number order, pulling and reinserting misfiled items, running RFID/barcode inventory passes against holdings lists, reporting missing items, straightening rows and resetting bookends.

Physical processing of newly received materials in the technical-services workroom: checking items against the invoice/order record, applying spine labels, barcodes and RFID tags in house-standard positions, property stamping, applying mylar jackets or plastic covers, inserting security strips, then routing to the shelving area.

Minor mending and repair of damaged collection items: taping torn pages, re-gluing hinges and loose spines, tipping in pages, repairing paperback covers, replacing DVD/CD cases and cleaning or resurfacing scratched discs, judging which items to repair versus refer for withdrawal or rebinding.

Periodicals and newspaper maintenance: checking in arriving issues against the serials record, date-stamping, placing current issues in slanted display racks, pulling superseded issues to back-file storage, discarding or preparing runs for binding.

Weeding, withdrawal and shifting: pulling items from a librarian's withdrawal list, stripping labels and property marks, boxing items for discard or the book sale, and shifting ranges of volumes along the stacks to rebalance shelf space.

A public copier/printer/self-check kiosk faults: staff open panels and drawers, extract crumpled or torn jammed sheets from rollers and the feeder, reseat the toner or duplex unit, clear the error code, run a test page, and post an out-of-order sign or log a vendor call if it will not recover.

Routine restocking of consumables: fetch reams from the supply closet, fan and load paper into copier and printer trays, swap a toner cartridge, replace receipt/label rolls in the self-check and print-release stations, and empty the coin/card box.

Daily upkeep of the public computer stations: power up or shut down machines at opening and closing, restart frozen PCs, reseat or replace mice, keyboards, headphones and cables, check the print-release station and clear stuck jobs, and confirm each station is usable.

Cleaning and checking equipment: wipe scanner platen glass, copier surfaces, monitors and keyboards, dust the microfilm/microfiche reader and AV gear, test lamps and functions, and note items needing repair.

tasks.label: Repair books using mending tape, paste, and brushes or prepare books to be sent to a bindery for repair.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Library workroom/technical services bench: mending torn pages in circulating books with document repair tape — worker opens the volume, aligns the two edges of a ragged tear flat, cuts and applies a thin transparent mending strip on one or both sides, burnishes it down without wrinkles or obscuring text, trims overhang at the fore-edge.

Hinge, spine and cover repairs on hardcovers and paperbacks: applying binder/hinge tape along a split hinge, re-gluing a loose or cracked spine with PVA applied by brush, reattaching a detached cover, clamping/weighting the book while the paste dries, then cleaning squeeze-out.

Reattaching loose or fallen-out leaves and small signatures: brushing a thin line of paste along the gutter edge, tipping the page back into exact register with adjacent leaves, pressing under weight, and checking that the text block still opens.

Surface repair and reinforcement of processed items: replacing torn book pockets, date-due slips and damaged spine/barcode labels, re-taping or replacing loose mylar/plastic jackets, and reinforcing hinges of new paperbacks before they go into circulation.

Bindery prep for bound monographs: pulling volumes flagged as too damaged for in-house repair, verifying title/barcode against the record, changing item status in the ILS/bindery software, inserting a printed routing slip, and packing the volumes into the bindery crate or cart for pickup, done at a workroom staging table.

Bindery prep for serials and problem items: gathering loose periodical issues from the holding shelf, arranging them in chronological order, checking the run for missing issues, removing ads/covers per policy, writing detailed spine-lettering and binding-style instructions on the bindery slip, and bundling the set.

Hand-delivering a small number of specific items to a particular department or staff member elsewhere in the building — a paged volume to the reference desk, reserve items to the circulation desk, interoffice mail, invoices, an AV kit or laptop — with a direct handoff or drop at a designated spot.

Retrieving requested materials from closed stacks, a locked storage room, compact/high-density shelving or a remote storage annex: locating the specific call number on the shelf, pulling it, and bringing it back to the service desk or reading room within the patron's wait window.

Moving bins/totes of interlibrary loan and branch-transfer materials, plus incoming delivery crates and mail sacks, between the workroom and the loading dock or mailroom for courier pickup, and bringing incoming bins back — heavy loads on book trucks, flatbed carts or dollies, through service corridors and freight elevators.

Delivering or retrieving materials outside the building: walking or carting a bag/box of books, deposit collections or documents across a campus quad, parking lot or city block to another building or department, and handing them off there — outdoor pavement, curbs, ramps, weather.

tasks.label: Assist in the preparation of book displays.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Public library: assistant builds a new themed display (e.g., 'Banned Books Week', 'Beach Reads'). Works from a librarian's booklist or subject/call-number list, pulls 15-30 titles from the open stacks onto a book truck, wheels it to a display table or shelf endcap on the public floor, and arranges the books face-out on easels/acrylic stands with a printed topper sign, while patrons move around the area.

Ongoing display maintenance: several standing displays (new fiction, holds pickup, staff picks) are checked daily; the assistant pulls remaining items forward, fills gaps left by checkouts with comparable titles fetched from the stacks or a holding cart, re-faces spines-out books to face-out, removes damaged/mis-themed items, and tidies the surrounding area.

New-arrivals / featured shelf: books just processed or returned are placed face-out on a designated display bookcase, slatwall, or spinner near the entrance; the assistant loads them from a book truck, spaces them evenly, adds shelf-talker labels, and keeps the unit filled and level throughout the shift.

Decorative display work, common in school and children's departments: backing a bulletin board with paper, cutting and stapling die-cut letters and shapes, hanging seasonal decorations and mobiles, staging props (stuffed animals, pumpkins, fairy lights, fabric) around the books, and assembling three-dimensional themed elements.

Locked exhibit/display case: assistant lays out an exhibit of fragile or unique material (local history photos, artifacts, realia, memorabilia, small framed items) on risers and cloth inside a glass case, positions typed caption cards next to each object, and locks the case.

instances.label: Sole-staff open-hours shift at a small rural/village branch: unlock and open the building, turn on lights and public PCs, staff the circulation desk (check items out and in, take fine/print payments, register new patrons and issue cards after checking ID/proof of address), answer walk-up questions and locate items on the shelves, reshelve returns between patrons, then cash out, secure the building and set the alarm; supervising librarian is at another location and reachable by phone/email.

Assistant in charge of a small urban/suburban neighborhood branch while the branch librarian is off-site: steady patron traffic at the desk, holds pickup shelf management, courier deliveries arriving mid-shift, meeting-room and study-room bookings, occasional patron behavior incidents and lost-item disputes, plus routine shelving and end-of-day statistics reported to the off-site supervisor.

Limited-hours, low-service express/deposit location (storefront, community center, grocery, senior center, transit lobby) with a small rotating collection: essentially circulation only — patrons take out and return popular titles, pick up items sent from the main library, minimal reference or program work.

Closed-hours or back-of-house operation of the branch with no public present: unpack the courier totes, check in returned and transiting items, sort them to holds, transit-out, and shelving destinations, print and match hold slips, shelve carts into the stacks in call-number order, shelf-read for misfiles, pull expired holds and pack outgoing totes.

Facility, technology and program duties of running the branch: troubleshooting the public computers, printer, copier and Wi-Fi for patrons, setting up and taking down chairs/tables/craft supplies for a storytime or community meeting, tidying the children's area, putting up displays, reporting a leak or broken lock to facilities, and opening/closing/securing the building around these.

tasks.label: Perform accounting and bookkeeping activities, such as invoicing, maintaining financial records, budgeting, and handling cash.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: At the circulation desk of a public library: a patron pays an overdue/lost-item fee, a print/copy charge, a replacement-card fee or a room-rental fee in cash. The assistant takes bills and coins, makes change from the till, prints or writes a receipt, and posts the payment to the patron's account in the ILS.

End-of-shift/end-of-day till work in the staff workroom: count the cash drawer down to the standard float, reconcile the count against the ILS/POS fee report, note over/short, complete the deposit slip, bag and seal the deposit, and secure it in the safe or hand it to a courier/city finance runner.

Periodic coin and petty-cash duties: unlock and empty coin boxes from public copiers, printers and vending, collect a Friends-of-the-Library book-sale cash box or program petty cash, count and roll/sort the coin, and record the proceeds against the appropriate fund.

Technical-services invoicing: a shipment of books/AV arrives, the assistant opens the cartons, checks items against the packing slip and purchase order, matches the paper or emailed vendor invoice, codes it to a fund line, enters/receives it in the acquisitions or accounting system, and routes it for payment.

Desk/office bookkeeping on the computer: maintaining spreadsheets and ledgers of fines, fees, donations and fund expenditures; tracking encumbrances against materials and program budget lines; running monthly reports and compiling figures for the librarian's budget request. No physical object is handled beyond keyboard, screen and occasional filing.

instances.label: Routine cash transaction at the teller window or drive-up: an account holder presents a deposit slip and a stack of bills, or requests a withdrawal; the clerk verifies the account/ID, counts the currency in or out, authenticates notes, posts the transaction to the core system and hands over a receipt. Check work at the window: depositing one or several checks (verifying endorsement and payee, imaging/encoding, applying hold rules, giving cash back) or cashing an on-us check for a customer after ID verification, counting out the requested denominations.

Issuing instruments and printed items: cashier's/official checks, money orders, counter or temporary checks, deposit slips, instant-issue debit cards — collecting funds, printing the item on secure stock, obtaining signature, and handing it to the customer with a receipt.
Vault-side customer service: escorting a customer into the safe deposit area, dual-key box access, retrieving and returning the box to a private booth, and logging the access.

instances.label: Routine safe-deposit access at a retail bank branch: renter presents ID, signs the access record; clerk pulls the signature card, takes the guard key, escorts the customer into the vault, turns guard key plus renter key to open the box door, removes the metal box and places it in a private booth, then re-inserts and relocks the box and logs the access.

New box rental: after the lease is signed the clerk selects an available box, records the box and key numbers, hands the customer the two stamped keys, explains that the bank keeps no duplicate, and admits the customer to the vault/booth for the first loading of the box.

Non-routine access requiring judgment and legal review: joint renters or deputies, power of attorney, access after the renter's death or under court order, delinquent-rent boxes scheduled for forced drilling — clerk verifies authority documents, arranges the locksmith drilling, and witnesses/records an inventory of contents.

Lost or damaged key: clerk verifies the renter's identity, explains the lock-change charge, orders replacement keys/lock from the vendor, arranges drilling if both keys are gone, issues the new keys, and updates the key records before readmitting the customer.

Assisted access where the physical burden is on the clerk: a large or heavy box (10x10 or drawer type) that must be carried to the booth for an elderly or mobility-limited renter, or a customer who needs the box brought out and returned for them.

Problem access: sticky or jammed lock, bent or worn key, box that will not seat back in its slot, renter who cannot manage the booth procedure and needs hands-on help — clerk troubleshoots at the box and, if needed, calls the vault vendor.

tasks.label: Perform foreign currency transactions and sell traveler's checks.

instances.label: Retail bank branch / exchange counter: a customer preparing for a trip buys a mainstream foreign currency (EUR, GBP, CAD, MXN, JPY) in cash, typically a few hundred to a couple thousand USD. Clerk quotes the rate, checks ID, debits the account or takes USD cash, counts out the foreign banknotes, prints the receipt.

Returning traveler sells back leftover foreign banknotes at the branch counter: mixed denominations, sometimes two or three currencies, notes possibly worn or folded. Clerk sorts and counts them, checks authenticity, refuses coins and unacceptable notes, computes the buy rate and pays out USD.

Advance order of a mainstream currency the branch does not keep in the drawer: clerk takes the order and enters it in the FX system, then days later, at pickup, verifies the customer's ID, counts the notes out with the customer, obtains the signature and hands over the cash.

Advance order and handover of an exotic or rarely traded currency (e.g. Vietnamese dong, Kenyan shilling, Chilean peso): sealed pack arrives from the vault/wholesaler, clerk verifies the shipment against the invoice, counts unfamiliar notes, and hands them over at the counter.

High-value or exception FX work at the counter: cash exchange at or above reporting thresholds or for a business customer (ID scrutiny, CTR/recordkeeping, possible refusal), foreign-currency drafts or foreign checks taken in for collection, and redemption of legacy traveler's cheques requiring a countersignature witnessed in person and endorsement.

Selling the travel-money instrument itself: traveler's checks are no longer issued by any major provider, so in practice the clerk sells and issues the substitute — a prepaid multi-currency travel money/debit card personalized and handed to the customer in the branch, loaded with the destination currency, with serials recorded and the customer's signature obtained.

instances.label: Medical/dental/veterinary front desk: patient checks out and pays a copay or outstanding balance by credit/debit card or mobile wallet; receptionist runs the card on the counter terminal, hands or prints a receipt, and posts the payment to the practice-management system.

Cash payment at a service counter (salon, auto shop, gym, small clinic, community office): receptionist quotes the amount, takes bills and coins across the counter, counts change from the drawer, issues a printed receipt, records the sale in the POS, and reconciles the drawer at shift end.

Hotel / spa / fitness front desk settlement: guest or member checks out, folio or service charges are settled on a card, an itemized invoice/receipt is printed or emailed, keys returned, and the account closed in the property-management system.

Check payments: a client hands a check over the counter, or checks arrive by mail; receptionist verifies amount and payer, stamps/endorses, writes a receipt, posts the payment to the account, and batches the checks for deposit with a deposit slip.

Remote payment taken at the desk: caller reads a card number over the phone, or an emailed/online invoice payment must be applied; receptionist keys it into the virtual terminal, emails or mails a receipt, and records it in the ledger. No object is handled.

Exception and negotiation cases: refunds and voids, split payments across insurance and patient, payment plans and deposits, disputed or mismatched balances, discounts/coupons/gift certificates, patients who cannot pay today — resolved in conversation at the desk and then recorded.

instances.label: Purely electronic record maintenance at the reception workstation: entering and updating client/patient/visitor details, appointment and call logs in the practice-management, EHR or CRM system from information taken by phone or in person; no paper artifact is involved.

Medical, dental or clinic front desk: patient-completed intake and consent forms, ID and insurance cards are collected, copied/scanned and indexed into the EHR, then the paper is filed into the chart or shredded per retention policy; work happens in bursts between arrivals.

General office or corporate reception: incoming paper documents (invoices, correspondence, signed forms, delivery slips, timesheets) are sorted and filed into labeled folders in cabinets in alphabetical/date order, and pulled and refiled when staff request them.

File-room upkeep in a school, law, insurance or government office: pulling and refiling folders, purging inactive files, boxing and labeling records for archive or off-site storage, and keeping the box/index list accurate.

Maintaining paper logs and registers at the desk: visitor sign-in sheets, key and equipment sign-out logs, package/mail receipt logs — handwritten entries during the day, then sheets collected, dated and filed.

Setting up a new client/patient/employee file: assembling a folder with the required blank and completed forms, applying the label/tab with the correct identifier, and inserting it in the proper sequence in the cabinet.

tasks.label: Collect, sort, distribute, or prepare mail, messages, or courier deliveries.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Front-desk receipt of courier/parcel deliveries: driver arrives at a corporate lobby, clinic or leasing office; receptionist accepts the parcels, signs/scans, logs each item against a recipient, stacks them in the package area, and notifies the recipient.

Sorting a batch of incoming mail behind the front desk or in a small mailroom: letters, flats, magazines, junk mail, accountable mail and small parcels split into departmental slots or employee pigeonholes by name.

Distributing mail and packages around the premises: pushing a cart or carrying items to departments and individual desks on several floors, using elevators, handing parcels to recipients or dropping items in in-trays.

Preparing outgoing mail and courier shipments: folding and stuffing letters into envelopes, sealing, metering/stamping, boxing an item, printing and applying a FedEx/UPS airbill, staging the pile for the afternoon pickup.

Taking phone or walk-in visitor messages and relaying them physically: writing a message slip and placing it on the recipient's desk or handing it (or a dropped-off document) to the right staff member.

sources.title: OPEX® Mail Matrix® Automates The Mailroom At Liberty University

sources.title: OPEX Mail Matrix Intelligent Mixed Mail Sorter

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic parcel induction/sortation. It handles the same objects (mixed small parcels), reads the label to identify the destination, and places each item in the correct bin — the physical core of logging and shelving inbound parcels by recipient.

sources.title: Automated Delivery Unit Sorter (ADUS) - U.S. Postal Facts

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Medical/dental or professional-office waiting room: between visitors, the receptionist squares up magazine and brochure stacks on the side tables, pushes chairs back into line, fluffs/repositions cushions, and re-hangs a fallen sign. Small, light, loose items; no fixed positions; must be done quickly during business hours around waiting patients.

Corporate or clinic lobby: clearing away what visitors leave behind — used coffee cups, water bottles, food wrappers, stray papers and newspapers — into the trash/recycling, and wiping crumbs or rings off the coffee table and counter. Items vary in shape and are scattered on tables, seats and the floor.

Reception-area plant care: watering the potted plants on the counter, floor and shelves on a routine schedule, checking soil, pinching off dead leaves, and wiping up spilled water. Plants sit at varied heights around furniture in an occupied office.

Refreshing lobby consumables: refilling the coffee/water station, restocking cups, lids, stirrers and sanitizer, replenishing the brochure rack and business-card holder, and taking empties back to the pantry. Repetitive fetch-and-place of standard stock items along a fixed indoor route.

Busy hotel/large corporate lobby appearance upkeep: quick vacuum or spot-mop of a tracked-in spill, straightening entry mats and stanchions, emptying the small lobby waste bin, general floor tidiness check during a shift with continuous foot traffic.

sources.title: Helix 02 Living Room Tidy
sources.claim: Figure's Helix 02 model drives an F.03 humanoid through an end-to-end, autonomous living-room tidy: picking up scattered toys into a bin, tossing a pillow back onto the couch, spraying and wiping a dirty surface, and side-stepping between coffee table and couch while manipulating.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tidying a living room. Same class of work as straightening a reception area — restoring scattered light objects (pillows, small items, papers) to their places and wiping surfaces, at aesthetic rather than metric precision, while walking around seating furniture.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: tidying/cleaning up an unfamiliar room. Comparable objects (cups, dishes, clothes, clutter on tables and floors) and comparable low precision; a lobby is a more constrained and repeatable version of the same setting.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: operating a beverage station all day. Same objects (cups, dispensers, small stock items) and same station-side handling required to keep a lobby coffee/water station stocked and presentable, sustained over a full shift.

instances.label: Airport/rail/bus terminal information or ticket counter: keeping the floor of the immediate customer area presentable while the facility is open — picking up dropped litter, dust and debris around the counter, kiosks and queue line, and spot-mopping a spilled drink before passengers walk through it.

Ticket/information counter during operating hours: wiping and sanitizing the countertop, boarding-pass scanner, card reader, monitor and phone between customers, moving tags, forms and personal items aside and replacing them, without wetting live equipment.

Clearing customer debris from the information area: collecting cups, wrappers, discarded boarding passes and baggage-tag backings from the counter, shelf and nearby seats, and emptying the small wastebasket behind the desk into a larger receptacle.

Visitor information center or travel desk: straightening and restocking brochure and timetable racks, replenishing forms, maps and pens, pulling outdated flyers, and organizing supplies behind the counter so the display stays presentable through the day.
Cleaning vertical and glass surfaces of the information facility: the booth's glass partition and door glass, fingerprinted signage and kiosk screens, and dusting counter front panels and shelving.

It shows machine cleaning of hard surfaces at building-standard quality, but only for pre-mapped, waterproof, item-free surfaces, which is why it substantiates counter wiping only when the surface is presented clear and fixtured (E1).

sources.title: Report: AMP Robotics' Business Breakdown & Founding Story

The objects are the same class of loose litter and the grasping precision is comparable, but the items must arrive presented on a purpose-built conveyor line, so it substantiates only the fixtured (E1) counterfactual.

sources.title: Restocking robots deployed in 300 Japanese convenience stores
sources.claim: Telexistence's TX SCARA restocking robot operates autonomously under its GORDON AI to replenish beverage display shelves in hundreds of FamilyMart convenience stores, with remote human recovery only when it fails.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: replenishing and straightening a customer-facing display rack. Comparable pick-and-place precision and a face-out display standard, but the robot is rail-mounted inside a purpose-built refrigerated case with stock presented in crates, so it substantiates the E1 counterfactual only.

sources.title: Skyline Robotics deploys Ozmo window cleaning robot in New York City

sources.transferJustification: Related task: cleaning glass and flat vertical surfaces to a commercial standard with a force-controlled arm. Transfer holds where the pane is presented to the machine on a rig; Ozmo is a facade-mounted system and cannot move through a terminal interior, so it supports E1 only.

sources.title: π0.5: a VLA with Open-World Generalization
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 model drove a mobile manipulator to tidy and wipe in kitchens and bedrooms it had never seen, but the developers state it is far from perfect ... frequently errs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wiping spills and putting stray items away. It is the closest published capability to counter tidying in a human setting, but the developers' own reliability caveat and lab/demo maturity keep it below worker quality for a staffed public counter.

tasks.label: Open or close information facilities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Airline or rail ticket-and-information counter in an airport terminal or major station: at shift start the agent unlocks the counter and back office, boots ticketing/bag-tag terminals and printers, loads ticket stock and forms, switches on counter and queue signage, sets out stanchions and brochures; at close logs out, secures ticket stock and cash drawer, locks cabinets and gates, kills lights.

State highway welcome center or downtown visitor information center: unlock exterior doors and disarm the alarm, turn on lights, A/V displays and coffee, open restrooms, restock hundreds of brochure and map slots, raise flags and set out an A-frame sidewalk sign, tidy the lobby; at close reverse each step, empty donation/cash box, lock all doors and arm the alarm.

Freestanding tourist information kiosk or booth in a plaza, sidewalk, cruise pier apron, or event site: unlock and raise the shutters or fold-down panels, wheel out the sandwich-board sign and brochure stand, open the umbrella, plug in power, hang the day's schedule; at close pack everything in, shutter and padlock the kiosk.

Hotel, resort, or cruise-line tour and shore-excursion desk in a lobby: unlock the desk and display cabinet, power up laptop/printer/card reader, set out tour brochures, price sheets and sign-up boards, unlock the ticket drawer; at close secure tickets, vouchers and cash, log off and lock the desk.

Intercity bus or ferry terminal ticket and information office: raise the security grille, unlock the waiting room and ticket windows, load ticket/receipt stock into printers, draw and count the starting cash bank from the safe, switch on departure boards; at close cash out, make the safe drop, lower the grille, lock up and set the alarm.

sources.title: Boston Dynamics releases Spot and Orbit 5.1 with new Spot Cam - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot runs scheduled autonomous inspection and off-hours security-patrol missions inside industrial facilities and can autonomously traverse access-controlled doors, with beta customers' robots having opened 2,500 doors.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous facility patrol/lock-up rounds in a structured work facility. It shows door traversal and scheduled premises rounds transfer, but not the unlock/power-up/stock/secure manipulation sequence that makes up opening or closing an information facility.

sources.title: Restocking robots deployed in 300 Japanese convenience stores - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Telexistence's TX SCARA autonomously restocks customer-facing refrigerated display shelves from crates in a purpose-built rail-mounted cell installed in hundreds of FamilyMart stores, with remote teleoperated recovery only when it fails.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: readying a customer-facing display for service by loading standardized items into fixed rack positions. In a fixtured, purpose-built presentation (E1), loading brochure/map racks, form trays and ticket stock is the same class of repeatable pick-and-place from presented stock into known slots.

sources.title: AVMC is Revolutionizing Healthcare Operations with Innovative Collaboration
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi operates autonomously in hospitals, mapping the building, using an arm to open multiple door types including badge-access doors, riding elevators and delivering/restocking supplies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous mobile-manipulation service rounds in a structured human facility. It shows door and elevator handling plus item transport carry over, but Moxi does not unlock/lock premises, operate equipment power, arrange displays, or handle cash, so it does not substantiate the whole open/close routine at E2.

sources.title: Tidel R1800 Cash Recycler - Safe and Vault Store.com
sources.claim: Cash recyclers are deployed machines that mechanically count, validate and secure banknotes, automating the start-of-shift and end-of-shift cash processes in cash-intensive businesses.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: the cash-bank draw at opening and the count/drop at closing. A purpose-built cash-handling machine performs the physical counting and securing of notes that is part of opening and closing a ticket/information office.

sources.system: Costa Coffee automated robotic coffee station

sources.claim: Costa Coffee's fully automated robotic coffee station operates unattended and self-cleaning for up to seven days ... human intervention at US airports and college ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bringing a small public-facing service point into and out of service each day. It substantiates that when a service point is purpose-built around the machine, opening/closing routines (power-up, self-check, shutdown, securing) run without a human, but only for a machine-designed kiosk, not a human-run information office.

sources.title: A VLA with Open-World Generalization | Physical Intelligence
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 policy autonomously controls a mobile manipulator to tidy kitchens and bedrooms in homes never seen in training, but the authors note it frequently makes semantic and motor errors.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: generalist pick-and-place tidying in unstructured settings. It marks the frontier of open-world manipulation and shows why unstructured or human-standard open/close routines (keys, alarms, equipment power, cash) are not yet completed at worker reliability.

tasks.label: Provide boarding or disembarking assistance to passengers needing special assistance.

instances.label: Airport departure, passenger who cannot walk the jetbridge or reach the seat unaided (WCHS/WCHC): agent collects them at check-in or gate, pushes the wheelchair through the concourse, down the jet bridge, transfers them onto a narrow aisle chair, wheels them to the row, lifts/pivots them into the aircraft seat, positions belt extender and stows their carry-on, then removes the chair before doors close.

Airport arrival/disembarking: agent waits at the aircraft door with wheelchair and aisle chair after all other passengers deplane, transfers the passenger out of the seat into the aisle chair and then into the wheelchair, pushes them up the jetbridge through the concourse, waits at baggage claim, lifts their checked bags off the belt, and delivers them to the curb, connecting gate, or a family member.

Ambulatory-but-limited passenger (most common wheelchair-service request): agent seats them in a wheelchair after security and pushes them through the concourse, elevators and moving walkways to the departure gate, checks in with the gate agent, and parks them in gate seating; the passenger transfers themselves and walks onto the aircraft at pre-board.

Non-wheelchair special assistance: sighted-guide arm escort of a blind passenger through the terminal and down the jetbridge to their seat with an orientation to the row and call button; steadying a frail elderly passenger on foot; escorting an unaccompanied minor or a passenger with a cognitive disability to the gate and handing them over to cabin crew with paperwork.

Rail, intercity bus or ferry: clerk meets a wheelchair passenger on the platform or at the bus/ferry berth, positions and deploys a portable or powered ramp/lift over the gap, helps push and align the chair aboard, secures it in the designated space or ties it down, and radios the destination station to arrange the reverse operation.

Remote stand or adverse-condition boarding: passenger taken airside by van to an aircraft parked on the ramp and boarded by ambulift or carried up air stairs in wind, rain or cold; or ferry/cruise gangway boarding on a tidal slope with luggage.

instances.label: Courier/forwarder terminal or will-call counter: a customer, driver or agent needs a specific held parcel, carton or document envelope. Air cargo / bonded terminal: pull stored cargo - a built ULD or loose skids in a high-bay or racked store - for re-flight, a customs exam, or release to a trucker, respecting seals, bonded status and flight cut-off times.

Trace of a shipment reported missing that is in fact still in the facility: check the last scan/WMS record, then physically search the storage area - walk or scan the racks, staging lanes and OS&D shelf, read labels and barcodes - find the mis-slotted or mislabeled freight and correct the record.

Trace of a shipment that has left the facility or was never received: pull scan history, call and email origin/destination terminals, drivers and the interline carrier, have other sites search their docks and trailers, chase paperwork, and either recover the freight or document it as lost for a claim.

Terminal yard / intermodal or dock area: locate a stored trailer or container holding the shipment among yard slots, hook it, connect air lines, pull it out of the parking row and spot it at a dock door or hand-off point, updating yard inventory.

Open-deck / oversize freight in a carrier yard or at a shipper's site: chains, binders, ratchet straps, edge protectors, corner blocking and tarping of machinery, steel, lumber or crated oversize cargo, outdoors in weather on varied ground.

Fragile, high-value or odd-shaped pieces: agent pads and cushions items before shipment — blankets, foam, bubble/paper cushioning, void fill in cartons and crates, corner protectors — at a packing bench or in the terminal's crating area.

Air cargo terminal acceptance / import breakdown: loose and palletized pieces are weighed and measured, piece counts checked against the air waybill and manifest, packaging inspected for ready-for-carriage condition (leaks, torn cartons, labeling, DG marks), and non-conforming or damaged shipments rejected.

Freight forwarder / 3PL warehouse receiving of palletized, shrink-wrapped freight: handling-unit count and label/PRO check against the packing list, gross-weight verification, exterior damage inspection at the unit level (pallet not opened), discrepancies recorded and damaged units set aside.

Port or rail intermodal interchange: container/chassis and seal numbers verified against the interchange/booking documents, exterior of the box inspected for dents, holes and door damage, equipment interchange receipt issued, and damaged or wrong-seal containers refused.

instances.label: Warehouse / freight-forwarder shipping dock: received palletized goods staged on the receiving dock are moved by counterbalance forklift or powered pallet jack to WMS-assigned rack or floor storage locations, or to a specific department's staging lane. Standard GMA pallets, shrink-wrapped, weights up to ~2,500 lb, flat concrete floor shared with other lift trucks and walkers.

LTL / trucking terminal cross-dock: palletized or skidded freight pulled from an inbound trailer is routed across the dock to the correct outbound door, bay stripe, or hold area according to destination and next departure, using forklift or pallet jack, under time pressure during a dock shift.

Air cargo terminal: accepted/received palletized freight or built-up ULDs are routed from the acceptance/breakdown area to a flight build-up position for the first available flight, or to racked pallet/ULD storage, using forklift, ULD transporter, slave pallets and transfer decks.

Loose, non-palletized or irregular pieces: loose cartons, wooden crates, drums, tires, oversize or odd-shaped pieces, and re-stacked/broken-down freight moved by hand truck, four-wheel cart, or forklift-with-slip-sheet to a shelf, bin, floor storage area, or a specific department, often requiring restacking and manual judgment about placement.

Special-handling shipments: perishables to the cooler, pharma to cold chain, dangerous goods to the segregated DG store, valuables to the security cage, live animals or AOG parts to a designated area — each routed to a controlled storage area after a condition/paperwork check, hand-carted or forklifted with extra care.

tasks.label: Assemble containers and crates used to transport items, such as machines or vehicles.

instances.label: Freight forwarder / crating area of a terminal warehouse: agent measures a machine (e.g., a CNC unit, generator), cuts lumber and plywood, nails together a skid base, side panels and a lid to build a one-off export crate, then bands and stencils it. Terminal or depot: erecting/assembling standard reusable transport containers — collapsible plastic/wire-bound crates, folding bulk bins, sleeve-and-lid pallet boxes — from folded or flat stock, in quantity, to standard dimensions.

Inside a loaded sea container or trailer in the yard: agent cuts dunnage lumber and nails chocks, cleats and bracing to the container floor/walls to block and brace a vehicle or heavy machine, adding straps and airbags, working in a confined, dark, uneven space.

On-site crating at a customer's plant or job site: crew travels out and builds a crate in place around a machine standing on the customer's floor, working around obstructions, power drops and other equipment, with layout and access differing at every site.

tasks.label: Maintain a supply of packing materials.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume parcel/LTL terminal or dock pack line: agent sees carton, stretch-film and dunnage stock at the pack/build stations running low, retrieves full pallets of corrugate/film/void-fill from the terminal's racked stock area with a pallet jack or forklift, stages them beside the stations and pulls empty pallets back. Marked lanes, forklift and foot traffic, standard pallets.

Piece/case-level restocking of consumables at pack stations and supply shelves: cutting down a pallet and filling bins with assorted box sizes, loading tape rolls into dispensers, hanging bubble/void-fill rolls, refilling label stock, poly mailers, strapping seals and markers. Objects vary in size, weight and floppiness; bin positions are only approximate.

Inbound supply delivery: a trailer of pallets of cartons, stretch film and pallets/skids arrives at the dock; agent unloads with a forklift, checks quantities against the packing slip/BOL, and puts the pallets away in the stock racks or floor lanes of the terminal.

Periodic stock check and reorder: agent walks the racked supply area and dock counting on-hand pallets and cases of cartons, film, strapping and labels, compares against minimum levels, and issues a purchase order or internal requisition to the vendor.

Air cargo terminal build-up area: keeping build-up stations supplied with empty ULD pallets/containers, cargo nets, straps, corner boards, shrink wrap and plastic sheeting; retrieving empties from ULD storage and staging them beside workstations amid tug and loader traffic.

Small trucking terminal or freight-forwarder office: cramped supply closet/mezzanine with no fixed locations; a parcel delivery of assorted supplies is hand-carried in, unboxed and stacked wherever room exists, and the counter is restocked with airbill sleeves, tape, labels and small cartons.

tasks.label: Direct or participate in cargo loading to ensure completeness of load and even distribution of weight.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Parcel/express sort hub (courier terminal): agent oversees and pitches in on loading loose parcels of random size, weight and shape from sortation belts into line-haul trailers or containers - building tight stable walls, keeping heavy pieces low, verifying by scan that every piece for the destination is aboard before the door is sealed.

Motor-freight (LTL) terminal or freight-forwarder cross-dock: agent directs forklift/jack loaders stuffing a trailer or ocean container with a heterogeneous mix - banded pallets, loose crates, drums, tires, odd-length pieces - tiering and floor-stacking, placing load bars, checking piece counts against the bill of lading and keeping weight balanced front-to-rear and side-to-side within axle limits.

Air cargo terminal: agent builds up or supervises build-up of ULD pallets/containers from mixed shipments per the load plan - respecting contour, ULD max weight and floor-loading limits, netting/strapping the pallet, reconciling pieces and weight against the air waybill, then releasing the ULD to the ramp for aircraft loading and weight-and-balance sign-off.

Distribution-center or manufacturer outbound shipping dock: agent directs loading of uniform palletized product into standard dry vans per a WMS load plan - pallet positions, single vs. double stack, heavy pallets over the axles - and verifies pallet/case counts against the BOL before sealing.

Non-standard/outdoor loading: flatbed, oversize or project cargo, breakbulk and machinery loaded at open yards, rail ramps or a customer's site - placing pieces with a lift truck or crane for even weight distribution, then blocking, bracing, chaining/strapping and tarping in weather, with no fixed layout.

tasks.label: Pack goods for shipping, using tools such as staplers, strapping machines, and hammers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Boxing outbound goods at a packing/shipping station in a freight terminal or 3PL warehouse: selecting a carton, placing conveyable customer goods inside, adding paper/air void fill, closing with tape or staples, weighing and labeling. Standard, repeatable cartons and mostly regular-shaped goods.

Unitizing freight at the dock: stacking cases (often mixed sizes/SKUs) onto a pallet or skid, then securing the load with stretch wrap and/or plastic or steel banding from a strapping machine, adding edge/corner protectors, and staging the completed unit load for pickup.

Heavy/export packing: assembling or closing wooden crates, boxes and skids around machinery, oversized or odd-shaped freight using hammer, nails, screws and steel banding; blocking, bracing and bolting the item down inside the crate; ISPM-15 marking. Each item is different.

Custom protective packing of small fragile goods that still move through a repeatable, conveyable carton format (e.g., electronics, bottles) needing cushioning pads or void fill top and bottom before sealing.

Custom protective packing of fragile, high-value or awkward items that do not fit a standard format: cutting foam and bubble to shape, double-boxing, suspending art/instruments/lab equipment, building internal supports by hand at the counter or bench.

Repacking and re-securing problem freight found on the dock: re-taping or re-stapling burst cartons, restacking a collapsed or leaning pallet, re-banding shifted loads, overpacking leaking or non-compliant (incl. hazmat) shipments before they can move.

tasks.label: Attach address labels, identification codes, and shipping instructions to containers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Freight forwarder / parcel-freight terminal shipping station: printing shipping and barcode ID labels from the TMS and sticking them onto individual cartons and parcels of varied size at a bench or alongside a conveyor; high volume, flat corrugated surfaces, label must be scannable and correctly oriented.

Dock/warehouse floor of an LTL or 3PL terminal: applying handling-unit / PRO-number / master shipment labels and placards to shrink-wrapped pallets and skids staged on the dock, often on two adjacent sides, before loading.

Container/trailer-level identification in the yard: attaching or updating hazmat placards, container ID and routing markings, seal numbers and document holders on intermodal containers and trailers parked at the terminal, outdoors in weather.

tasks.label: Open cargo containers and unwrap contents, using steel cutters, crowbars, or other hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cross-dock or air-cargo terminal floor: agent cuts the plastic or steel banding and slits/strips the stretch film from an inbound palletized shipment (skid or ULD pallet) so the freight can be inspected, counted, relabeled or re-worked; pallets sit where the forklift dropped them, film is irregularly wrapped, people and lift trucks moving nearby.

Warehouse/receiving office: agent uses a box cutter or steel snips to open corrugated cartons and cases (top or side), pulls back inner poly bags/void fill to verify contents, check for damage or concealed shortage, retrieve packing lists, then repacks or re-tapes.

Loading dock or container yard: agent cuts a bolt/cable seal with steel cutters, releases the locking bars and swings open the doors of an ocean container or trailer (sometimes rusted, door-bulged or shifted-load), records the seal number, and pulls back any load-securing wrap/liner at the doorway.

Freight terminal or customs exam area: agent pries open nailed wooden crates or plywood boxes with a crowbar/pry bar (project cargo, machinery, artwork, exam holds) without damaging the contents, opens inner packaging, then re-closes/re-secures the crate.

Unstructured location: opening and unwrapping at a customer's site, a curbside truck, or an open yard — cutting tarps, banding and dunnage on flatbed or irregular loads, in weather, on uneven ground, with no fixed layout or institutional control.

instances.label: Scheduled multi-stop lab-specimen route by car: courier drives a fixed circuit of physician offices, draw stations, urgent cares and nursing homes, parks, walks in, retrieves specimen bags/coolers from a designated fridge or front desk, signs the log, keeps samples at temperature, and delivers the batch to a central/reference lab receiving window.

STAT / on-demand urgent run: dispatched to move blood products, urgent chemistry or micro specimens, or tissue between a hospital blood bank, a satellite ER and a reference lab under a time deadline, in traffic, day or night, with chain-of-custody paperwork and hand-to-hand transfer to lab or nursing staff.

Intra-hospital / intra-campus messenger runs: moving specimens from nursing units and urgent care to the lab, medications from the inpatient pharmacy to floors, and charts between departments, on foot or with a cart, through corridors, elevators and badge-access doors of a single hospital or connected campus.

Medical / clinical-lab courier loads a car or small cargo van at a hospital or reference-lab dock: insulated coolers, specimen racks and UN3373 biohazard bags, dry-ice shippers and blood-product boxes, checked against a pickup manifest, kept upright and secured, cold chain preserved.

In-house / company messenger loads a company car or van at a corporate mailroom or campus dock with interoffice mail bins, sealed pouches, banker boxes and tubes for a fixed inter-building run, checking each item off a route list.

On-demand courier for a pharmacy, retailer, auto-parts store or office-supply shop loads a personal car or small van at the shop's back door or at the curb: bags, totes, loose and oddly shaped items, often double-parked on the street, in whatever weather and layout the site presents.

Dangerous-goods loading: courier loads regulated items - medical/industrial gas cylinders, lithium-battery shipments, dry ice, small quantities of chemicals or radiopharmaceuticals - verifying labels and shipping papers, segregating incompatible classes, blocking/bracing so nothing shifts, placarding the vehicle where required.

instances.label: Mid-route refueling of a gasoline/diesel courier car or van at a public self-serve filling station: pull into a pump lane, pay/authorize with fleet card, open the fuel door and cap, insert the nozzle, fill to full, replace cap, record gallons/odometer on the fuel log. Done several times a week in all weather, at varying stations along the route.

Refueling at the employer's depot fuel island / fleet card pump inside a controlled yard at start or end of shift: park at the island, authorize, fuel the van, note mileage and fuel used on the vehicle sheet.

Plugging in and charging an electric courier van or car: park in the depot charging bay (or a public DC charger stop), open the charge port, insert the connector, confirm the session started, and unplug/stow the cable when charged.

Under-hood fluid check and top-up in the depot lot or wherever the vehicle is parked: open hood, pull and read the engine-oil dipstick, check coolant overflow, brake fluid and washer reservoir levels, add oil or washer fluid from a jug as needed, close hood, note any low or leaking fluid for the shop.

Pre-trip walkaround on the van: check tires for damage and gauge pressure at each wheel, add air from the depot hose or station air pump, check headlights/brake lights/turn signals, wipers, mirrors, look under the vehicle for drips, and report defects.

Bicycle, e-bike, scooter or motorcycle courier maintenance done at home, at the messenger office, or curbside: pump tires, lubricate and check the chain, check brake pads and cable tension, tighten fasteners, top up motorcycle oil and chain lube.

instances.label: Walking route through a residential neighborhood: reader goes yard to yard reading wall-mounted electric and gas meters at single-family homes, opening gates, working around parked cars, shrubs, snow, mud and loose dogs, keying the register digits into a handheld unit at each stop.

Residential water meters set in below-grade curb boxes or pits: reader locates the buried box, pries/unlocks the cast-iron or plastic lid with a pentagon key or hook, clears dirt, grass, insects or standing water, reads the odometer/dial register in the hole, replaces the lid and enters the read.

Inside reads at homes and small buildings where the meter is in a basement, garage, utility closet or behind a locked door: reader gains access, descends stairs, works in dim cluttered space, reads the register and records it, often on a scheduled appointment or re-read.

Meter rooms and meter banks at apartment complexes, commercial buildings, campuses and industrial plants: institution-controlled premises with a fixed layout; reader works down a bank of many electric/gas/steam meters, matching each register to an account number and logging readings on a handheld.

Vehicle-based drive-by AMR route: reader drives an assigned pattern of streets at prescribed speed with a mobile radio collector on board that interrogates ERT/radio meter transmitters; reads are logged automatically and the route file is uploaded at end of shift.

tasks.label: Walk or drive vehicles along established routes to take readings of meter dials.

instances.label: Suburban residential walking route: reader walks block to block reading curbside water meter pits (lift or flip the lid, clear mud/debris, read the register dials) and side-of-house gas/electric dials; fenced yards, dogs, parked cars, snow, overgrown grass, addresses that differ house to house.

Drive-and-walk route in low-density or rural service territory: reader drives a company vehicle between scattered properties and farms, parks, walks up gravel drives to meter sets, reads dials, keys readings into the handheld, then drives to the next stop over many miles.

Multifamily property: reader enters an apartment or condo building with a key/access code and reads a bank of 8-40 water, gas, or electric meters in a basement, meter closet, or exterior meter alley; tight aisles, stairs, poor lighting, registers at varying heights.

Commercial/industrial customer premises: reader checks in at a business, warehouse, plant, or institution, follows site safety rules, and reads large-format meters or compound meters in a mechanical room, yard, or vault, recording index and demand readings.

Interior meter at a private residence: older home with the water or gas meter in the basement or crawl space; reader knocks, is admitted by the occupant (or uses a scheduled appointment), walks through the home, and reads the dial with a flashlight.

Dense urban walking route: reader covers downtown blocks on foot among pedestrians and traffic, reading storefront meters, sidewalk vault meters, and alley-mounted meter banks, some requiring a lid pull or gate access.

tasks.label: Verify readings in cases where consumption appears to be abnormal, and record possible reasons for fluctuations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High/low-bill exception flagged for a single-family home: reader returns to the outdoor wall- or side-mounted electric or gas meter in the yard, confirms meter ID matches the account, re-reads the register, checks for an obviously stuck/damaged dial, broken seal, obstruction or vacancy, and enters a reason code plus note in the handheld. Conditions: fenced yards, gates, dogs, vegetation, weather, varying meter locations.

Water utility exception: curbside/parkway meter pit. Reader pries off a cast-iron or plastic pit lid, clears dirt, water or insects, reads the register and the low-flow leak indicator, checks whether the dial spins with fixtures off (customer-side leak) and whether the register is fogged/stopped, then records the probable cause. Conditions: buried, silted, sometimes flooded pits at the curb or in the parking strip.

Apartment complex or strip-mall meter bank in a locked meter room, basement or exterior alcove: reader verifies which socket/meter belongs to the flagged account (crossed-meter or meter-exchange errors are a common cause), re-reads the correct register, checks meter number against the account, and records the finding. Institution-controlled premises with a fixed layout and standard meter banks.

Large commercial/industrial customer (plant, hospital, campus, large gas set): reader verifies the index/demand register, confirms the CT/PT multiplier or gas corrector factor applied to the reading, looks for a stopped register or damaged meter, checks with on-site facility staff about process changes, and records the reason for the consumption swing.

Meter located inside the premises or behind locked access at a residence (basement, utility closet, under-house gas set): reader arranges access with the occupant, enters, reads the register, looks for causes such as a running toilet, space heater, new appliance or seasonal use, and records the explanation on the exception record.
