roles.title: Postal Service Mail Sorters, Processors, and Processing Machine Operators
aliases: Computer Forwarding System Markup Clerk (CFS Markup Clerk)
Small Package and Bundle Sorter Clerk (SPBS Clerk)
roles.description: Prepare incoming and outgoing mail for distribution for the United States Postal Service (USPS). Examine, sort, and route mail. Load, operate, and occasionally adjust and repair mail processing, sorting, and canceling machinery. Keep records of shipments, pouches, and sacks, and perform other duties related to mail handling within the postal service. Includes postal service mail sorters and processors employed by USPS contractors.

tasks.label: Clear jams in sorting equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Letter-sorting machine (e.g., DBCS/AFCS) jams during a run in a USPS processing & distribution center: machine faults and stops, operator reads the fault location, opens transport covers/doors, pulls crumpled and torn letters out of rollers, belts and stacker pockets, verifies no fragments remain in the path, re-sleeves or re-feeds recovered mail, closes covers and restarts the run — under throughput pressure on a dispatch clock.

Flat sorter (AFSM 100 / FSS) jam: bulky catalogs, magazines or polywrapped flats jam in the feeder magazine, transport or bin; operator reaches into the feeder/transport, extracts torn or accordioned flats and loose contents, checks belts and guides, restores damaged pieces to processable condition and restarts.

Package sorting machine (APBS/SPSS/PILS-type) jam: a parcel wedges at induction, a diverter, or a chute mouth; operator stops the belt, frees or lifts out the package (sometimes heavy, irregular, or with a broken/spilled contents), clears the backed-up parcels behind it, re-inducts them and restarts the sorter.

Conveyor / tray-and-tub or sack handling system jam: trays, tubs, gaylords or sacks jam on a takeaway conveyor, stacker, or tray-management line; operator reaches or climbs to free the jammed load, straightens or re-stacks it, clears the queue and restarts the conveyor.

Severe or complex jam: mail wound around rollers or wedged deep inside the transport, requiring lockout/tagout, hand tools, opening or partially removing guards/panels, retrieving shredded pieces, coordination with maintenance, and rewrapping/reporting damaged mail before the machine can be returned to service.

sources.title: DHL Supply Chain Achieves First Commercial Deployment of Boston Dynamics' Stretch Robot to Unload Trailers and Containers in the Warehouse
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Stretch is a commercially deployed autonomous mobile manipulator that unloads boxes from trailers and containers and can recover fallen boxes — the nearest deployed capability to freeing a stuck/misplaced package, but it works on free-standing box stacks on the floor of a trailer, not inside sorting machinery.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: trailer unloading with fallen-box recovery. It does not transfer to jam clearing: Stretch grasps intact boxes on an open floor with suction, whereas jam clearing requires opening machine covers, extracting crumpled/torn mail from between rollers and guides in confined machine interiors, and verifying the transport path is clear before restart.

sources.title: Amazon introduces 'Blue Jay' warehouse robot that performs multiple tasks at once
sources.claim: Amazon's newest deployed sortation robots are arm-based pick-and-place systems that sort and consolidate packages from conveyors and totes; no capability to diagnose and clear jams inside sorting machinery is described.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: package sortation by robot arm in a purpose-built cell. It does not transfer: the arms pick presented, free-standing items from conveyors/totes; nothing in the reporting shows fault diagnosis, cover opening, or extraction of jammed items from a machine transport path.

sources.title: Continuous Improvement of Mail Processing Operations — USPS Office of Inspector General
sources.claim: Jams in USPS mail processing equipment remain a routine operational problem tracked as a human-managed performance metric at processing plants, indicating jam clearance is still a manual operator activity.
sources.transferJustification: Context, not a positive capability claim: it establishes that jam clearance in USPS plants is handled within human-operated mail processing operations, with no robotic jam-clearing system reported.

sources.system: Anti-jamming means for a pocket of a mail sort machine (patent)
sources.title: Anti-jamming means for a pocket of a mail sort machine (US 4718660)
sources.claim: Automatic jam handling in high-speed sortation and document machines is addressed by built-in anti-jam and self-clearing mechanisms described in patents, not by any named deployed robotic system that clears jams the way an operator does.
sources.transferJustification: Related mechanism: in-machine jam prevention. It does not substantiate the task: it prevents a jam from forming rather than locating and extracting mail already jammed in the transport, and it is a patent disclosure rather than a demonstrated or deployed system.

tasks.label: Operate various types of equipment, such as computer scanning equipment, addressographs, mimeographs, optical character readers, and bar-code sorters.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Letter mail on automation at a USPS processing & distribution center: the clerk stages APCs/hampers of letter trays at a DBCS/DIOSS/AFCS, pulls and unsleeves trays, dumps and jogs the letters, and keeps the feeder ledge continuously supplied through a run at tens of thousands of pieces per hour, pulling out non-machinable pieces.

Flat mail on a flat sorter (AFSM 100 type) in a plant: opening bundles of flats, prepping them into trays, and keeping the machine's feed stations supplied so the OCR/barcode reader can sort at rated throughput.

Sweeping the output of letter/flat sorters: removing accumulated stacks from stackers/output bins, placing them into letter trays or flat tubs, labeling and sleeving trays, and loading full trays onto pallets/APCs for dispatch.

Operating package sorting machines (single-induction package sorters, APBS, regional/matrix sorters, delivery-unit sorters): dumping containers onto bulk flow, singulating and inducting parcels label-up onto the induction belt, and pulling sorted parcels off chutes into sacks, gaylords or rolling containers.

Using barcode scanning equipment to record processing and dispatch events: scanning individual parcels, trays, placards and containers with handheld/mounted scanners at the machine and on the dock, and keying item/route data into terminals.

Running and tending a machine through a sort: loading/changing the sort program at the console, monitoring throughput, reject and read rates, clearing jams and misfeeds in the transport and stackers, making minor adjustments (feeder settings, belts, cleaning sensors) and restarting the run.

tasks.label: Sort odd-sized mail by hand, sort mail that other workers have been unable to sort, and segregate items requiring special handling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Manual distribution in a P&DC/RPDC: clerk works nonmachinable, odd-sized letters, flats and bundles (rigid mailers, tubes, square/oversized envelopes, poorly wrapped pieces) out of a hamper into a manual case or bin bank by ZIP separation, then ties out and labels the separations. Most pieces carry printed labels or legible addresses; volume is high and continuous.

Parcel operation in a plant or annex: clerk hand-sorts irregular/nonmachinable parcels rejected by or bypassing the package sorters — padded mailers, tubes, sacks, oddly shaped or poorly wrapped boxes, most under about 50 lb — into hampers, gaylords or containers by destination, scanning as required.

Exception/reject mail: pieces that the machines and other workers could not sort — torn or damaged pieces, spilled or re-wrapped contents, illegible handwriting, obliterated or unreadable labels/barcodes, incomplete or wrong addresses requiring lookup, forwarding/nixie research — resolved piece by piece, sometimes re-labeled or repaired, then dispatched.

Segregating service-class and accountable items out of the flow: Registered, Certified, insured, signature-service and Priority Mail Express pieces identified by label/barcode are pulled, scanned and placed in designated containers or the registry cage for separate dispatch.

Segregating problem items: leaking, crushed or damaged parcels, live animals and perishables, suspicious pieces, and undeclared or improperly packaged hazardous materials are spotted in a mixed flow, removed by hand, contained, and routed to the appropriate special-handling procedure.

Delivery unit / small post office back room: clerk hand-sorts odd-sized mail, machine rejects and parcels into carrier route separations and hampers, pulls accountable pieces for the carriers, in a cramped room whose layout varies from site to site.

tasks.label: Direct items according to established routing schemes, using computer-controlled keyboards or voice-recognition equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Keying/induction station on a bundle-and-small-parcel sorter (SPBS/APBS) at a USPS processing & distribution center: the clerk pulls each bundle or small parcel from a rolling container or belt, reads the address, keys the 2-3 digit destination code on the machine keyboard, and places the item in the carrier/tray so the sorter drops it at the right bin. Mixed sizes, polybags, mailers, small boxes; machine-paced, plant floor with staff working alongside.

Package sortation to routes or dispatch at a delivery unit, annex, or USPS-contractor facility using a scanner/keypad or voice-directed prompt: the worker reads or scans the label, is told (or keys) the route/destination, and places the piece in the correct route hamper, cage, or sack. Mixed parcel sizes, seasonal surges, tight floor space.

Letter/flat processing machine operation at a plant: operator feeds flats or letters into a flat sorter or barcode sorter, keys sort codes or ZIP information for pieces the reader cannot handle, and directs them into bin separations at machine pace (thousands of pieces per hour), clearing jams and re-feeding.

Video/image encoding keying (remote encoding center style console): operator views digital images of letters and packages whose addresses the processing machines could not read - handwritten, exotic, change-of-address - and keys the address data that determines the piece's routing. No contact with the physical mail; strict keystroke-rate and accuracy standards.

Exception and reject handling at a plant keying console: pieces rejected by the automated readers or mis-sorted - torn or smudged labels, hand-addressed or incomplete addresses, foreign-format addresses, non-machinable irregular parcels and sacks. The clerk interprets the address, keys the routing, and dispatches the item to the correct container.

tasks.label: Check items to ensure that addresses are legible and correct, that sufficient postage has been paid or the appropriate documentation is attached, and that items are in a suitable condition for processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Automated letter-mail operation at a USPS processing & distribution center: collection and presorted letters are worked on facer-canceler and barcode-sorter lines; each piece must be checked for a stamp/indicia (postage present and sufficient), a legible address that matches a valid delivery address, and suitability for machine processing (not too thick, stiff, oversized, torn or rigid). Failures are culled to reject bins, postage-due/no-postage pieces separated.

Flats and large envelopes at a plant: worker inspects magazines, catalogs and oversize envelopes for a complete, legible address, adequate postage or permit imprint, and condition (torn polywrap, loose or bulging contents) as pieces are prepared for and run on the flats sorter or cased manually.

Parcels and packages at a plant, annex or sorting & delivery center: check that the shipping label/barcode is readable and complete, that postage paid matches actual weight/dimensions/service, and that the package is intact and machinable (not crushed, leaking, unwrapped, oversized or hazardous); divert damaged, shortpaid or non-machinable items to rewrap, postage-due or manual handling.

Manual, reject and nixie mail: pieces the automation could not handle - hand-addressed illegible letters, incomplete or wrong addresses, mangled/unwrapped pieces needing rewrap, unstamped or shortpaid pieces needing postage-due markup, foreign-language or oddly shaped items. The clerk examines each piece individually, decides legibility/correctness/condition and dispositions it (lookup, forward, return, repair, dead mail).

Dock/acceptance check of bulk mailings and containers: verify that pallets, rolling containers, trays and sacks of customer mail carry the required documentation (mailing statement/PS Form 8125, placards, container labels), that the labels are correct and readable, and that the containers and their contents are in suitable condition before induction into processing.

tasks.label: Bundle, label, and route sorted mail to designated areas, depending on destinations and according to established procedures and deadlines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Regional processing & distribution center: sweep sorted letters/flats out of the output bins of a letter or flat sorter into trays and tubs, apply the machine-generated tray label, sleeve/lid and strap the tray, and set it on the takeaway conveyor for its destination separation — continuous flow, mixed thicknesses, dispatch deadlines.

P&DC: containerize — stack full, labeled trays/tubs by destination into All-Purpose Containers, hampers, or onto pallets, apply the container placard/label, and close out the container per the dispatch scheme.

P&DC: route the built, labeled containers, hampers and pallets of sorted mail across the workroom floor (shared with employees, tuggers and forklifts) to the designated staging area or dock door in time for the scheduled dispatch trip.

P&DC parcel/bundle operation (SPBS/APBS/parcel sorter): sort small parcels and bundles of mail to destination bins, verify or apply labels/scans, drop them into sacks, hampers or wire containers, and close and stage the container for its destination.

Manual/exception work: residual, rejected, damaged, oversized or misrouted mail — hand-facing and hand-tying/banding bundles, writing or applying a label, deciding the correct separation from the label list, and carrying the bundle to the right container or area.

Small delivery unit, annex, or USPS-contractor consolidator site: bundle and label mail/parcels for carrier routes or outbound dispatch and stage them in the designated area; smaller floor, more varied layout, mixed containers arriving.

Sacks and pouches (Priority/periodical/international, ORM sacks): release the sack closure or cut the plastic tie/lock, empty contents into a hamper or onto a belt without damaging the reusable sack or its contents, then attach a new sack tag/label or reuse the label holder. Lower volume than containers but still routine.

Dispatch side on the dock: placard/label pallets, rolling stock and strapped-and-wrapped tray stacks with destination placards, route tags and barcoded labels before loading; may involve cutting straps or shrink wrap on inbound pallets first. Standard USPS containers, printed placards from Surface Visibility scanners.

tasks.label: Rewrap soiled or broken parcels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: At the rewrap table of a USPS processing & distribution center: a corrugated parcel that has split at a seam or lost its tape on the sorter arrives in a hamper; contents are still contained and the address label is legible. The clerk assesses it, tapes it shut or slides it into a clear rewrap bag, and returns it to the mailstream.

A parcel that burst open in the sorter, with contents partly or wholly spilled onto the belt or into a tub. The clerk gathers the loose items, matches them to the torn wrapper and its label, judges whether the goods are still dispatchable, selects a new box or bag, repacks, seals and relabels.

A damaged parcel whose address label is torn, soaked, or missing and whose barcode will not scan. The clerk researches the addressee (opens the parcel to find a packing slip or invoice, or looks up remnant data), prints/writes a new address, applies it, and rewraps the parcel; otherwise routes it to the Mail Recovery Center.

A soiled, leaking, or contaminated parcel (broken liquid container, crushed food, unknown powder/odor). The clerk isolates it, wipes or contains the spill, double-bags or over-boxes it, attaches a damage/apology notice, and decides whether it goes forward, to hazmat, or to disposal.

Torn padded mailers, flats, and small packets whose wrapper has failed but whose contents are intact; the clerk slips each into a plastic rewrap bag or overwrap with a 'we care'/damage notice, ensuring the address remains readable, at a plant rewrap station or a post office back room.

Broken-open bundles, burst sacks, or an oversize/irregular parcel (bike box, tote, banded bundle) that has come apart in handling; the clerk re-bands, re-straps, or over-wraps the unit so it can be re-dispatched on a pallet or in a container.

Retail window / back office of a Post Office: a customer presents a batch of stamped mail (e.g., 60-150 wedding invitations) and requests hand-canceling; the clerk hand-stamps each decorative, sometimes lined or embellished envelope without smearing ink onto the address or artwork, then trays them as nonmachinable.

Hand-canceling stamped parcels and small packages at an acceptance or plant work station: irregular boxes, padded mailers and tubes of varying size and rigidity, stamps placed anywhere in the upper area of the top face; worker locates the stamps, presses the canceling stamp firmly enough for a legible mark on soft or uneven surfaces, and moves the parcel to a hamper or conveyor.

Clean-up canceling during or after a machine run: pieces pulled from the mailstream with uncanceled or misplaced stamps, jam-damaged or rewrapped pieces, and mail returned from the reject bin; worker inspects each piece, decides whether it still needs a cancellation, and applies the hand stamp at the machine side or repair/rewrap station.

Philatelic / special-event cancellation: first-day-of-issue covers or pictorial postmarks applied by hand at a philatelic window or temporary event station; collectors' covers must receive a clean, legible, correctly positioned impression, sometimes handed back rather than mailed.

sources.title: DHL Group signs MOU with Boston Dynamics for additional 1,000-robot deployment

sources.transferJustification: Related task: cycle counting. It is the same act as this task's second half - machine-reading labels on goods and comparing them against the system record to flag discrepancies - performed unaided in an ordinary warehouse.

sources.title: Corvus Robotics Brings Autonomous Inventory Management System to Lights-Out Warehouses

sources.title: How Amazon Robotics is working to eliminate the need for barcodes

sources.transferJustification: Related task: pre-ship condition and attribute inspection. It substantiates the damage/attribute-checking half of shipment examination on a machine-fed line, with automatic isolation of non-conforming items.

tasks.label: Requisition and store shipping materials and supplies to maintain inventory of stock.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Distribution center / large warehouse shipping department: clerk watches min/max levels of bulk shipping materials (corrugated cartons, pallets, stretch wrap, void fill, strapping), raises requisitions in the WMS/ERP, and when the supplier truck arrives puts the palletized supplies away into bulk racking with a powered pallet jack or forklift, then draws pallets down to replenish pack lines.

Manufacturing plant or mid-size warehouse supply crib: assorted cases of tape, labels, poly mailers, banding and stencils arrive mixed on one pallet or as LTL/parcel cartons; clerk reorders from a vendor catalog, breaks the load down, hand-shelves cases and part-cases into shelving with partly filled, variably spaced bins, labels locations, and counts stock.

Retail store or small e-commerce operation back stockroom: clerk orders mailers, boxes and tape online from a supplier, receives a handful of parcel-carrier cartons at the back door, carries them into a crowded stockroom shared with returns and seasonal goods, stacks or shelves them wherever space allows, and updates a spreadsheet or simple inventory app.

Institutional mailroom or hospital/office shipping-and-receiving supply room: clerk requisitions envelopes, mailers, labels, ribbon and box stock through purchasing, stores them in cabinets and on shelves in a small supply room, and issues quantities out to departments while keeping the stock record.

E-commerce fulfillment center packaging supply: clerk keeps corrugate, bag rolls and label stock flowing to automated pack-out equipment - ordering to forecast, storing incoming pallets and rolls in bulk racking, and staging/delivering them line-side to carton erectors and baggers.

sources.title: Seegrid Lift RS1 Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR)

sources.transferJustification: Storing shipping supplies in a warehouse is pallet putaway and line-side delivery of the same unit loads (pallets of corrugate, wrap, pallets themselves) that the Palion Lift moves and stacks.

sources.title: Seegrid AMRs Surpass 17 Million Autonomous Miles Driven in Customer Facilities

tasks.label: Pack, seal, label, or affix postage to prepare materials for shipping, using hand tools, power tools, or postage meter.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume e-commerce/parcel pack station in a distribution center: picked consumer goods arrive in totes at a bench; clerk selects a right-size carton or polybag, adds void fill, tapes/seals it, applies the printed carrier label, and sets it on the takeaway conveyor. Mixed SKUs, high throughput, standard corrugate and label stock.

Manufacturing/wholesale shipping department end-of-line: repeat-SKU finished goods are case-packed, the carton taped or glued shut and case-labeled, then stacked on a pallet, strapped or stretch-wrapped with power/pneumatic tools, and a pallet placard/shipping label applied before dock staging.

Small business, retail back room, or office mailroom: low-volume, heterogeneous outbound items (returns, samples, spare parts, documents) packed by hand into varied or reused boxes, envelopes and mailers, taped with a hand tape gun, weighed on a desk scale, and franked with a postage meter or thermal label printer; work is interleaved with other clerical duties.

Cold-chain or regulated shipments (mail-order pharmacy, perishable food, lab/specimen kits): order contents placed in an insulated liner or cooler with gel packs or dry ice, carton sealed, and compliance labels (temperature, hazmat/UN, Rx) applied within a controlled facility on a deadline.

Repeat-SKU fragile or breakable goods (glassware, bottles, ceramics, small electronics) packed with molded inserts, partitions or cushioning into shipping cartons, sealed and labeled in the shipping area of a warehouse or plant.

One-off high-value, oversized or irregular items (machinery, lab or medical equipment, awkward assemblies) needing bespoke protection: measured and cut cushioning/foam, blocking and bracing, double-boxing or a custom wooden crate built and fastened with power tools (nailer, banding tool), then stenciled/labeled for export.

tasks.label: Weigh or measure materials, equipment, or products to maintain relevant records, using volume meters, scales, rules, or calipers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machine shop / metal or plastics plant: worker pulls parts off machines at set intervals, measures diameters, lengths and features with calipers, micrometers or bench gauges, and logs the dimensions on inspection sheets or into the quality system; parts vary by job order.

Warehouse shipping/receiving dock: worker weighs cartons, cases and pallets on floor, bench or pallet scales, measures dimensions with a rule or tape for freight documentation, counts units, and records weights and quantities on receiving/shipping records; mixed carton sizes arrive on pallets and trailers.

Food, beverage or consumer-goods plant: worker weighs ingredient batches and finished packages, performs net-content checks against declared weight, and records weights on batch/production logs; product moves on packaging lines in a sanitary plant.

Bulk commodity facility (grain elevator, quarry, scrap or recycling yard): worker weighs loaded and empty trucks on a weighbridge or measures load volume, takes a sample of the load, and issues/records the weight ticket and net quantity; trucks arrive through an outdoor yard lane in all weather.

QA/assay laboratory or sample room: worker collects samples of product or raw material, weighs them on a balance, measures volumes, labels and logs each sample with its weight into the records; sample containers and racks are standard lab ware.

Yard or jobsite field measurement: worker tallies and measures varied materials as found — lumber and log tallies, pipe and rebar lengths, equipment dimensions, odd-lot loads — using a tape, rule or portable scale outdoors, and records the tally sheet.

tasks.label: Collect or prepare measurement, weight, or identification labels and attach them to products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food/consumer-goods plant packing line: worker weighs each variable-weight pack on a scale, the scale-printer produces a weight/price/lot label, and the worker sticks it on the package before it moves to case packing; hundreds of packs per shift, indoor plant floor, standard trays and films.

Distribution-center outbound area: cartons and unit loads are weighed/dimensioned, worker prints carrier shipping labels and SSCC pallet placards at a workstation printer and applies them to the correct carton faces or pallet sides before loading; fixed layout, standard cases and pallets.

Mill or fabrication plant: after weighing/measuring, worker prepares heat/lot ID tags for heavy or irregular items (steel coils, bundles, billets, lumber packs, pipe, castings) and attaches them by adhesive, staple, or wire tie; hot, dusty plant floor with overhead cranes and forklifts.

Warehouse receiving dock/stockroom: clerk checks in assorted incoming goods (mixed cartons, drums, crates, totes), weighs or counts them, prints or hand-writes ID/inspection labels and attaches them to items as they sit on pallets or on the dock floor; mixed sizes and packaging, no conveyor presentation.

QC sampling: worker collects samples of product or raw material into bags, bottles, or tubes, prepares identification labels (lot, time, station), attaches them to the sample containers, and logs them; plant QC lab or clinical lab bench with standard containers.

Outdoor yard or field: weighing or measuring loads, bins, bundles, or produce lots and attaching identity tags outdoors (lumber/scrap yard, grain or produce site, harvest bins) in variable weather, on uneven ground, with site-to-site layout differences.

tasks.label: Examine products or materials, parts, subassemblies, and packaging for damage, defects, or shortages, using specification sheets, gauges, and standards charts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Distribution-center/warehouse inbound receiving: checker meets pallets and cartons pulled off a trailer at the dock, compares against the packing list/ASN, counts cases (Ti-Hi), looks for crushed, torn, wet or leaking cartons and broken pallets, and records shortages/damage for a carrier claim.

In-facility stock audit/cycle count in a warehouse or stockroom: checker rides a lift or walks racking and floor-bulk lanes, verifies pallets/cases against WMS records, notes shortages, mislocated or expired stock and visibly damaged packaging, and records discrepancies.

Manufacturing plant in-process or final inspection: checker takes parts and subassemblies from a bin, machine or line, checks dimensions and features with calipers, micrometers and go/no-go gauges against a specification sheet, inspects visually for burrs, scratches, missing components, and logs measurements/defects.

Outbound order and packaging check before dispatch (fulfillment center, DC or plant shipping area): verify the right items and quantities are in the carton/order, check labels, seals and packaging integrity for damage, and record the result before shipment.

Sampling and grading of food/agricultural or bulk commodities (produce packhouse, food plant, grain elevator, mill): draw or receive a sample, examine it against a standards chart for defects, foreign material, size/colour, grade it and record the result.

Checks at uncontrolled outdoor sites: verifying a delivered load of lumber, pipe, steel, drywall or salvage/scrap on a truck bed, laydown yard or construction site against a delivery ticket, looking for transit damage and shortages in mixed, unfixtured loads and variable weather/lighting.

tasks.label: Collect product samples and prepare them for laboratory analysis or testing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production-line sampling inside a food, beverage, plastics or consumer-goods plant: each hour or batch the sampler walks the floor, pulls a grab sample from a filler, chute, hopper, tote or finished case, fills and caps a labeled cup/bottle/bag, records lot, line and time, and carries the samples to the on-site QA lab.

Incoming bulk commodity receiving at a grain elevator, feed mill, oilseed or ethanol plant: sample every arriving truck or railcar (probe or stream sampler), divide the sample on a Boerner/riffle divider, run moisture and test weight, bag and label a file/retain sample for the lab, and enter grade data on the ticket.

Bulk liquid and chemical sampling at a chemical plant, tank farm, terminal or refinery: go to sample points, tanks, reactors, drums, tank trucks or railcars, purge the line or open the hatch, draw with a thief/bomb or closed-loop valve into labeled bottles or cylinders, seal, log the sample, and deliver it to the plant lab.

Heavy-industry high-temperature and bulk-solids sampling: molten steel/iron lance or disc samples in a melt shop, clinker, raw meal and cement samples in a cement plant, ore or coal from a conveyor; the sample is cooled, cut/ground or bagged, identified, and sent to the plant lab (often by pneumatic tube).

Liquid pickup sampling at producer sites: a bulk milk hauler/sampler agitates the farm bulk tank, dips or ports a representative sample into vials, labels and ices them, records temperature and weight, and delivers the vials with the load to the plant lab; each farm's milk house differs.

Off-site or stored-lot spot sampling at varied locations: coring stored lots in customer warehouses, digging samples from scrap or aggregate piles at a yard, sampling produce in coolers or grain/fertilizer in barge or ship holds; sampling points are chosen on the spot and differ site to site.

tasks.label: Maintain, monitor, and clean work areas, such as recycling collection sites, drop boxes, counters and windows, and areas around scale houses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Interior housekeeping of a scale house / weigh-station booth at a landfill, quarry, grain elevator or transfer station: wiping the counter and ticket-window glass (inside and out), dusting around the indicator/printer, sweeping and mopping mud tracked onto the floor, emptying the wastebasket. Clutter (papers, tickets, keyboard, radio, mugs) sits on the counter and the booth is small and occupied during shifts.

Sweeping and clearing spilled material and debris from the truck-scale deck and the paved apron around the scale house: grain, aggregate, mud clods, blown litter, cardboard. Outdoor, at a facility-controlled yard with truck traffic; done between weighings or at shift end so the scale reads true.

Maintaining a recycling collection / drop-off area at the site: picking up loose litter and windblown material around the drop boxes, moving items left outside the containers into the correct box, clearing overflow and stray bulky items (bags, boxes, a broken chair), keeping the lanes walkable. Mixed, unpredictable objects; public members drive up and unload.

Monitoring rounds of the work area: walking or driving the scale house surroundings, drop-box pad and collection site to spot spills, hazards, blocked lanes, full or damaged containers, and contaminated/improper drop-offs; noting and reporting what needs attention.

Periodic wash-down of hard surfaces: hosing or pressure-washing the concrete pad around drop boxes and the scale approach, rinsing spilled material off the deck and curbing at an institution-controlled outdoor site.

Upkeep of site fixtures: restocking supplies and forms in the booth, replacing or straightening signage on drop boxes, repositioning bins, cleaning out the inside of a drop box or container, and small repairs.

tasks.label: Compare product labels, tags, or tickets, shipping manifests, purchase orders, and bills of lading to verify accuracy of shipment contents, quality specifications, or weights.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Inbound receiving check at a warehouse/DC dock: worker checks pallets and cartons coming off a trailer against the bill of lading, ASN and purchase order — counts units, reads case/pallet labels and SKUs, notes damage, shortages and overages, and records the receipt.

Outbound order/load verification in a DC: worker checks staged or racked pallets and cases and their labels against the packing list/shipping manifest and order before loading, flagging mis-picks, wrong SKUs and mislabeled cases.

Outbound weight/dimension verification: worker weighs packed cartons or parcels and compares the weight (and dims) against the order or shipping spec to catch pick errors and carrier-compliance problems before shipment.

In-plant production/QC check: worker verifies product labels, tags, tickets, lot/date codes and net weights on finished packs or cases against the order and quality spec, pulling or rejecting nonconforming product and logging results.

Truck scale / bulk materials: worker weighs loaded and empty trucks at a scale house, grain elevator, scrap or aggregate yard, samples or grades the load where required, and compares the scale ticket weight and commodity to the bill of lading or load manifest.

Freight terminal, cross-dock or parcel hub: worker reconciles freight bills and manifests to the pallets and parcels handled at the dock, captures weights/dimensions, and flags shortages, overages, mislabels and damage.

It is the same act as this task's core — reading product labels and tags on stored freight and comparing them to the document of record (WMS-held ASN/PO data) to flag mismatches — on the same objects and in the same warehouse setting.

tasks.label: Remove from stock products or loads not meeting quality standards, and notify supervisors or appropriate departments of discrepancies or shortages.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Distribution-center/warehouse receiving: checker inspects inbound mixed pallets and floor-loaded freight against the BOL, pulls crushed, leaking or short-dated cases off pallets onto a quarantine/salvage pallet, keys the damage and case shortages into the WMS and notifies the receiving supervisor and vendor. Forklift traffic, shrink-wrap, heterogeneous cartons.

Manufacturing/packaging plant QC checkpoint: worker weighs and checks packaged units coming off the line (fill weight, seal, label/date code), pulls underweight, mislabeled or damaged units off the belt into a hold cage, records the count on the QC/production record and alerts the line supervisor or QA of the out-of-spec run.

Food processing plant or produce packinghouse grading: sampler draws samples from incoming lots and running product, culls rotten, undersized or foreign-material-contaminated product from bins and belts, records grade and defect percentages and notifies QA, the shipper or grower of the off-grade lot.

Retail/club store or grocery backroom: receiver-checker walks stock and shelves, removes damaged, expired or short-dated packaged goods into a reclaim/salvage cart, scans them out of inventory, and reports the shrink and vendor shortages to the store manager. Customers and staff present, varied packaging.

Bulk/heavy materials yard (scrap metal, recycling MRF tipping floor, lumber yard, grain elevator, aggregate): sampler inspects or samples an inbound load, segregates contaminated or out-of-grade material out of the stream or downgrades/refuses the load, logs the result on the scale ticket and notifies dispatch or the buyer. Outdoor or open-shed, weather exposure, truck traffic.

Field or job-site check: worker inspects materials delivered to a construction site, farm or customer yard (or field-harvested product), sets aside broken, wet or off-spec items for return, tags them, and phones or emails the office/supplier about the discrepancy or shortage. Layout differs site to site, no fixed equipment.

tasks.label: Inspect products and examination records to determine the number of defects per worker and the reasons for examiners' rejections.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel/sewn-goods or textile plant: the checker collects garments and fabric pieces pulled by line examiners, spreads them on an audit table, identifies the defect (skipped or broken stitch, seam pucker, stain, hole, misaligned pattern), matches each piece to the sewing operator's bundle ticket, and tallies defects per operator and reason on the daily quality report.

Food/beverage/CPG packaging plant: the checker samples product and reviews packages rejected by line inspectors (underweight, bad seal, crooked or wrong label, damaged pack), verifies each rejection against the inspection sheets, and records counts of defects by reason, line, shift, and the inspector/operator responsible.

Discrete manufacturing (machined, molded, or assembled parts; PCB assemblies): the checker works through reject bins and re-inspects parts with gauges, calipers, and visual standards, confirms or overturns the examiner's rejection, classifies the defect (burr, short shot, scratch, solder bridge, missing component), and attributes counts to the responsible operator/station in the quality log.

Grading and packing facility (produce packinghouse, poultry/meat plant, sawmill/planer mill): the recordkeeper audits product downgraded or culled by human graders, verifies the defect call against grade rules (bruise, rot, foreign material; knots, splits, shake), and compiles per-grader defect counts and rejection reasons.

Warehouse/distribution center or shipping department: the checker examines returned or customer-rejected cartons and items alongside packers'/checkers' inspection records, determines why each was rejected (damage, wrong item, short count, wrong label), and tabulates errors per packer or checker for the accuracy report.

tasks.label: Store samples of finished products in labeled cartons and record their location.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food/beverage/CPG plant: QA checker pulls retain units of each production lot off the packaging line (bags, bottles, pouches, trays), places the required count into a carton, marks/prints the lot code and date on the carton, shelves it in the retention room by date, and logs the shelf/bay location in a spreadsheet or QA system.

Pharma/nutraceutical/cosmetic GMP site: reserve samples in sealed primary containers are packed into labeled cartons, barcode-scanned, moved into a controlled-access, temperature-monitored retain room, and the rack/shelf position recorded in LIMS/ERP with chain-of-custody entries.

Chemical, plastics, or feed plant: retain samples of bulk lots drawn at fixed process sampling points into jars/bags, labeled with lot and sampling data, boxed by campaign, stored on racks in a sample archive room, and the position logged in plant records.

Warehouse/DC or receiving-inspection area: sample units of finished goods (incoming or outgoing) are placed in labeled cartons and put away in a designated storeroom bay/rack, with the carton and its slot recorded in the WMS/ERP.

Mill or durable-goods plant (textile, metals, paper, building products): physical specimens of finished output (swatches, coupons, cores, small parts) of varied shape and weight are boxed in labeled cartons and archived in a specimen storeroom; location recorded in a log or database.

Outdoor receiving yard or field-side sampling (grain elevator truck probe station, packinghouse yard, remote delivery point): samples drawn from trucks or piles are bagged, boxed in labeled cartons, and stashed in a sample shed, trailer, or truck, with the location noted on the ticket/log.

tasks.label: Count or estimate quantities of materials, parts, or products received or shipped.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Inbound dock at a distribution center or plant: as a trailer/container is unloaded (floor-loaded cartons or palletized freight), count the cases/pallets received, scan or read labels, verify the count against the bill of lading/packing list, and record shortages, overages and damage.

Outbound shipping area of a DC or plant: count and verify cases/cartons/pallets staged and loaded against pick lists and BOLs before the truck leaves, confirming order quantities and recording the shipped count.

Warehouse racking, stockroom bins or retail/wholesale sales floor: count quantities of received stock held in storage locations (cycle counts, wall-to-wall physical inventory, putaway verification), reconciling on-hand quantities to WMS/ERP records.

Manufacturing stockroom or receiving bench: count small parts and components (fasteners, electronic parts, castings) in totes/bags/cartons, typically by weigh-counting on a counting scale or hand-counting a sample, to verify supplier counts of received lots or quantities issued/shipped.

Outdoor industrial yard (aggregate plant, scrap yard, grain elevator, cement/sand terminal): estimate quantities of bulk material received or shipped by gauging pile volumes and truck/rail loads, and record tonnage for inventory and shipping documents.

Outdoor yard or jobsite delivery of irregular heavy goods: tally lumber packs, pipe joints, logs on a truck, or steel bundles received or shipped, counting pieces on stacks and loads in the open, in variable weather and stacking arrangements.

instances.label: Wholesaler/manufacturer distribution center: worker reads an order ticket/pick list, walks racks and bins to pick eaches and cases of mixed SKUs, counts or weighs to verify quantity against the ticket, packs into a carton with packing slip, weighs and labels the parcel, and stages it on the outbound dock for the carrier.

Manufacturing-plant stockroom or parts crib: fills internal and customer orders for components and hardware, weigh-counts small fasteners/parts on a counting scale to hit the ordered quantity, bags and labels with part and lot numbers, records the issue, and forwards the kit to shipping or to a production line.

Product-sample fulfillment desk (textiles, coatings, food, chemicals): pulls sample stock or fills small jars/bottles/envelopes with a weighed or measured quantity, labels with lot/batch data, logs the sample in the sample record, and packs it into a mailer for USPS/UPS pickup.

Lab/QC retained-sample shipment, routine case: retrieves standard tubes/retains from a sample library or freezer per a request ticket, aliquots or repacks into standard vials, applies barcode labels, boxes them with coolant, logs chain of custody, and hands off to the courier.

Lab/QC retained-sample shipment, non-routine case: variable containers, hazardous-material or dry-ice cold-chain shipments requiring regulated packaging, declarations and one-off documentation before courier handoff.

Bulk loadout at a feed mill, grain elevator, chemical or aggregate plant: fills an order by weighing bulk product into bags, totes or a truck on a scale, verifies net weight against the order ticket, palletizes/secures the load, records weights on the scale ticket and releases the shipment.

Manufacturing / food or beverage processing plant: the weigher-checker moves bins, totes, carts, drums and racks of raw material or finished product between the weigh/inspection point and the processing line, packaging area, or cooler/warehouse, using carts, tuggers, or by placing loads on conveyors. Quality-control sample runs: the sampler collects small containers (bottles, jars, sample bags, pressurized cylinders, plates) at a production line, tank or receiving point and carries them across the plant, mill, or lab building to the testing laboratory several times per shift; some plants use pneumatic tubes or carts. Indoor corridors, doors, elevators.

Outdoor bulk facility (grain elevator, feed mill, aggregate/scrap/lumber yard, river or rail terminal): samples are drawn from arriving trucks or railcars in the driveway and must get to the scale-house/grading lab, and bagged retains are moved to storage. automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Daily filing of incoming paper into case files: opening mail, sorting pleadings/correspondence/discovery, removing staples and punching, placing each document in the correct client-matter folder in date order, and refiling folders in the office file room's cabinets.

Document intake into the electronic case file: prepping paper (staples, torn edges, mixed sizes), batch scanning, applying client/matter and document-type metadata in the DMS (iManage/NetDocuments), QC of images, and organizing the electronic folder structure.

Building trial, closing, or deposition binders and exhibit sets: copying heterogeneous originals (photos, oversized exhibits, certified copies), collating, inserting printed index tabs, punching, loading three-ring binders, labeling spines, and preparing the index.

Physical law library upkeep in a firm library: reshelving reporters, treatises and digests left on tables, checking in and shelving new volumes and advance sheets, shelf-reading to correct misfiled call numbers, and inventory.

Updating looseleaf services and pocket parts: filing replacement pages into looseleaf binders page by page, pulling superseded pages, inserting new pocket parts into hardbound volumes and discarding old ones.

Closed-file records management: pulling the completed matter's file, purging duplicates and drafts, packing records cartons, labeling/barcoding and indexing them, transferring to the storage room or offsite records vendor, and retrieving files/boxes on later request.

tasks.label: Mail, fax, or arrange for delivery of legal correspondence to clients, witnesses, and court officials.

instances.label: Routine outgoing first-class correspondence from a law office: print a transmittal/cover letter plus enclosures (copies of pleadings, discovery responses, invoices), collate the set, fold, insert into a window or firm envelope, seal, run through the postage meter, and place in the outgoing mail tray for carrier pickup. Volumes of a few to a few dozen pieces a day, varying page counts and enclosure combinations.

Certified mail / registered mail / service by mail: prepare the letter and enclosures, generate the certified barcode label or green card, affix to the envelope, apply postage, log the tracking number in the case file, take it to the post office or hand to the carrier, and later file the return receipt or delivery proof with the proof-of-service record.

Overnight courier or messenger dispatch: assemble the document packet into a FedEx/UPS envelope or box, print and affix the airbill/shipping label, book the pickup or arrange a local messenger/process server, and hand the package off at reception, dropbox, or the building dock.

Fax or electronic transmittal of paper-origin documents: feed a hard-copy signed letter, pleading, or exhibit set into a fax machine/MFP or production scanner, transmit to the court clerk, opposing counsel, or client, and save the transmission confirmation to the file.

Bulky or customized packages: judge's courtesy copies, tabbed exhibit binders, three-ring sets with dividers, original wet-signed documents accompanied by filing-fee checks, oversize exhibits, USB drives or CDs, each assembled to court- or client-specific instructions with a cover letter and packing note, then boxed for messenger or process server.

Hand-carrying documents: walking a filing packet or correspondence to another floor of the office building, to a nearby courthouse filing window, or to opposing counsel's office down the street; presenting it to a clerk or receptionist and obtaining a conformed copy or signed receipt.

instances.label: Routine small-batch copying in the law-office copy area: 2-20 loose letter-size pages (a letter, a signed contract, a filed pleading), 1-3 copies via the MFP document feeder; secretary carries originals from her desk, loads the feeder, selects settings on the touchscreen, retrieves output, staples, and puts copies in the client file or on an attorney's desk.

Copying originals that are stapled or clipped, or several documents at once: remove staples/clips, run each document, re-staple the originals in original order, staple each copy set, keep sets separated, occasionally duplex or reduce/enlarge.

Bulk copying for court filing, service, or discovery: a 200-800 page document copied in 3-6 collated sets, hole-punched or stapled/bound, spot-checked for legibility, skipped or double-fed pages, then boxed or delivered against a filing deadline.

Non-standard originals on the platen: bound deposition transcripts or books, fragile/aged or torn records, small items (checks, IDs, receipts, photos), oversized plats or exhibits - placed and repositioned one at a time with zoom/contrast adjustment.

A copy job interrupted by machine trouble: paper jam mid-run, toner or paper out, a crumpled or mis-fed original; the secretary opens the machine, clears the paper path, replaces toner or reloads trays, re-runs the missing pages, and verifies each set is complete.

Offsite copying: at a courthouse clerk's counter, a client's home or business, or a records storage site, using unfamiliar found equipment or a portable scanner/copier, with no fixed layout and originals in whatever condition the file is in.

Equipment malfunctions beyond a quick fix: reading the error code and service ticket details, calling or ticketing the copier/telecom vendor under the service contract, scheduling and escorting the technician, arranging a workaround device in the meantime, verifying the repair and logging it.

instances.label: Purely electronic records work at a workstation: creating and naming folders in a shared drive/SharePoint/DMS, filing emails and attachments, saving and versioning correspondence, updating attendance and personnel spreadsheets or database records. No physical object is handled; the output is an organized, retrievable electronic file set.

Routine hard-copy filing in a general office: sorting the day's incoming correspondence, invoices, signed forms and reports, removing/adding fasteners, labeling folders, and filing each document in the correct folder in lateral or vertical cabinets in a shared file room, keeping the sequence correct.

Digitizing paper into the electronic system: preparing batches (removing staples and clips, straightening, inserting separator sheets), feeding a sheet-fed scanner or MFP, then naming, indexing and filing the resulting images in the document management system, and shredding or refiling the originals.

Pulling and refiling records on request: locating a requested folder among thousands in the file room or storage cabinets, checking it out to a requester, delivering it, and refiling it correctly on return.

Periodic reorganization and archiving: setting up new file categories and labels, purging files under a retention schedule, boxing and labeling inactive records, and moving boxes to a storage room or off-site records center with an index of contents.

Maintaining attendance and log records from paper: collecting sign-in sheets, timesheets or visitor logs, transcribing the marks/entries into the attendance or payroll system, and maintaining the paper log binder.

Fault handling: paper jam or misfeed mid-run — open the copier doors, extract crumpled or torn sheets from rollers/fuser, replace a spent toner cartridge, and re-run the spoiled copies.

instances.label: Day-to-day desk scanning in an employer's office: worker takes a stack of loose paper (letters, signed forms, invoices, memo drafts), pulls staples and clips, squares the sheets, loads the ADF of a desktop/multifunction scanner, picks resolution/duplex/OCR settings, scans to the network, and the captured text/data lands in the word processor or records system for revision. Mixed sizes and paper quality; occasional jams and rescans.

Backfile conversion project: boxes of archived files pulled into a records room, prepped (unstapling, unfolding, taping tears, inserting separator/patch sheets, batch tickets), run in batches through a production sheet-fed scanner, then indexed and the extracted fields loaded into the document management system for editing. High volume, tight deadlines.

Exception originals: bound reports and books, brittle or oversized documents, carbon copies, photographs and pasted-in graphics, receipts, ID and insurance cards. Each item is positioned individually on a flatbed platen or book cradle, scanned one page at a time, cropped/deskewed, and imported into the document being prepared.

Point-of-capture entry at a service counter or records desk: forms handed over by patrons/staff, barcoded file jackets, marked/OMR forms and ID cards are passed through a desktop scanner or barcode/card reader into the records system while the worker watches the capture on screen and corrects rejected or misread fields.

Off-site or home-based work: a remote typist or one working at a client's premises scans handwritten copy, rough drafts, or client paperwork with a small desktop scanner, portable sheet-fed scanner, or phone camera on whatever surface is available, then imports and edits the text. Layout, lighting, and equipment vary site to site.

instances.label: Refilling paper in a shared office laser printer/MFP: carry a ream from the supply cabinet, pull out the tray, strip the wrapper, jog and align the stack, set the side/rear guides for letter or legal, close the tray and confirm the size on the panel. Machine sits among desks and foot traffic in a normal office.

Replacing consumables on an office MFP: open the front door or side panel, pull the spent toner/ink cartridge (or waste toner bottle, staple cartridge), unbox and shake the replacement, seat it until it latches, close the door, run a test/calibration page, and box the old unit for recycling pickup.

Operating the printer/copier for a job: release or queue the job at the panel or driver, pick tray, duplex, collate and finishing options, watch the run, then retrieve, sort and keep the output sets separated for distribution.

Loading blank or special media into equipment: inserting blank discs, backup tapes, memory cards or USB media into a drive or duplicator, and loading envelopes, labels, letterhead or preprinted forms into a tray or a specialty printer, with the right orientation and settings.

Keeping a high-volume copy-room/production machine running in a law office, agency or word-processing pool: feeding it cases of paper through a long run, swapping toner and staples mid-job, and unloading finished stacks from the output/finisher.

Fault recovery on an office printer: the machine reports a jam or misfeed, so the worker opens covers and the duplexer, pulls crumpled or torn sheets out of the rollers and fuser area, finds fragments, reseats the tray, clears the error and reprints the missing pages, or reseats/replaces a worn pickup roller.

tasks.label: Gather, register, and arrange the material to be typed, following instructions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Law firm / government administrative office: typist collects paper rough drafts, handwritten notes and marked-up corrected copy from in-trays and colleagues' desks, date-stamps each item, records it in a job register (job number, originator, deadline), and sorts the items into priority folders on the desk before typing.

Fully digital intake: source material arrives as emailed attachments, scanned PDFs and uploaded digital dictation files; the worker downloads and renames files, logs each job in a tracking spreadsheet or workflow queue, and orders the queue by deadline and instructions. No physical object is handled.

Records/forms batch prep: a batch of paper forms, mail-in applications, charts or correspondence arrives (often still in envelopes); the worker opens and extracts contents, checks items against a request/manifest list, removes staples and clips, collates and orders the pages, and attaches a batch cover sheet or barcode registering the batch for typing/data entry.

Central file room / storage retrieval: the worker pulls existing case files, charts or prior correspondence needed as source material, checks them out in the file log or tracking system, and brings the assembled set in order to the typing station.

Ad hoc gathering across the premises: walking to other departments to collect handheld dictation recorders or USB/cassette media and missing attachments or signed originals from staff, docking/uploading the audio, assigning job numbers, and matching each recording with its accompanying paper worksheet before typing.

sources.title: Document Scanning & Digitization Services | Ripcord AI-Powered Robotics

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic document digitization prep. The physical work is identical to the typist's gather/register/arrange step — taking loose paper, folders and envelopes as received, separating and de-stapling pages, identifying and ordering them, and registering each record by index/category so it is queued for downstream keying. Same objects (loose sheets, folders, mail), same page-level precision, same output (a registered, ordered set of source material).

sources.title: Ripcord uses robotics to digitize records, processes and avoid paper waste — The Robot Report
sources.claim: Ripcord runs robots at production scale in its Hayward, California facility, using them to sort pages and remove staples much faster than human operators, with people involved in fewer steps than a conventional document-processing facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: high-volume paper record preparation and sorting. Sorting individual pages and de-stapling at production reliability is the manipulation core of gathering and arranging material to be typed; throughput and error rates are commercially accepted by enterprise customers.

sources.claim: Independent trade press confirms Ripcord's machines are physical robots that scan documents autonomously, including staple removal, serving large enterprise customers.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes autonomy (not teleoperation) for the Ripcord workcells cited above for paper gathering, de-stapling and indexing.

The machine reads each piece, matches it against a database (register) and places it into the correct destination bin (arrange) — the same operations on the same objects (mixed paper mail and forms) that a typist performs when registering and arranging incoming material for typing.

sources.claim: The FBI's Central Records Complex uses a fleet of automated robots and one of the world's largest automated storage-and-retrieval systems to file away and retrieve paper case files held in bins; file requests are made electronically and the robots service them.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: retrieving requested paper case files from records storage. This is the 'gather' step of the typist instance — locating and bringing the requested file set, with automatic location logging (register) — performed on the same objects (paper case files/folders) at institutional reliability, in a purpose-built robotic storage grid.

sources.title: Autonomous Robots Installed at Upstate Medical University — Aethon
sources.claim: Aethon TUG autonomous mobile robots are deployed in fleets in hospitals (e.g., 14 at Upstate Medical University, VA hospitals, Stanford) to transport medicines, supplies and records in closed carts along mapped routes; they transport material but do not pick, register or collate documents.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to characterise the ceiling of deployed capability inside human work facilities (E2): autonomous transport of closed carts along mapped corridors, with no manipulation of loose paper, no registration and no collation — hence it cannot complete these instances at E2.

Freelance desktop publisher working at a home office: inserting a client's flash drive, memory card, or disc into a home computer or an external drive on a cluttered domestic desk, sometimes needing an adapter or cable hookup first.

tasks.label: Lift and unload containers of mail or parcels onto equipment for transportation to sortation stations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Parcel hub / presort facility: unloading a floor-loaded trailer or ocean container of loose parcels and cartons at a dock, placing them onto an extendable/telescoping conveyor that feeds the sortation system; mixed box sizes and weights up to ~50 lb, arranged as human loaders stacked them.

Mail/e-commerce processing facility: lifting mail tubs, letter trays, totes and cases off pallets, hampers, dollies or carts and setting them onto an induction conveyor or sorter feed belt; repetitive, high volume, stacks arranged by hand.

Inside the facility: loading filled containers/tubs/parcels onto transport equipment (wheeled carts, GoCarts, pallets, tugger trains, AMRs) at the dock and unloading them again at the sortation stations; flat floors, marked aisles, employees moving around.

Exception handling: bulging or deformable mail sacks, oversize/odd-shaped or over-50-lb parcels, damaged or wet containers, items handled at an open dock in heat/cold, requiring two-hand grabs, re-stacking and judgment about damage.

tasks.label: Clear jams in sortation equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Folder-inserter jam in a corporate, university, or hospital mailroom: machine faults and displays a jam location; clerk opens side covers and deck plates, releases roller pinches/platen handles, pulls crumpled or partly torn sheets and envelopes out of the paper path, checks that no paper fragments remain, closes covers, reconciles the damaged piece and re-runs it.

Misfeed/jam in a mailing machine, postage meter feeder, tabber, labeler, or address printer in a small office mailroom: damp or double-fed envelopes stuck in the feed deck or sealer, clerk frees the envelope, wipes/adjusts feed rollers and separators, resets the meter count and restarts the run.

Jam in a high-speed letter/flat sorter or barcode sorter at a presort mail service bureau or lettershop: mail wedged in the transport or a stacker pocket, operator opens transport doors, extracts several bent or torn pieces, culls damaged mail, re-feeds the recovered pieces and restarts the sort run without losing count integrity.

Parcel jam on a sortation conveyor, diverter, or chute in a shipping/mailing operation or campus distribution center: an oversize, unstable, or burst package is wedged at a shoe sorter or chute mouth; worker hits E-stop/lockout, reaches or climbs into the line, frees the package (sometimes recovering spilled contents), inspects for debris, and restarts the line.

Recurring or severe jam requiring tools and partial disassembly: shredded paper, label adhesive, or shrink wrap wrapped around rollers/belts; worker removes guards, extracts debris, decides whether to adjust the machine or call maintenance, and logs the downtime/damaged mail.

sources.title: All about Clear Jam In The Inserter - Quadient
sources.claim: Clearing a paper jam in a production inserter is documented by the OEM as a manual operator procedure: open covers, unlatch release handles, swing open assemblies, and pull out jammed paper — no robotic mechanism performs it.
sources.transferJustification: Directly describes the task instance (jam clearing on mail inserting equipment) and shows it is performed by a human operator, not by any machine subsystem.

sources.title: Shipping & Mailing Inserting Relay 2500, 3500, 4500 Inserting System user guide
sources.claim: Mailing-system OEM safety documentation frames jam clearing as a hands-on human procedure requiring judgment about stopped mechanisms and gentle extraction of jammed material.
sources.transferJustification: Same task on the most common mail machine class in this occupation; confirms the recovery step is manual on current commercial equipment.

sources.transferJustification: Describes the parcel-sortation instance of this task and attributes the physical clearing step to human operators even in automated sortation lines.

tasks.label: Place incoming or outgoing letters or packages into sacks or bins based on destination or type, and place identifying tags on sacks or bins.

instances.label: Corporate/office mailroom: clerk works from hampers and tables of incoming mixed mail (letters, flats, interoffice envelopes, small parcels), reads names/departments and drops each piece into departmental pigeonhole bins or hampers on a human-height rack; bins carry department/floor tags that the clerk swaps as routes change.

tasks.label: Release packages or letters to customers upon presentation of written notices or other identification.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corporate/institutional mailroom or reception counter: an employee or visitor arrives with an arrival-notice email/slip or shows a company badge; the clerk locates the parcel or accountable letter on the mailroom's open shelving or in a bin, verifies the name, hands it across the counter, and logs the release or collects a signature.

Outgoing mail collection and consolidation: emptying building drop boxes and departmental outgoing trays at end of day, then separating the collected pieces by class and carrier (USPS metered, presort, UPS/FedEx, interoffice) and staging them in trays/bags at the dock for carrier pickup.

University/hospital/government central receiving dock: a contractor or courier truck backs in with palletized freight and standard containers (USPS all-purpose containers, letter/flat tray stacks strapped to skids, cartons). Irregular and exception intake: canvas sacks, wheeled hampers, loose bulk mail, oversized/odd-shaped or heavy items, cold-chain or high-value items, plus shortages, damaged loads, mis-consigned or COD/signature-restricted deliveries that must be counted, refused or annotated, and resolved on the spot with the driver.

Street-level acceptance at a building with no dock: the courier hands off containers at the curb, sidewalk, or lobby in whatever weather and pedestrian traffic exists; clerk counts and signs there, then carts the load through public/shared space and a freight elevator to the mailroom.

tasks.label: Add ink, fill paste reservoirs, and change machine ribbons when necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corporate/office mailroom: postage meter (e.g., Pitney Bowes SendPro C or mailstation) signals low ink. Clerk fetches the correct ink cartridge from the supply cabinet, opens the machine cover, releases the latch, removes and bags the spent cartridge, seats the new one, closes the cover, runs a test print/print-head alignment, and confirms the indicia is legible.

High-volume mail production center (presort house, university/hospital central mail): refill or swap the bulk ink supply on an inkjet addressing/imprinting head or tabber, purge and wipe the printheads, run a sample sheet, and check barcode/address print quality before restarting the run.

Filling the sealing-fluid / paste reservoir: open the tank lid on a folder-inserter, envelope sealer or moistener, pour E-Z Seal type solution to the fill line without overflowing, check the wick/brush or felt pad, wipe up drips, and test-seal a few envelopes.

Changing a ribbon: thermal-transfer ribbon on a shipping-label or tape printer, or a fabric/ink ribbon on an older imprinting, addressing or postage-tape machine. Remove the spent spool, thread the new ribbon through guides and around the take-up spool, tension it, close the head, and test print.

Replacing toner/drum in the mailroom's laser or label printer used for postage tapes, address labels and manifests: unbox and rock the cartridge, remove the seal, seat it in the machine, run a calibration page, box the spent cartridge for recycling, and log the consumable use.

instances.label: Production inserter line at a print/mail service bureau or in-house statement shop: operator watches finished mailpieces coming off a high-speed inserter, pulls samples, checks for missing/extra inserts, out-of-sequence or mismatched pages, unreadable postal barcodes, mis-sealed or scuffed envelopes; then determines the cause (feeder timing, worn separators, static, print file/collation error, envelope stock) so it can be eliminated.

Addressing/inkjet printing output on the mail line (envelopes, postcards, statement web): operator inspects printed addresses, indicia and IMb/Mailmark barcodes for streaks, dropouts, faint or misregistered print and skew; determines cause (clogged or failed nozzles, low ink, head height, paper skew) and how to eliminate it.

Office/campus mailroom desktop or mid-volume folder-inserter run (invoices, notices, enrollment letters): operator inspects folded and inserted pieces for misfolds, dog-eared or creased sheets, wrong document set in an envelope, unsealed flaps; determines cause (fold-plate setting, feeder gap, dry sealer, static, wrong stock) and corrective adjustment.

Postage meter / mailing machine output check: operator inspects metered indicia and permit imprints for faint, smeared or offset print, correct date and postage value, and checks flap sealing; determines cause (low ink, dirty or clogged printhead, dry/overfull sealer tank, envelope thickness) and how to eliminate it.

Tabbing/labeling/addressing machine output for a direct-mail drop: operator inspects wafer-seal/tab placement, label adhesion and skew, double-fed or torn pieces, and postal compliance of the finished piece; determines cause (tab head position, feeder pressure, static, stock curl) and adjustment needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corporate, university, or hospital mail center: clerk at a workstation keys recipient name, department, or mail-stop code into the mail-management/tracking system so each incoming item is assigned to the correct internal delivery route and route sheet.

Semi-automated letter/flat/parcel sorter in a presort or corporate mail facility: operator sits at a keying console and enters destination or bin codes for item images the machine's address reader rejected (video/remote coding), so the sorter diverts them to the right stacker.

Voice-directed sortation station in a shipping/fulfillment mailroom: clerk speaks ZIP, hub, or chute codes into a headset-based voice recognition terminal, which assigns the item to a route or lights the correct destination bin.

Presort/mailing-service operation: operator selects and loads the applicable sort plan or routing scheme on the machine controller and keys exception items (illegible, forwards, rejects, undeliverables) into the terminal for redirection.
Shipping/courier counter or dock terminal: clerk keys destination and service-level data into routing software to assign the parcel to a carrier lane or hub route and generate the routing label.

tasks.label: Wrap packages or bundles by hand, or by using tying machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corporate, campus, hospital or law-firm mailroom: clerk hand-packs varied outgoing items (documents, binders, samples, small parts, promo kits) into cartons, jiffy bags or padded mailers at a packing bench, adds fill, tapes and labels. Items and box sizes vary order to order; volumes are modest and interruptions frequent.

Sort station in a mail center: clerk gathers sorted letters/flats into bundles per department, route or ZIP and secures each bundle by hand with rubber bands, string or a banding tool, then places bundles into trays or sacks.

Mail production floor: clerk feeds stacks of mail, catalogs or inserted pieces (or filled trays/tubs) into a tying/banding/strapping machine, cycles it, checks strap placement and tension, and stages the finished bundles.

Protective wrapping of fragile, odd-shaped or high-value items (glassware, awards, electronics, artwork tubes) in bubble wrap or kraft paper with cushioning and void fill before boxing and sealing for shipment.
Dock/staging area: clerk strapping or stretch-wrapping bundles, trays, tubs or sacks onto pallets or skids to stabilize them for bulk-mail drop-off or carrier pickup.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corporate/institutional mail center service window: employees walk up to buy stamps, stamped envelopes, mailers and packing supplies; clerk quotes the amount, hands over the items, takes cash or charges the department cost center, gives change and a receipt, logs the sale.

University or hospital mail center counter accepting an outgoing package: clerk weighs and measures it, quotes carrier/service options and mailing charge, applies postage or prints a label, and runs a debit/credit card or campus-card payment.

Private shipping/mailbox retail store counter, routine transaction: customer picks a standard box, tape, bubble mailer or stamp booklet and a shipping service; clerk rings up goods plus mailing charge, takes card or cash, gives receipt and change.

Private shipping/mailbox store, consultative transaction: customer arrives with an unpacked, fragile or oversized item and questions about international/customs or insurance; clerk inspects the item, recommends box size and service, prices a custom quote, and accepts payment (sometimes by check).

Small business front desk/mailroom ad hoc stamp sale: clerk sells a few stamps or a metered-mail credit from a cash drawer, makes change from coins and bills, and reconciles the till and postage log at end of shift.
Roving interoffice round: clerk pushes a mail cart through office floors, takes stamp/postage requests at desks, hands over stamps or supplies, and collects cash or signed department charge slips.

Mail merchandise samples or promotional literature in response to requests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corporate/marketing mailroom, low-to-moderate daily volume: clerk works a queue of literature requests (web form, call center, trade-show leads), pulls the requested brochures, catalogs and price sheets from stock shelves, collates the kit, folds and stuffs a #10 or 9x12 envelope, seals it, prints/affixes the address label, runs it through the postage meter, and logs the request as fulfilled.

High-volume literature fulfillment run in a company mail center or lettershop: batch of hundreds to thousands of accumulated requests, variable enclosures per recipient, run on folding/inserting equipment with inline addressing and metering, then trayed/sacked and staged for USPS pickup.

Merchandise samples of small consumer goods (cosmetics packets, supplements, food samples, swatch cards, small SKUs) picked from bins or a sample room, placed in a poly mailer or padded envelope together with a literature insert, weighed, shipping label applied, and manifested with the carrier.

Bulky or irregular samples (hardware parts, fabric sample books, demo units, glass or fragile items) that need a right-sized carton, void fill/protection, dimension and weight capture, carrier label, and occasionally special-handling paperwork.

Ad hoc single request handled by a mixed-duty clerk at a desk in a general office: retrieve the item or brochure from a supply cabinet, hand-address or print a label, affix stamps or meter tape, and drop it in the outgoing mail bin.
