roles.title: Office Clerks, General
roles.description: Perform duties too varied and diverse to be classified in any specific office clerical occupation, requiring knowledge of office systems and procedures. Clerical duties may be assigned in accordance with the office procedures of individual establishments and may include a combination of answering telephones, bookkeeping, typing or word processing, office machine operation, and filing.

tasks.label: Operate office machines, such as photocopiers and scanners, facsimile machines, voice mail systems, and personal computers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Photocopying at a shared office multifunction printer: clerk carries a stapled 20-40 page report or a mixed stack of forms to the copier down the hall, removes staples, loads the document feeder (or lifts the lid for odd-sized/fragile originals), selects duplex/collate/staple/reduce settings on the touch panel, runs several sets, checks for skew or double-feeds, and retrieves and re-assembles originals plus copies.

Scanning/digitizing paper into PDFs: feeding invoices, personnel files, contracts, or receipts through an office scanner or MFP scan-to-email/scan-to-folder function, de-stapling and unfolding pages, rescanning misfeeds, then naming, indexing, and filing the resulting files in the document system.

Running other paper-path office machines: sending and retrieving faxes, running outgoing mail through a postage/folder-inserter machine, shredding confidential batches, laminating, binding/comb-punching, and printing labels — feeding stacks in, setting the machine, and collecting output.

Keying data from paper source documents into computer systems: reading invoices, forms, timesheets, or applications and entering fields into an ERP/records system or spreadsheet, with cross-checking against the paper original.

General personal-computer and phone-system operation: email, word processing, spreadsheets, calendar/scheduling, printing from applications, plus retrieving voice mail messages and forwarding or distributing them — output is entirely digital or verbal.

Keeping the machines running: refilling paper trays and specialty stock, swapping toner cartridges, clearing paper jams inside the copier, rebooting a frozen MFP, running cleaning cycles, and calling or waiting for the service technician.

sources.claim: Ripcord builds and commercially operates robotic cells that autonomously de-staple and scan paper documents at scale, run in its own dedicated digitization facilities in the US and Japan for enterprise customers.
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers the paper-handling core of the scanning/copying instances: unfastening stapled originals and feeding sheets through a scanning device at commercial quality and volume.

sources.claim: The Ripcord cell handles loose stacks of paper: an industrial robot with machine vision pulls staples and places sheets one at a time onto a ... for scanning at roughly one sheet per second.
sources.transferJustification: Same objects (loose and stapled office paper) and same manipulation (separating and feeding single sheets into a document machine) as clerical copying/scanning; the setting is a purpose-built robotic cell.

sources.title: Ripcord and VASTEC Merge to Scale AI-Powered Document Digitization

sources.transferJustification: Establishes present-day availability of the robotic paper-handling service and its extension from scanning to extracting indexed data from paper source documents (the keying-from-paper instance).

sources.system: Zund/RobotFactory sheet-handling cobot (and comparable Agfa, Durst systems)
sources.title: The Rise of Robotics: Automating Wide Format Print Production | FESPA
sources.claim: In commercial print production facilities, cobots from vendors such as Zund/RobotFactory, Agfa and Durst routinely load and unload sheets into presses and cutting tables, including registration steps so each sheet is placed precisely.
sources.transferJustification: Supplies the output side of copying/printing in a purpose-built cell: robotic loading of stock into a printing machine and removal of finished sheets, the same media handling a clerk does at a copier.

sources.title: Alphabet's X has 'Everyday Robots' test fleet that autonomously performs office maintenance tasks | 9to5Google
sources.claim: The most advanced autonomous mobile manipulation deployed inside real offices (Alphabet's Everyday Robots at Google Bay Area campuses) performed trash sorting, table wiping, cup grasping and door opening — not operation of copiers, scanners or other office machines.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound the E2 (as-found office) frontier: the tasks demonstrated are coarse cleaning and door opening, not de-stapling, feeder loading, touch-panel operation or jam clearing, so it does not transfer to office-machine operation.

sources.title: Figure-01: Humanoid Robot Learns to Make Coffee By Watching Videos
sources.claim: Figure 01 autonomously operated a capsule coffee machine end to end after learning from video — inserting the capsule, closing the lid and pressing the brew button — in a lab setting.
sources.transferJustification: Nearest general-purpose evidence for pressing controls on a human-designed machine; it is a single-button lab demo and does not cover multi-page paper handling, panel menu navigation, or output verification at an office MFP.

tasks.label: Maintain and update filing, inventory, mailing, and database systems, either manually or using a computer.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Front office of a clinic, law firm, school district or corporate department: the clerk sorts the day's accumulated paperwork (invoices, signed forms, correspondence, charts, receipts), matches each item to the right client/case/employee folder, creates and labels new folders, opens lateral or hanging-folder drawers and interfiles loose, stapled, mixed-size pages in sequence, and pulls and refiles folders requested during the day. Cabinets are crowded and folders are hand-labeled.

Desk work at a computer only: entering and correcting records in a database, spreadsheet or CRM/ERP (address changes, new customer/patient/student records, inventory quantities, vendor data), de-duplicating and cleaning mailing lists, running batch updates and verifying entries. No handling of physical objects beyond keyboard and mouse.

Office mailroom: opening and date-stamping incoming mail, sorting envelopes, flats and small parcels into departmental slots and mail bins, logging accountable items, preparing outgoing mail (folding, stuffing, metering), and updating the address/mailing-list database from returned mail and change-of-address notices.

Supply room or stockroom of an office, clinic or school: physically counting stock on shelves (paper, toner, forms, envelopes, PPE), comparing counts against par levels in the inventory spreadsheet or inventory-management software, updating quantities, flagging items for reorder, and putting away arriving deliveries.

Periodic records purge and archive: pulling folders past their retention date from cabinets, boxing and labeling cartons, updating the file index and retention log, and moving cartons to a basement storage room or staging them for offsite storage or shredding pickup.

sources.title: Ripcord uses robotics to digitize records, processes and avoid paper waste
sources.claim: Ripcord operates a purpose-built robotic facility where robots handle unstructured stacks of office paper (mixed sizes, staples, binders), sort and feed pages for scanning, and index them into a searchable digital records system at roughly a billion pages per year.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bulk records digitization. It is the physical core of maintaining a filing system - separating loose office paper item by item, classifying it with vision, and updating an indexed record system - on the same objects a clerk files, but in a machine-built facility.

sources.transferJustification: Same task family as mailroom maintenance: reading each mail item, looking it up in the address database, and physically placing it in the correct destination bin - the physical step of maintaining an office mailing/distribution system, in purpose-built equipment.

sources.title: Simbe's Tally Inventory Robot Deployed in Harmons Stores Following Pilot Success

sources.title: Pilot project takes automated inventory management to the next level | DC Velocity
sources.claim: Verity's autonomous inventory drones fly warehouse aisles unattended, scan barcode labels and photograph pallet locations, then transmit updated stock data to the warehouse management system; deployed commercially with logistics operators.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cycle counting stock. Structurally identical to maintaining an inventory record - locating stored items on shelving in a human work facility, reading their identifiers, and pushing corrected quantities into the inventory database.

sources.title: Restocking robots deployed in 300 Japanese convenience stores - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Telexistence's TX SCARA restocks refrigerated shelves with bottled and ... drinks in about 300 FamilyMart convenience stores, running autonomously under the GORDON AI with remote teleoperated recovery only when a problem occurs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shelf replenishment in a retail store. Putting away arriving supplies onto stockroom shelving is the same grasp-and-place of boxed/bottled consumables in an institution-controlled facility, with only occasional remote assistance.

sources.title: Swisslog Healthcare Partners with Diligent Robotics to Enhance Hospital Logistics
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi mobile manipulator is deployed in more than 25 ..., autonomously fetching and delivering supplies, medications and specimens over corridor routes, with more than one million deliveries completed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: intra-building item transport. Shows autonomous fetch-and-carry of small items inside a people-occupied institutional building - the transport component of mail distribution and supply/records movement - but not paper filing or counting.

sources.title: From case unloading to picking and beyond with DHL and Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Stretch performs autonomous case handling (unloading cartons from containers) in DHL warehouses, with ten robots in production use across three countries as of June 2025.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: carton handling. Moving labeled records cartons is the same object class and precision as case unloading, though Stretch works only on presented stacks in logistics facilities, not on office cabinets.

sources.title: Vertical Carousel Module (VCM) | Megamat Solution for Offices
sources.claim: Kardex Megamat vertical carousels are software-controlled automated storage and retrieval machines marketed for office file and record rooms; they hold the equivalent of many filing cabinets and deliver requested files to an operator access point.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physical file storage and retrieval. Shows purpose-built machinery handling the storage/retrieval half of paper filing under database control, though a person still inserts and removes documents at the access point.

sources.title: PP-Tac: Paper Picking Using Tactile Feedback in Dexterous Robotic Hands
sources.claim: Grasping single sheets from a stack with dexterous robot hands remains a laboratory research problem, with reported success rates around 87 percent, below clerical reliability.

instances.label: Front counter collection: at a small office reception window (medical/dental practice, school, municipal or utility office, storage or repair shop) the clerk takes a walk-in payment in cash, check or card, verifies the bills, makes change from a drawer, prints or writes a receipt, and posts the payment to the customer's account. Disbursing money: issuing petty cash to employees against approved receipts, funding tills/floats and event cash boxes, handing out paychecks or cash payment envelopes, paying a COD delivery, and logging each disbursement against the voucher.

Basic bookkeeping with paperwork at a desk: opening mail containing checks and invoices, sorting and coding paper receipts and invoices, keying them into QuickBooks or a spreadsheet, reconciling the monthly bank statement, and filing the paper in binders or cabinets.

tasks.label: Complete and mail bills, contracts, policies, invoices, or checks.

instances.label: Routine customer invoice/statement run in a small-to-midsize office (20-300 pieces, weekly or monthly): clerk generates the invoices in the accounting system, prints them at a shared office printer, checks amounts and addresses, folds and stuffs them into #10 window envelopes, seals, runs them through a postage meter or applies stamps, and puts them in the outgoing-mail bin for carrier pickup.

Accounts-payable check run: clerk prints checks on MICR/preprinted stock from the accounting system, matches each check to its remittance stub/invoice copy, routes for authorized signature, verifies payee and amount, stuffs and seals double-window envelopes, meters postage, and mails; secure handling and no mismatches required.

Ad-hoc single items: complete an individual form, contract, policy endorsement, or one-off bill (fill in fields, attach the right enclosure, confirm the signature is present), copy for the file, hand-address or print a single envelope, apply postage - sometimes certified mail/return receipt - and drop it in outgoing mail or take it to the post office.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Office multifunction copier/printer fails mid-job: paper jam, misfeed, low or streaking toner, empty tray. The clerk walks to the copier alcove, reads the panel code, opens doors and drawers, pulls crumpled or torn sheets out of rollers and the fuser/duplexer, reseats or swaps a toner cartridge, reloads paper, closes panels, power-cycles, and runs a test print to confirm the fix.

A coworker's desktop or laptop has a software problem: application freezes or crashes, a file won't open, print queue stuck, wrong printer driver, email/VPN/login or password issue, pending updates. The clerk sits at the user's desk, operates mouse and keyboard, checks settings, clears the queue, reinstalls a driver, reboots, and confirms the user can work.

A desk-side connection fault: network cable unplugged or loose at the wall jack or NIC, patch cord in the wrong port, dead network link. The clerk traces the cable under the desk, reseats or re-patches it, and confirms connectivity is restored.

A desk-side peripheral or power fault: blank monitor, dead keyboard/mouse/headset/webcam, docking station not detected, power strip switched off, laptop not charging. The clerk checks power and USB/HDMI connections in cluttered footwells, swaps in a spare peripheral or dock from the supply cabinet, power-cycles, and verifies the user's setup works.

Shared office machines other than PCs and copiers: conference-room projector or video-conference system not showing a laptop over HDMI/wireless display, desk phone or headset not registering, shredder jam, scanner feeder misfeed, postage/label machine or laminator fault. The clerk goes to the room, tries cables/inputs/settings, clears the jam, and restores service before a meeting.

Problem exceeds the clerk's ability: they document symptoms, run the vendor's guided diagnostics, phone IT or the copier/equipment vendor, arrange service, meet and escort the technician, hand over or pack and ship the failed unit, set the user up on a loaner, and verify the repair when it returns.

instances.label: General office / in-house copy room: operator squares a stack of 20-200 loose letter- or legal-size originals (memos, invoices, forms of mixed condition), sets the paper guides, drops the stack in the ADF feed tray of a walk-up copier/MFP and starts the run, clearing occasional misfeeds and re-feeding skewed sheets.

Production scanning bureau or digital mailroom: shift-long batch work at a high-volume production scanner - taking prepped batches off a cart, loading the elevator feed tray repeatedly, keeping batch separators/patch sheets in order, re-feeding rejected sheets, against throughput and image-quality targets.

Document prep and single-sheet feeding of problem originals: pulling staples, clips and bindings, unfolding creased or torn pages, taping repairs, then feeding sheets one at a time into the feed rolls of a scanner or copier so nothing jams or tears.

Library / archive / records digitization lab: positioning bound volumes, ledgers, loose photographs and archival documents on the copy table or cradle beneath an overhead camera, squaring them to registration marks, turning pages and repositioning between exposures without damaging the item.

Oversize and special originals: bound newspaper volumes, maps, blueprints and engineering drawings laid on a large copy table under an overhead camera or fed into wide-format feed rolls, aligned by hand and often re-shot.

On-site / mobile scanning job in a client's storage room, basement or field office taken as found: boxes stacked on the floor, no fixed layout, portable scanner set up on a folding table, originals of unknown condition fed by hand.

instances.label: In-house or commercial copy/print center: operator runs high-speed production copiers/printers — loads paper stock into trays and high-capacity feeders from cartons/pallets, keys or downloads the job (counts, duplex, tabs, stapling), monitors run quality, clears misfeeds and jams, replenishes toner, and unloads/checks finished sets for multiple concurrent jobs on varied stock.

tasks.label: Clean machines, perform minor repairs, and report major repair needs.

instances.label: Routine cleaning of a photocopier/MFD or duplicator in an office or in-house copy center: wipe the platen glass and document feeder, dust the exterior and control panel, wipe toner dust off accessible feed rollers and paper-path guides, empty the waste-toner container.

Clearing paper jams and misfeeds on a high-volume copier, duplicator or finisher: open doors and side panels, pull levers, extract crumpled or torn sheets from rollers/fuser/stapler-finisher, verify no scraps remain, close panels and reset the machine.

Consumable and small part replacement: swap toner or drum cartridges, staple cartridges, waste-toner bottles; replace worn pickup/feed rollers, o-rings or belts using simple hand tools; run the machine's calibration/test print afterward.

Mailroom/bindery machine upkeep: on folder-inserters, collators, addressing machines and postage meters, brush out paper chaff and dust, oil/lubricate points, replace worn feed tires, adjust paper guides and separators, clear feed jams.

Diagnosing a fault beyond minor repair and reporting it: notice streaked copies, grinding noise, repeat jams or an error code, check the machine, then log a service call to the vendor/facilities with a description of the symptom and code, and tag the machine out of service.

instances.label: In-plant/commercial copy or print center: operator runs a guillotine (programmable) paper cutter — jogs and squares piles of printed sheets, sets or recalls the cut program, clamps and makes a sequence of cuts to trim jobs to final size, checks squareness/size, and offloads trimmed lifts. Runs range from a few hundred to several thousand sheets with frequent job changeovers.

Print shop or mailroom: operator sets up and runs a buckle/knife folding machine for letters, brochures and signatures — sets fold plates/rollers for the fold pattern, loads the feeder pile, makes a test fold, runs the job, clears misfeeds and double-feeds, and jogs/stacks folded output onto pallets or into boxes.

Copy center bindery: operator runs a collator/booklet-making line (tower collator feeding a saddle stitcher-folder-face trimmer) — loads bins with collated sets, sets stitch positions and trim, runs the job, clears jams and misfeeds, checks page order and stitch placement, and offloads finished booklets.

Print/copy center: operator runs a paper drilling/punching machine (three-hole drill for binder inserts, or punch for wire/comb binding) and a perforating unit — sets hole pattern and backgauge, lifts stacks into the machine, drills/punches each lift, clears chips, and stacks punched output.

Print shop: operator runs a pad/tablet making operation — counts and jogs sheets into pad-size lifts with chipboard backs, loads them into a padding press or automated hot-melt padder, applies/sets adhesive, lets pads set, then breaks/cuts the padded block into individual pads.

Mail production room: operator runs a high-volume folder-inserter/collating line for statements or direct mail — programs the job, loads document and insert feeders, monitors OMR/barcode integrity, clears jams and misfeeds, reruns exceptions, and boxes/trays the sealed pieces.

tasks.label: Maintain stock of supplies, and requisition any needed items.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corporate/agency copy center or mailroom: operator makes a routine round of the copiers, printers and mail machines and the adjoining supply closet, visually checking levels of letter/legal/11x17 and colored stock, toner/ink cartridges, staples, envelopes and labels against par levels, then enters a requisition in the purchasing system.

Point-of-use replenishment: pulling reams and cases of paper, toner cartridges and other consumables out of the central stockroom, moving them by cart across a floor or building, and stocking the cabinets/shelves beside each machine so the machines never run dry mid-shift.

In-plant print shop or high-volume duplicating operation: bulk paper delivery arrives at the dock on pallets/cases; operator verifies quantities against the packing slip, moves pallets with a jack or hand truck into the stockroom, stacks and rotates stock, and breaks cases down onto racks.

Long-tail specialty consumables and vendor handling: tracking dozens of model-specific toner/drum/ink SKUs, binding combs, laminating film, photographic media and chemicals; checking condition and expiry, boxing used cartridges for return, placing SKU-specific orders and chasing backorders.

Periodic full physical inventory or cycle count of the supply room before a busy period: counting every item on the shelves, reconciling counts with the stock records, and requisitioning quantities needed to bring stock back to par.

tasks.label: Prepare and process papers for use in scanning, microfilming, and microfiche.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Back-file conversion at a document imaging/records service center: worker pulls files from boxes, removes staples, clips, binder rings and rubber bands, unfolds and flattens creased sheets, mends torn edges, sorts into batches, inserts barcode/separator sheets, loads production scanner hoppers, clears jams and rescans rejects, then re-boxes or shreds. Mixed weights and sizes of ordinary office paper, carbonless forms, receipts.

Day-forward in-house scanning in a business office or back office: small mixed batches of invoices, applications, HR forms and signed contracts brought to a departmental scanner or MFP; destaple, straighten, remove sticky notes, scan duplex, check image quality on screen, name/index the file, then re-staple and refile or place in shred bin.

Mailroom / digital-mail operation: open incoming envelopes, extract and unfold contents, discard envelopes or retain as an image, separate checks and remittance stubs, prep and feed into the scanner, route images to the correct queue. High daily volume, deadline-driven.

Healthcare HIM or law-firm records unit: prepare patient charts or case files for scanning/microfilming - remove two-prong fasteners, tabs and adhesive labels, photocopy odd-size items (EKG strips, ID cards, half-sheets) onto letter carriers, order pages, insert document-type separator sheets, scan and index to the chart. Confidential material, chain-of-custody rules.

Library/archive or government records unit preparing fragile historical material for imaging or microfilming: loose-leaf registration cards, ledgers and bound volumes; remove rusted fasteners, flatten, place targets and index/eye-mark sheets, capture on planetary camera or book scanner, verify frame counts and film/image quality.

Oversized and damaged material prep: D/E-size engineering drawings, maps and blueprints that must be unrolled and weighted, brittle or water-damaged records requiring tape repair, encapsulation or de-binding before large-format scanning or microfilming; each item judged and handled individually.

instances.label: In-plant/small-shop offset duplicator operator: after a run, strips the paper or aluminum plate off the duplicator drum, wipes ink off with plate cleaner, applies gum/preservative, slips it into the job envelope and files it in the plate cabinet by job number for reprints.

tasks.label: Move heat units and clamping frames over screen beds to form Braille impressions on pages, raising frames to release individual copies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Braille press / duplication room of a nonprofit braille producer or state library for the blind: a long production run of thermoform (Brailon) copies from one braille text master — place master on the screen/vacuum bed, lay a Brailon sheet, close the clamping frame, slide the heat unit over, dwell, apply vacuum, raise the frame, strip the formed copy and stack it, repeated dozens to hundreds of times.

School district / agency transcription office: small runs of 1–10 thermoform copies of worksheets, tests or handouts from freshly brailled masters, with frequent master changes, mixed page sizes, and a same-day deadline for a student's class.

Tactile graphics and maps: thermoforming over a raised-line or collage master (glued textures, string, thin 3-D objects); careful master positioning, adjusted heat/dwell so fine detail forms without scorching, gentle release of the hot sheet so dots and textures are not crushed or torn, then visual/tactile check of fidelity.

Large-format or heavy-gauge work on a big-bed machine (e.g., 15x20 in maps, charts, thicker Brailon): heavier clamping frame and longer heat cycles, followed by trimming, hole-punching and collating of the released copies into sets.

Problem cycles during a run: warped, scorched, or incompletely formed copies from vacuum leaks, master misalignment, or wrong dwell; the operator re-seats the master, adjusts timer/heat, discards rejects and re-runs until copies meet the reading-quality standard.

sources.system: ILLIG IC-RDKP 72k automatic pressure forming machine
sources.date: 2026-07 (page retrieved); machine line commercially available for years

sources.claim: Commercial industrial thermoformers run the full forming cycle — actuated clamping frame, heating, vacuum/pressure forming over a mould, and part release — automatically at high cycle rates in a fenced production machine, which is the same physical process as Brailon braille duplication over a braille master.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic vacuum/pressure thermoforming of thin plastic sheet over a mould with a clamping frame. Braille thermoform duplication is the identical process (Brailon sheet clamped over a braille master, heated, vacuum-formed, frame raised, copy released); braille dot relief (~0.5 mm) is far coarser than the surface detail industrial thermoformers routinely reproduce, and the machine both clamps and releases parts without an operator.

instances.label: Row-crop/produce farm: supervisor walks the field during harvest or thinning, watching a 15-30 person crew for PPE use, knife/tool handling, heat-illness signs, water/shade breaks, and safe distance from tractors and harvest rigs; verbally corrects violators on the spot in Spanish or English.

Logging site: supervisor observes fallers, skidder and loader operators for hard hats, chaps, eye/ear protection, escape routes, and safe working distances under the canopy and around machinery; stops unsafe work and issues a verbal warning or sends a repeat violator home.

Commercial fishing vessel or aquaculture pen: deck boss watches crew during gear setting and hauling for PFD/immersion-suit use, keeping clear of winches, lines and net drums, and safe knife/hatch practices; shouts warnings over engine and weather noise and pulls a violator off the deck.

Nursery, greenhouse, or packing shed: supervisor monitors workers around conveyors, forklifts, sprayers and chemical mixing areas for respirators, gloves, lockout practices and re-entry intervals; corrects violations and re-instructs the worker.

Livestock, dairy, or feedlot operation: supervisor watches handlers in alleys, chutes, milking parlors and around silage equipment for safe animal-handling positioning, PTO/guard compliance and confined-space rules; warns workers who cut corners.

Follow-up and formal discipline: supervisor documents repeat violations, delivers a written warning or suspension in a meeting with the worker (and sometimes HR or the crew leader), reviews the rule violated, and covers the incident in the next toolbox/tailgate safety talk.

tasks.label: Observe animals for signs of illness, injury, or unusual behavior, notifying veterinarians or managers as warranted.

instances.label: Confinement dairy (100-2,000 cows): herd supervisor walks freestall barns and watches cows at the parlor/robot each day, looking for mastitis, off-feed or non-milking cows, lameness, injuries, and calving trouble; flags animals and calls the herd vet.

Beef feedlot or backgrounding yard: pen riding once or twice daily through pens of 100-300 head, spotting early bovine respiratory disease signs (droopy ears, nasal discharge, gaunt flank, altered gait), pulling suspects to the hospital pen and notifying the consulting vet/manager.

Pasture/rangeland cattle or sheep: supervisor checks stock spread over hundreds to thousands of acres by truck, ATV or horseback, looking for downed, cast, injured, sick, birthing or missing animals in variable terrain and weather; reports to owner/vet.

Commercial poultry house (broiler, breeder or layer): daily walk-throughs of houses holding 20,000-50,000 birds, counting and removing mortality, culling, spotting lame, panting or respiratory-affected birds and abnormal flock distribution; reports to complex manager or service technician.

Swine barn (finishing or sow unit): pen-by-pen daily check for scours, coughing, lameness, prolapse, tail bites and off-feed pigs, marking pigs for treatment and notifying the farm vet or production manager.

Aquaculture site (catfish/tilapia ponds, trout raceways, hatchery tanks, or marine net pens): observing feeding response, swimming behavior, surface/flashing behavior, lesions or parasites and daily mortalities; notifying fish health specialist or manager.

tasks.label: Observe fish and beds or ponds to detect diseases, monitor fish growth, determine quality of fish, or determine completeness of harvesting.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pond farm (channel catfish, baitfish, tilapia, hybrid striped bass) in the Delta/Southeast: supervisor drives levee roads on daily rounds, watches feeding response at the feed line, scans banks and surface for sick, circling or dead fish, and nets moribund fish for closer examination or lab submission. Outdoor earthen ponds, turbid green water, weather and wildlife present.

Hatchery, raceway or indoor RAS facility (trout, salmon smolt, bass, ornamentals): supervisor walks tanks and raceways checking fry/fingerlings for fungus, gill problems, abnormal swimming and mortalities, dip-nets sample fish to weigh and measure for growth against the feed chart, and checks size uniformity before grading. Clear water, fixed layout, controlled access.

Shellfish beds and leases (oyster, clam) intertidal or subtidal: supervisor works from a boat or the flats, pulling bags/cages or sampling bottom stock to check for gapers and mortality, disease and fouling, measures shell size and meat condition to judge growth and market readiness. Tidal, variable bottom, weather-dependent.

Harvest supervision at a pond seine, bed dredging, or pen crowding: supervisor inspects the catch coming aboard or into the live-haul truck for size uniformity, sores, off-flavor and blemishes, and judges whether the harvest is complete — whether marketable fish remain in the pond or stock remains on the bed — before releasing the crew.

Marine net-pen site (Atlantic salmon in Maine, kampachi in Hawaii, offshore cages): supervisor observes fish through surface behaviour, underwater cameras or a dive, counts sea lice and mortalities, assesses condition and wounds, and tracks average weight/biomass to set feeding and harvest timing. Moored pens at a permitted, company-controlled site.

instances.label: Logging crew: supervisor runs a pre-shift tailgate/toolbox safety meeting at the landing or shop, covering OSHA/state logging safety regulations, PPE, escape routes, hazard trees, and incident review; verbal instruction plus handouts and sign-off sheets.

Field instruction of a new or less-experienced cutter in felling and bucking: explaining and showing face-notch and back-cut geometry, hinge wood, wedging, lean assessment, bucking bind and escape paths, then watching the trainee's cuts and correcting technique on the spot in standing timber.

Training an operator on machinery — skidder, knuckleboom loader, forwarder, or farm tractor — by walking through controls and pre-operation checks, riding along or coaching from the ground on yarding, decking, and loading technique, and evaluating the trainee's proficiency.

Agricultural/aquacultural crew leader briefing seasonal or new hires at the start of a season on tractor and implement operation, PTO and rollover hazards, chemical and machinery safety rules, often bilingually and with a mix of demonstration and Q&A.

Administrative side of training: reviewing updated regulations and company procedures, preparing lesson content or videos, documenting competency evaluations and certifications, and debriefing individual workers after a near-miss or performance issue.

tasks.label: Treat animal illnesses or injuries, following experience or instructions of veterinarians.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dairy/confinement cattle: a cow flagged sick (metritis, pneumonia, retained placenta) is restrained at a headlock or parlor exit and given the systemic injectable drug and dose specified in the herd health protocol the veterinarian wrote; treatment and milk-withhold are logged and repeated on schedule.

Dairy/confinement cattle: non-injectable individual treatments per veterinary instruction - intramammary mastitis tubes, oral drenches and boluses (ketosis, bloat), IV calcium for milk fever, hoof block/wrap for a claw lesion, cleaning and dressing a laceration or abscess.

Beef feedlot/backgrounding yard: supervisor rides pens, pulls cattle showing respiratory disease, foot rot or pinkeye, runs them into a hydraulic squeeze chute, checks temperature, administers the prescribed injectable antibiotic/anti-inflammatory, tags and records, and moves the animal to a hospital pen for re-check.

Range/pasture cattle and small ruminants: locate a sick or injured animal in a paddock or corral, catch and restrain it, then pare and treat foot rot, dress a wound or calving injury, treat a prolapse, or drench - work done in the open with portable equipment and variable footing.

Swine and poultry confinement barns: inject individual sick or lame pigs and dress tail-bite wounds and hernias, mix medication into a group's drinking water per the veterinarian's prescription, and walk houses to identify, treat or cull moribund birds.

Aquaculture farm site: carry out the health treatments in the site's fish health plan on stock in cages or tanks - control and removal of sea lice and other parasites, bath or in-feed medication, and vaccination of the stock.

tasks.label: Inspect crops, fields, or plant stock to determine conditions and need for cultivating, spraying, weeding, or harvesting.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Row-crop supervisor (corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton) makes an in-season scouting round over several hundred acres: walks/drives transects to assess stand and vigor, weed escapes, foliar disease and insect pressure, and growth stage, then decides which fields need a herbicide/fungicide/insecticide pass or cultivation this week. Open fields, variable terrain, weather, wide area to cover.

Fresh-market vegetable or berry field supervisor walks blocks before/during harvest to judge maturity, size and quality by block, decide which blocks the crew cuts or picks today and which need another day, and flag weed or pest pressure needing cultivation or spraying. Open in-soil beds, plastic mulch, irrigation lines, crews working nearby.

Orchard or vineyard supervisor inspects blocks ahead of harvest passes: fruit maturity, color/size distribution and crop load per tree or vine, to set picking sequence and crew assignments. Outdoor trellised or tree rows, uneven ground, canopy occlusion.

Orchard or vineyard supervisor makes a pest-and-disease scouting round: examines canopy and undersides of leaves for mildew, mites, scale, borers, checks traps, and assesses ground weed pressure, then determines spray timing and material. Requires close-up, hands-on canopy examination across blocks.

Greenhouse or propagation nursery supervisor inspects plant stock on benches/trays/pot beds: germination and dropouts, uniformity and growth stage, pests and disease spots, dryness, and saleable readiness, then directs spraying, spacing, watering or shipping. Indoor structure with fixed rows, standard trays/benches, controlled access.

Forestry supervisor inspects a plantation or stand: seedling survival and vigor, competing brush needing release treatment, insect/disease damage, and whether a stand or block is ready for thinning/harvest. Rough terrain, slash, brush, no maintained layout.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Irrigation/water-management move on a row-crop or hay farm: the supervisor plans and works with a 2-4 person crew to break down portable hand lines or wheel lines, pull suction and discharge pipe, load a portable pump/filter station, haul it across fields and farm roads to a new field, then set, level, couple, prime and pressure-test the system. Mud, uneven ground, ditches, fences, weather-driven timing.

Logging show move: supervisor coordinates a crew relocating yarder/tower, loader, skidders and support equipment to a new landing - unrigging skyline, guylines, blocks and straps from stumps and tail trees, walking or lowbedding machines over steep skid roads, then re-setting the tower, anchoring guylines, stringing skyline and rigging the carriage before production resumes.

Indoor plant/facility setup: nursery, greenhouse, hatchery or packing-shed supervisor coordinates moving and re-erecting equipment inside a company building - potting/seeding lines, conveyors, graders, benches, pumps, tanks - unbolting from floor, disconnecting power/water lines, moving on pallet jacks or forklifts, re-anchoring, leveling, reconnecting utilities and test-running.

Aquaculture/fishing gear relocation: supervisor coordinates crew and vessel/crane to move net pens, cages, moorings, feed lines and dockside handling gear to a new lease or site, or to strike and reset processing/grading gear; work over water, on decks and docks, with lines, shackles and chain, under weather and tide constraints.

Field machinery move between farms or fields (custom harvest, tillage, spraying crews): supervisor coordinates removing headers/toolbar wings, folding and pinning implements, disconnecting hydraulic and electrical couplers, loading on trailers or road-transporting, then reassembling, greasing, calibrating and test-running at the new site's yard and field.

instances.label: Row-crop / produce field walk-or-drive: a crop farm supervisor moves through planted fields checking stand and emergence, weed and insect pressure, disease spots, irrigation and drainage problems, and crop stage, to decide what crews should spray, cultivate, irrigate or harvest next. Ranch/pasture round: a livestock foreman drives or rides pastures and range checking fence lines and gates for breaks, water tanks/troughs and floats, mineral feeders, forage condition and cattle, to determine fence repair, water hauling, feeding or moving work. Large, unimproved outdoor acreage.

Logging site or forest tract / outdoor fishery site inspection: a logging or fishing supervisor walks an active cutting unit, landing, skid trails and haul roads (or a fishing/aquaculture site and its gear) to judge ground conditions, hazards, timber, road damage and gear condition, and assign the day's work. Site taken as found, changes daily.

Machinery and equipment check in the shop or equipment yard: pre-season or pre-shift inspection of tractors, harvesters, sprayers, ATVs, chainsaws and implements — tires, hoses, belts, fluid levels, leaks, guards, wear parts and damage — to generate the repair, service and parts list. Farm-controlled shop/yard, standard equipment.

Buildings and production facilities: barns, poultry/dairy houses, greenhouses, packing sheds, hatchery/aquaculture rooms — checking structure and doors, ventilation and heating, lighting, feeders and waterers, bedding/litter, leaks and sanitation, to determine repair, cleaning and adjustment work. Institution-controlled, fixed layout.

Supplies check in storage buildings: counting and inspecting seed, feed, chemicals, fertilizer, fuel, parts, packaging and PPE on racks and pallets, spotting damaged, expired or short stock, to determine ordering and restocking work. Enclosed farm storage/warehouse.

instances.label: Periodic walk-through of an active irrigation installation on farmland: crews trenching with a backhoe/plow, laying mainline PVC or poly, glued/fused joints, valves and drip or sprinkler laterals. Supervisor checks line routing against the plan, trench depth and bedding before backfill, joint workmanship, fitting sizes, and safety, and directs the crew or contractor to correct deviations. Muddy, rutted, changing field conditions with running equipment.

Overseeing erection of a horticultural building at a nursery/greenhouse operation (hoop house, gutter-connect greenhouse, headhouse or pack shed): checking foundation/anchor layout, frame plumb and squareness, purlin and glazing/poly installation, vents, heaters and electrical rough-in against drawings; verifying material deliveries and contractor progress; flagging defects for rework. Partially enclosed, cluttered active build site.

Commissioning and acceptance of a finished irrigation system: charging the mainline, pressure-testing, walking each zone with the controller running, looking and listening for leaks and blown fittings, checking emitter/nozzle flow and coverage, adjusting sprinkler heads and pressure regulators, then signing off or issuing a punch list. Outdoor field/orchard, wet ground, spray.

Routine progress documentation and status reporting on an ongoing farm construction project: a scheduled visit to record what has been built since the last visit, capture photos/measurements of as-built work versus the plan and schedule, quantify earthwork or installed lengths, and produce the record used for the owner/manager progress report and pay applications. Outdoor site, largely observational.

Overseeing smaller farm infrastructure builds by contractors: pump house and well hookup, drainage tile installation, culvert or farm road work, tank pads, fencing for a new planting. Supervisor verifies grade/depth, alignment, materials and connections, coordinates access and utility locates, and accepts the work. Remote, rough, unimproved ground.

Field crew shift start-up and shutdown: supervisor hands out pruners, knives, hoes, gloves/PPE and orchard ladders from a crew truck or field trailer to individual workers, then counts, inspects and stows everything at day's end. Roadside/field-edge staging, no fixed layout.

Farm shop / equipment yard: supervisor assigns tractors, ATVs, sprayers and implements to operators — issues keys, confirms the unit is fueled and serviceable, then receives the machine back at day's end and checks its condition and fuel.

Nursery, greenhouse or packing shed: supervisor issues carts, trolleys, trays and containers to crews at their work stations and retrieves them when the run is finished. Fixed indoor/covered layout controlled by the operation.

Fishing vessel or aquaculture site: supervisor issues gear (knives, gloves, foul-weather gear, dip nets, totes, buckets) to the crew dockside or on deck before the trip/shift and collects, rinses and stows it afterwards.

instances.label: In-field breakdown during fieldwork (also on a fishing vessel deck or logging landing): supervisor is called to a stopped tractor, combine, baler, skidder or deck winch, diagnoses the fault by look/sound/feel, and works alongside the operator to fix it — replace a burst hydraulic hose or belt, splice a chain, free a plugged header or net drum, replace a bearing or shear bolt — using hand tools, jacks and salvaged parts on uneven ground, in dust, mud or spray, with the crop or catch waiting.

Hands-on setup or field adjustment of an implement with tools before or between passes: setting planter seed depth and row cleaners, swapping and calibrating spray nozzles and checking output per acre, squaring and leveling a tillage tool, setting header height/reel position, adjusting mower blades or cutter bar, tightening chains and belts — done at the field edge or in the farmyard on the machine as it sits.

Keeping a working machine adjusted to hold output quality during operation: watching grain loss, tailings and grain damage behind a combine and changing fan speed, sieve and concave settings; holding sprayer boom height and application rate; maintaining planter row-unit downforce as soil conditions change across the field. Supervisor directs the operator to make these settings changes on the go.

Scheduled service and minor repair in the farm shop or equipment yard, machine brought in and parked: grease points, change oil, fuel and hydraulic filters, sharpen mower blades or saw chains, change or repair a wheel/tire, weld a cracked bracket, replace lights and wiring, charge batteries — a mixed list of jobs on varied makes and ages of equipment, with parts and tools on hand.

Irrigation and field infrastructure repair: locating and fixing a leak in mainline or drip tape, replacing sprinkler heads and clogged emitters, unsticking or re-aligning a center-pivot tower, servicing a well or booster pump, repairing gates and fence-line feeders — outdoors in the field or orchard, often in mud and standing water, with the crew held up.

Fixed equipment inside a livestock barn, dairy parlor, greenhouse or packing shed: adjusting or repairing auger feeders and waterers, ventilation fans and controllers, milking units and vacuum lines, greenhouse irrigation booms and heaters, grading/conveyor lines — indoors on a known layout, but with animals, plants or product present and production continuing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Slaughter-line postmortem inspection in a meat or poultry establishment: examining every carcass and its viscera at line speed for disease, contamination and defects, directing trim/retain/condemn actions and checking humane handling.

Facility compliance verification in a food, dairy or seafood processing plant: walking the plant during operations, checking equipment and product-contact-surface sanitation, temperatures, pest control and employee practices, collecting samples, reviewing HACCP/SSOP records and writing noncompliance records.

Grading and condition inspection of commodity lots at packinghouses, egg plants, cold storages and terminal markets: drawing samples from cartons or lines of fruit, vegetables, nuts, eggs, processed products or fish fillets, scoring defects against grade standards and certifying the lot.

Grain and oilseed inspection at country elevators and export terminals: probing trucks, railcars or barges, dividing samples, determining moisture, test weight, damaged kernels, foreign material and insect infestation, and assigning the grade.

Field compliance inspections of operations taken as found: farms, orchards, nurseries, dairies, feedlots, pesticide applicators, organic operations, timber harvest sites and fishing vessels or docks — driving to the site, observing practices and equipment, sampling crops/animals/soil/product, interviewing the operator and writing findings.

Measurement and grading of logs and landed fish at log landings, mill gates and docks: scaling truckloads of logs for volume and grade, or grading landed fish and shellfish against size/quality standards.

tasks.label: Inspect the cleanliness and practices of establishment employees.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: USDA FSIS in-plant inspector on a beef/pork/poultry slaughter and fabrication floor: during the shift, walks the kill floor and cut lines observing employees' sanitary dress (frocks, hairnets, beard nets, gloves), hand and glove washing, knife/steel sterilization at the 180F cabinet, and handling that could contaminate carcasses; wet, cold, noisy, slippery, with moving lines and knife-wielding workers; judges regulatory significance and writes a noncompliance record discussed with plant management.

Inspector at a further-processing / ready-to-eat or egg-products establishment: observes gowning and hand-hygiene at entry and during production, glove changes after contact with floors or raw product, employee traffic between raw and RTE zones, eating/drinking/jewelry rules, and personal-hygiene practices at workstations; documents findings and verifies corrective actions.

Produce packinghouse / packing-shed inspection under the FSMA Produce Safety Rule or a buyer audit: observes sorting and packing-line workers' hand-washing at stations, glove and apron use, hair restraints, sick-worker and cut/wound policies, and handling of packed product; interviews workers and supervisors and records observations.

Grade A dairy farm/milking-parlor inspection: observes milkers' hand cleanliness and glove use, udder prep and towel handling, clean outer garments, and sanitary handling of milk-contact equipment; farm layouts differ site to site, with live animals, manure, mud and variable lighting.

Seafood/fish processing plant sanitation-HACCP inspection: observes employee hygiene on wet, slippery filleting and picking lines - hand-washing frequency, glove and apron condition, cross-contact between raw fish and finished product, use of hand-dips - and documents sanitation-control deficiencies.

On-farm harvest crew inspection in an open field or orchard: observes harvesters' hygiene practices, use of portable toilets and field hand-wash units, cleanliness of gloves, harvest knives and bins, and adherence to worker health/hygiene requirements; terrain, weather and crew position change continuously.

sources.system: Spot (with Orbit AI inspection), Boston Dynamics
sources.title: Cargill Deploys Boston Dynamics' Robot Dog at Amsterdam Facility | Food Engineering
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot performs autonomous inspection rounds inside a food-processing plant (Cargill Amsterdam Multiseed crush and refinery), capturing thermal, acoustic and visual ... on equipment; the deployment covers machine condition and hazards, not judgments about employees' hygiene practices.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous mobile inspection rounds inside a food plant (an E2 facility). It establishes navigation and sensing in this environment, but it does not transfer to inspecting employees: the robot evaluates fixed equipment against thermal/acoustic thresholds, whereas the task requires observing moving people's behavior (hand-washing technique, glove changes, cross-contamination) and rendering a regulatory compliance judgment.

sources.system: Spot with Orbit AI visual inspection
sources.title: Spot at Cargill | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' published Cargill case study describes Spot's optical camera as capturing snapshots for visual safety checks and its acoustic sensor as detecting leaks - equipment- and hazard-oriented checks, with no capability described for assessing worker hygiene practices.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (autonomous plant inspection). Cited to show the scope of what the most capable deployed inspection robot actually judges - gauges, leaks, thermal anomalies - which does not include employee cleanliness or work practices.

sources.system: AI hand-hygiene monitoring (depth sensors/computer vision), Stanford / Lucile Packard Children's Hospital
sources.title: Improving Hospital Hand Hygiene: The Solution May Lie with AI | Stanford Medicine
sources.claim: The closest demonstrated automation of human hand-hygiene compliance monitoring uses fixed ceiling cameras with computer vision in a hospital, not an embodied robot; such camera/software systems are excluded from consideration as robotic systems.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated monitoring of personnel hand-hygiene compliance. It cannot substantiate a positive judgment here because it is a fixed-camera software system with no physical embodiment, and it scores a single scripted behavior rather than performing an inspector's roving assessment and documented compliance finding.

sources.developer: Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) researchers
sources.title: An Autonomous Robot-Aided Auditing Scheme for Floor Cleaning (Sensors)
sources.claim: Research mobile robots that audit cleanliness are limited to assessing floor/surface cleaning quality in a mapped area; they are laboratory prototypes and do not observe or evaluate people's hygiene practices.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous auditing of cleanliness. It does not transfer: the audited object is a static floor surface sampled by a touch/vision sensor, whereas this task requires continuous behavioral observation of workers and a regulatory judgment about their practices.

tasks.label: Verify that transportation and handling procedures meet regulatory requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Livestock humane-handling verification at a slaughter establishment: inspector stands at the unloading chute and holding pens, watches drivers and plant crew unload cattle/hogs, checks for downers, overcrowding, injured animals, improper prod use and trailer condition, and documents compliance or writes a noncompliance record (HATS Category II truck unloading).

Refrigerated or dry-van food shipment check at a processing plant, packinghouse or distribution center dock: inspector opens the trailer, checks interior cleanliness, off-odors, infestation, damage and pre-cooling, verifies pulp/air temperatures and reefer settings, watches loading/stacking practice, and clears or rejects the load under sanitary-transport requirements.

Bulk carrier stowage/handling examination at a grain elevator, river terminal or export dock: inspector examines empty truck hoppers, railcars, barge holds or ship holds for residues, insects, odors, leaks and unsafe loading practice before loading, and issues a pass/fail determination on the carrier.

Off-facility handling verification at farms, ranches, live-haul poultry catching, livestock auction yards, nurseries or roadside/checkpoint stops: inspector observes catching, penning and loading practices in the yard or field, checks vehicle condition and load segregation, and verifies the movement meets health/quarantine requirements.

Records and procedure verification at the establishment: inspector reviews bills of lading, wash certificates for previous loads, temperature logs and reefer downloads, health/quarantine certificates and written transport SOPs, interviews the driver and plant staff, and records the verification finding.

sources.title: Spot at Cargill | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot quadruped runs autonomous inspection rounds inside a Cargill oilseed crush and refinery plant, doing routine maintenance inspections and visual ...; this is autonomous facility equipment inspection, not verification of transport/handling procedures or regulatory determinations about how people handle loads.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous rounds-based inspection inside a food facility (E2). It is the closest deployed robotic inspection capability, but it reads gauges and looks for equipment/safety anomalies on fixed routes; it does not open trailers, judge livestock handling, or issue regulatory compliance findings, so it does not transfer to whole-task completion.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic work inside a trailer interior in a purpose-built bay (E1). It shows a machine can enter a presented trailer, but it runs a fixed cleaning program and produces a cleaning certificate, not an examination for odors, residues, infestation, temperature and loading practice with an accept/reject regulatory determination.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated condition checking of arriving transport equipment at a terminal gate. It is a fixed camera/software system, not a robotic system acting on the physical world, and it checks container exteriors only, so it cannot substantiate robotic completion of this task.

tasks.label: Collect samples from animals, plants, or products and route them to laboratories for microbiological assessment, ingredient verification, or other testing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Slaughter/meat-poultry or other food processing establishment: inspector walks the production floor, selects a carcass, trim combo, ground product or RTE lot, aseptically collects a sponge swab, excision or scoop sample, places it in a sterile labeled bag/bottle, completes chain-of-custody paperwork, packs it with coolant and ships it to the FSIS or contract microbiology lab.

Grain, oilseed or feed lot sampling at a country elevator, terminal, warehouse or export house: obtaining a representative sample from a truck, railcar, barge or loading stream (probe, pelican or mechanical stream sampler), then routing the sample to the grading/inspection laboratory for grade, mycotoxin or GMO testing.

Field, orchard or nursery visit: inspector walks a block taken as found, selects symptomatic or randomly designated plants, cuts leaves/stems/fruit or collects insects, bags and labels each sample with location data, and ships to a plant diagnostic or residue laboratory.

Live animal sampling on a farm, feedlot, livestock market or ante-mortem pen: restraining animals and drawing blood, taking nasal/oral swabs, fecal or ear-tissue samples, labeling tubes per animal ID, and submitting to a veterinary diagnostic laboratory.

Dairy sampling: collecting bulk-tank milk samples in a farm milkhouse and tanker/silo samples at a receiving plant (and individual-cow samples for component/somatic-cell testing), preserving, icing and routing them to a certified dairy laboratory.

Packinghouse, cold store, port-of-entry or warehouse: pulling designated packaged units or cases from an imported or domestic lot for residue, ingredient-verification or microbiological testing, sealing and labeling the sample, and forwarding it to the laboratory.

tasks.label: Examine, weigh, and measure commodities, such as poultry, eggs, meat, or seafood to certify qualities, grades, and weights.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Poultry plant grading line: grader stands at the chilled whole-bird distribution/cut-up line, examining ready-to-cook carcasses moving on shackles for conformation, fleshing, bruises, broken wings, feathers, skin tears and discoloration, checking individual bird weights, and assigning A/B grades and downgrade routing at high line speed.

Red-meat slaughter plant: beef carcasses in the grading cooler are evaluated at the ribbed 12th rib for marbling, ribeye area, fat thickness and yield grade, with hot carcass weight from the rail scale; in pork plants, carcasses are classified for lean yield/backfat on the line, and grade/class and weight are certified per carcass.

Shell egg packing plant: grader oversees/performs candling of eggs for cracks, leakers, blood spots, dirt and interior quality, weighs eggs into size classes (jumbo through peewee), verifies carton net weight and grade markings, on a continuous grading line running tens of thousands of eggs per hour.

Seafood/fish processing plant line: examining fillets, portions or whole fish for size, visible defects, bones and foreign material, weighing and size-grading the product stream, and verifying declared net weights of finished packs.

Cold-storage warehouse or plant holding room lot certification: locating and sampling cartons from stacked pallets of frozen or packaged meat, poultry or seafood, opening cases, counting and weighing units, checking net weight after deglazing, and examining/thawing samples for dehydration, discoloration, odor, packaging and labeling defects to certify the lot.

Off-site points: dockside fish landings and buying stations, live-bird or egg receiving points, farm and small-processor visits, and retail/point-of-sale net-weight checks — commodities presented loose, in totes, bins, or vessel holds under variable weather and lighting.
