automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steep-slope Pacific Northwest / Northern Rockies hand falling of large conifers: after felling and limbing, the faller walks the stem in slash and brush, decides bucking points, then checks each cut log for correct length plus trim allowance (tape or measuring stick) and for quality — butt rot/conk, catface, shatter or breakage from the fall, excessive sweep — re-bucking or culling defective segments before the yarder takes them.

Hand falling of smaller-diameter conifers in thinning, salvage or machine-inaccessible ground: stems bucked to standard mill lengths, faller verifies each log against the length/diameter spec sheet and discards broken, rotten or crooked segments to pulp. Ground is uneven, weather and light variable.

Eastern/Appalachian hardwood falling: quality judgment dominates. After felling, the faller reads surface indicators (bumps, seams, holes, sweep, stain) to place bucking cuts and to sort each log into veneer, grade sawlog, tie or pulp classes, measuring lengths with a tape on brushy, sloping ground.

Bucking at a roadside landing or log deck after whole-tree/stem skidding: the bucker trims ends, verifies lengths for the truck and mill, and sorts logs by grade and defect, working on a muddy, site-specific landing with skidders and loaders moving around.

Danger/hazard tree falling for fire crews, utility rights-of-way, or road clearing: after felling, the stem is bucked into manageable lengths for removal or scattering; assessment is coarse — checking soundness and that segments are the right length to handle, deck or leave.

Small woodlot, land-clearing or firewood jobs for private landowners: felled stems cut to sawlog or firewood lengths, faller checks piece lengths and rejects rotten or hollow sections, often working alone with a chainsaw in varied ground.

sources.title: MiCROTEC - CT Log
sources.claim: MiCROTEC's CT Log computed-tomography scanner grades and sorts logs by quality from a full reconstruction of internal features and computes the optimal cutting solution in real time, inline in sawmills.
sources.transferJustification: Same judgment the faller makes on a bucked log — is the quality acceptable and where should it be cut — performed automatically on conveyed logs, including internal rot and knots the faller can only infer from surface signs.

sources.system: CT Log X-ray scanner + Logeye 900 stereo carriage scanners
sources.title: Cascade Hardwoods Adds Microtec CT Log Scanning | Timber Processing
sources.claim: A US hardwood mill (Cascade Hardwoods, Chehalis, WA) runs CT X-ray log scanning that detects internal defects including knots, cracks, ..., with the resulting segments optimized and sawn automatically downstream.
sources.transferJustification: Hardwood log grading (veneer/grade/tie/pulp) is the quality half of this task; the deployed scanner performs the defect assessment on the same species and log sizes an Appalachian faller sorts by eye.

sources.date: 2025 (product page; family in service for years)
sources.title: MiCROTEC - Logeye 302
sources.claim: MiCROTEC Logeye linear log scanners measure each log's diameter, length, volume, curvature and ... over- and under-bark and support automatic log sorting, grading and cutting optimization on sawmill lines.
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers the 'length is correct' half of the task plus sweep/taper defects, measured automatically on every log rather than by tape.

sources.system: Optimized bucking / merchandiser lines (laser profiling scan heads and optimizer-controlled saws)
sources.title: ABCs of Sawmill Scanning: Bucking & Merchandising - JoeScan
sources.claim: Sawmill bucking/merchandising lines convey each stem lengthwise through laser profiling scanners; an optimizer chooses cut lengths and the system also sorts logs to the appropriate line, and delivered logs are commonly scanned as they are offloaded from trucks to audit suppliers. In-forest bucking is normally done without any scanning or optimization.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes that the whole assessed-and-acted-on loop (measure length/geometry, decide correctness, cut and sort) runs automatically once logs are presented on a conveyor — the E1 presentation of this task.

sources.system: Ponsse Bear harvester with H8 head and Opti4G on-board bucking optimization
sources.developer: Ponsse (study by Labelle & Huß, Silva Fennica)
sources.title: Creation of value through a harvester on-board bucking optimization system operated in a spruce stand
sources.claim: A cut-to-length harvester's head measures stem diameter and length automatically and the on-board computer selects cross-cut points in the stand, but the machine is run continuously by an operator in the cab ... quality bucking is entered by the operator via hot-keys.
sources.transferJustification: Closest in-forest analogue: automatic length/diameter measurement of freshly cut logs, but embedded in an operator-driven machine and without automatic quality grading, so it cannot substantiate autonomous completion in the woods.

sources.developer: Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (La Hera et al.), Journal of Field Robotics
sources.title: Exploring the feasibility of autonomous forestry operations: Results from the first experimental unmanned machine
sources.claim: The first unmanned forest machine autonomously navigated forest terrain and picked up logs from the ground using computer vision, an experimental research platform for forwarding — not log grading or length verification.
sources.transferJustification: Shows the frontier of autonomy in the woods is log detection and handling; no autonomous assessment of log quality or length is demonstrated, supporting a negative E3 judgment.

sources.system: Camera/sensor-based root-rot detection on harvesting machinery
sources.developer: Research review, International Journal of Forest Engineering
sources.title: Predicting the occurrence of root rot in tree stumps based on harvester data
sources.claim: Sensor-based methods for detecting rot in freshly cut stems/stumps during harvesting remain research; no practical implementation has been made.
sources.transferJustification: Directly addresses automatic in-woods quality assessment of cut wood (rot), the quality half of this task, and shows it is not yet fielded.

sources.system: Autonomous logyard crane with Metris ANDI
sources.title: Log yard cranes | ANDRITZ
sources.claim: ANDRITZ supplies autonomously operated log yard cranes (Metris ANDI) that use laser scanners and cameras to determine the position and dimensions of loose wood and handle it 24/7 in mill wood yards.
sources.transferJustification: Nearest system operating on decked, unfixtured logs; it senses log dimensions for handling but performs no grade/length acceptance decision, so it supports handling in a purpose-built yard rather than the assessment task in a human facility.

sources.title: The new splitter-cutter measures logs entirely automatically | POSCH
sources.claim: Commercial firewood processors measure each log automatically with optical sensors as it is fed and control the saw so pieces are cut to length without offcuts.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the low-grade end of the task (verifying that cut pieces are the right length) with automatic measurement and cutting once the log is presented to the machine.

tasks.label: Appraise trees for certain characteristics, such as twist, rot, and heavy limb growth, and gauge amount and direction of lean, to determine how to control the direction of a tree's fall with the least damage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production felling of second-growth conifers on steep Pacific Northwest/Inland West ground: for each tree the faller walks up, sizes up head lean and side lean against a plumb reference, reads crown weight and heavy limbs, looks for conks, cat-faces, hollow butts and spiral (twisted) grain, sounds the stump area with an axe, checks wind, brush, adjacent leave trees and the intended lay, and settles on face-cut direction, hinge dimensions and whether wedges or a jack are needed to avoid breakage and hang-ups.

Manual felling on flatter southern pine plantation or mixed hardwood ground where machines can't operate (wet, small tracts, select cuts): faller judges lean and limb weight (hardwoods often heavily one-sided or forked), spots butt rot and old wounds, and picks a lay that drops the stem clear of leave trees and skid trails without breaking merchantable length.

Large-diameter or high-value timber (old growth, big hardwood sawlogs) with significant defect: heavy rot in the butt, pronounced twist, dead top or broken limbs; the faller must judge how much sound holding wood remains, whether the tree will barber-chair or split, and pick a bed and direction that preserves log value and keeps the stem from shattering.

Danger/hazard tree falling on fire lines, burned areas, roadsides and campgrounds: fire-weakened snags, dead tops, punky wood and unpredictable internal rot; the faller must appraise soundness from the ground, quickly, often in smoke or with limited approach, and decide direction of fall away from crews, roads and improvements, or decide the tree can't be safely felled by hand.

Right-of-way, utility corridor and near-structure work: tree must be threaded into a narrow lay away from conductors, fences, roads or buildings; faller gauges lean and limb loading against the required direction, decides how much wedging, rope/pull line or notch style is needed to swing the tree against its natural lean with least damage.

Storm-damaged and windthrown material: leaners hung in other trees, uprooted stems under tension, spring poles and broken tops; the faller reads tension and compression, root-wad behavior and hang-up geometry to decide the cutting plan and release direction.

sources.title: The World's First Drone Tree Harvest in a Real Forest - AirForestry
sources.claim: AirForestry's 6.2 m electric harvest drone completed an autonomous sequence in which it flew to position, identified a tree, harvested it and dropped it off; separate work harvested trees in a real production spruce stand. The autonomous end-to-end sequence was run on the company's test field.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous thinning harvest of small plantation stems. It does not transfer to this appraisal task: the drone grips and lifts the stem, so no lean/limb-weight assessment or hinge/face-cut plan governing a controlled fall is required, and no defect appraisal (rot, twist) is reported; the fully autonomous cycle ran on a purpose-built test field, not in the production stand.

sources.system: ANYmal D autonomous forest inventory system
sources.developer: University of Oxford Dynamic Robot Systems / ANYbotics platform
sources.title: Autonomous Forest Inventory with Legged Robots: System Design and Field Deployment (arXiv:2404.14157)
sources.claim: A legged ANYmal D robot autonomously surveyed a ~1 ha forest plot under canopy, detecting and measuring stems (diameter at breast height) without an operator, in real UK woodland.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous under-canopy tree measurement. Shows a robot can autonomously locate stems and measure diameter in a real forest, but the measured attributes stop at stem position/DBH; no internal rot, spiral grain, crown-weight or lean appraisal and no felling plan are produced, so it does not substantiate completion of this task.

sources.title: Towards Autonomous Robotic Precision Harvesting: Mapping, Localization, Planning and Control for a Legged Tree Harvester (arXiv:2104.10110)
sources.claim: A full-size hydraulic walking excavator fitted with a tree gripper autonomously navigated a GPS-denied forest and grasped standing trees, with reported end-effector accuracy around 30 cm; cutting/directional felling and defect assessment were not part of the demonstrated autonomy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous approach and grasping of standing trees by a harvester machine. It is the closest robotic analogue to working a tree in the woods, but the system reasons only about stem geometry for grasping; it does not appraise rot, twist or limb loading, nor plan a hinge and direction of fall.

sources.title: Kodama Systems uses robotics to mitigate wildfire risk - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Kodama Systems fits skidders and other forest-thinning machines with teleoperation and supervised-autonomy kits (lidar and cameras) for wildfire fuels-reduction work; the machines are remotely driven by human operators rather than felling and appraising trees on their own.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanized forest thinning with remote operators. Human operators remain in the perception-and-decision loop, and the automated element is skidding/hauling, so it cannot substantiate autonomous appraisal of tree defects or fall-direction planning.

sources.title: Ponsse launches the intelligent OptiFellingAssist solution to enhance precision, safety and productivity in timber harvesting
sources.claim: Ponsse's 2026 OptiFellingAssist is an in-cab operator assistance feature on manned cut-to-length harvesters that automates crane pre-tensioning and vertical movement during the felling cut; the human operator still selects the tree and controls the felling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine felling of standing trees. The state-of-the-art commercial 'felling assistant' automates only crane/saw mechanics under a seated operator; tree appraisal and fall-direction judgment remain human, showing the appraisal step is not automated even in mechanized harvesting.

sources.title: A robotic solution for safer tree trimming | Penn Today
sources.claim: Serpent Robotics is prototyping a rope-climbing, ground-controlled ... system for tree care so workers stay on the ground; it is an early prototype under human control, not an autonomous tree appraiser or feller.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic tree cutting in arboriculture. It is ground-controlled (teleoperated) and at prototype stage, so under the autonomy rule it cannot support a positive judgment for appraising trees and planning a controlled fall.

tasks.label: Clear brush from work areas and escape routes, and cut saplings and other trees from direction of falls, using axes, chainsaws, or bulldozers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steep-ground timber sale (PNW/Rockies): before cutting each large conifer the faller 'swamps out' the stump area with the chainsaw — cutting brush, limbs, small firs and vine maple around the trunk — then clears two escape routes at ~45 degrees behind the tree over slash, logs, stumps and uneven slope.

Flat to rolling second-growth or plantation stand: faller cuts light brush, ferns and 1-4 inch saplings from around each stem and along the working area with a chainsaw, moves cut material aside by hand, and keeps a clear walk-out path; stand is dense but relatively uniform.

Cutting saplings, small trees, snags and leaning stems out of the intended lay so the falling tree will not hang up, break, or shatter; requires reading the lay and selecting which stems in the fall path must go, then dropping them clear with saw or axe.

Eastern/Southern hardwood woods: dense understory of briars, vines, laurel and hardwood sprouts with poor visibility and soft or wet footing; faller must clear brush at the stump and cut two escape paths before each tree.

Heavy-equipment variant: a dozer (or excavator/skid steer with blade) pushes brush, small trees and slash out of a work area, landing approach or access route at the felling site, piling debris clear of the timber to be felled.

Agency or utility work under institutional control: fuel-reduction or hazard-tree felling along a maintained road corridor, utility right-of-way or developed recreation site, where access is controlled and ground is kept mown/graded; faller still clears brush at the stump and cuts escape paths.

sources.system: SAHA (Supervised Autonomous HArvester, based on RCM Harveri)
sources.developer: ETH Zurich Robotic Systems Lab / DigiForest consortium
sources.title: [2601.01282] SAHA: Supervised Autonomous HArvester for selective forest thinning
sources.claim: SAHA, a 4.5-ton small robotic harvester from ETH Zurich's DigiForest project, autonomously navigates real northern European forests and reaches targeted trees for selective thinning under supervised autonomy in field trials; it is a research prototype, and the reported capability is navigation and reaching/handling target stems, not swamping brush from a stump or clearing escape routes.
sources.transferJustification: Selective thinning of small stems in a real forest is the nearest related task to cutting saplings from the direction of fall: same environment, similar objects. It does not transfer to the whole instance, however — the machine targets merchantable stems mapped in advance with a harvester head, and neither cuts low brush around a stump nor opens escape routes, and it is a supervised research prototype rather than production-quality work.

sources.system: Legged tree harvester (Menzi Muck-based precision harvester)
sources.title: Towards Autonomous Robotic Precision Harvesting: Mapping, Localization, Planning and Control for a Legged Tree Harvester
sources.claim: ETH Zurich's legged tree harvester autonomously navigated a GPS-denied natural forest and grabbed selected trees, but the demonstrated cycle stopped at grabbing; the authors state that a felling (cutting) application would require further hardware hardening.
sources.transferJustification: Closest autonomous in-forest manipulation of standing trees; cited to show that even the leading forest-manipulation demonstrations stop short of autonomously cutting stems, so they cannot substantiate cutting brush and saplings at a felling site.

sources.title: Kodama Systems uses robotics to prevent wildfires - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Kodama Systems retrofits commercial forest-thinning machines (skidders) with teleoperation and partial autonomy and ran them on a thinning project in the Stanislaus National ...; the deployed capability is remote operation of log skidding, not autonomous brush cutting or sapling felling.
sources.transferJustification: Forest-thinning machine automation in US timber stands is the industry state of the art most adjacent to this task; it is teleoperation of skidding, so it cannot support a positive judgment for autonomously clearing brush or cutting saplings.

sources.title: BurnBots at work: Bend Fire using robots to clear wildfire fuels in Deschutes River Woods - KTVZ
sources.claim: BurnBot's mulching machines used by Bend Fire to clear wildfire fuels (brush and shrubs) in Oregon are run by a technician walking behind with a remote control, i.e. teleoperated rather than autonomous.
sources.transferJustification: Brush and shrub clearing in wooded ground is essentially the same physical work as clearing brush from a faller's work area; the machine is continuously teleoperated, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.title: Southern Company deploys electric, semi-autonomous lawn mowers at power plants
sources.claim: Scythe Robotics' M.52 is a commercially deployed autonomous mower used by landscape contractors and at Southern Company power plant grounds; it autonomously cuts turf on maintained, institution-controlled properties, not woody brush or saplings.
sources.transferJustification: Autonomous cutting of vegetation at an institution-controlled site is the E2 analogue; it does not transfer to this task because it mows grass over open areas and cannot selectively cut woody saplings, swamp brush at a tree base, or open escape routes.

sources.system: RC Mowers R Series (remote-operated) and Autonomous Mowing Robots
sources.title: Robotic Mowing Solutions | Robotic Mowers | RC Mowers
sources.claim: RC Mowers' brush-capable machines (R Series, which cuts brush up to 1.5 inches diameter on steep slopes) are remote-operated, while its autonomous product line is limited to mowing expansive turf areas such as sports fields, parks, airports and campuses.
sources.transferJustification: Shows the commercial split as of 2026: machines that cut woody brush on rough ground are teleoperated, and the autonomous machines cut turf on maintained grounds; neither substantiates autonomous brush/sapling clearing at a felling site.

sources.system: AutoPlant autonomous site preparation and planting machine
sources.developer: Skogforsk / Bracke Forest / KTH / SLU (Vinnova project)
sources.title: Autoplant—Autonomous Site Preparation and Tree Planting for a Sustainable Bioeconomy
sources.claim: The Swedish AutoPlant project demonstrated a fully autonomous soil-scarification and tree-planting cycle at full scale in a real forest regeneration area, showing autonomous ground-engaging forest work is possible in cutover terrain, but the work performed is scarification and planting, not cutting brush or saplings.
sources.transferJustification: Nearest evidence of autonomous ground-engaging machine work on forest terrain (an E3 setting); it does not transfer to cutting brush and saplings, which requires selecting and severing woody stems with a saw around a specific tree.

sources.system: Built Robotics autonomy kit / Exosystem for dozers and excavators
sources.title: Built Robotics releases 1st fully autonomous construction machinery in US | Construction Dive
sources.claim: Built Robotics supplies autonomy kits that let dozers and excavators perform earthmoving tasks fully autonomously on construction sites, with the demonstrated tasks being trenching, excavating foundations and grading pads rather than clearing brush and small trees.
sources.transferJustification: Relevant to the bulldozer variant of the task — autonomous blade work on an unstructured site — but the demonstrated tasks are soil moving on prepared earthwork areas, not pushing, uprooting and piling brush, stumps and saplings while protecting the residual timber, so it does not substantiate completion.

tasks.label: Tag unsafe trees with high-visibility ribbons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Inside an active timber harvest unit before/during falling: the faller walks steep, brushy, debris-covered ground, judges each stem for hazard indicators (dead or broken tops, hanging limbs, conks/rot, cracks, heavy lean, root damage) and ties high-visibility flagging around the trunk at eye level so the crew can see it from a distance.

Flagging danger trees along haul roads, skid trails, landings and unit boundaries: better vehicle access and flatter ground, but still natural forest edge with slash, ditches and variable brush; ribbons tied on trunks that threaten the travel way or work area.

Post-fire salvage, blowdown or beetle-killed stands: dense concentrations of fire-weakened snags, leaners and hung-up tops in ash, ruts and downed material; large numbers of stems tagged in one pass, often with additional ribbon color coding for cut/leave or wildlife trees.

Hazard trees in developed or managed sites — campground loops, trailheads, roadside pullouts, utility rights-of-way: access roads and facilities are maintained by an agency or utility, but the tree cover and ground are natural; ribbons mark trees for removal and warn the public.

Ad-hoc mid-shift marking: after encountering a hung-up tree, widowmaker or unexpectedly rotten stem while cutting, the faller ribbons the tree and strings flagging across the approach to close off the danger zone until it is dealt with.

sources.title: Cascade Hardwoods invests in Microtec CT Log Scanning technology - International Forest Industries
sources.claim: MiCROTEC's CT Log X-ray computed-tomography scanner, installed at Cascade Hardwoods' Chehalis, Washington mill, automatically detects internal wood defects including rot and cracks in logs presented on the mill line, and passes the grading result downstream in real time.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated grading of stems for unsoundness. It substantiates the assessment half of 'tag unsafe trees' when the work is presented to the machine — same material (wood stems), defect classes that overlap a faller's concerns (rot, cracks), decided autonomously at line speed in a purpose-built setting.

sources.system: Samuel Coding & Labeling wood marking / automatic package tag systems
sources.title: Tech Update - Lumber Marking Systems - Forestnet
sources.claim: Samuel Coding & Labeling supplies automated wood-products marking equipment used in sawmills and planer mills, including ink-jet grade-mark systems and automatic tag systems that print labels and staple them onto finished wood packages.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: applying a durable visible tag/mark to wood in a mill. The physical act — fastening a high-visibility marker onto presented wood, legibly and repeatably — is the marking half of the faller task, performed by machine in a purpose-built line.

sources.developer: International Bar Coding Systems and Consulting
sources.title: Tech Update - Lumber Marking Systems - Forestnet
sources.claim: International Bar Coding's PA10G print-and-apply unit automatically prints and applies self-adhesive labels onto wood products moving through a mill line at over 300 pieces per minute, integrated with mill control systems.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic application of a physical marker to wood presented on a conveyor; demonstrates worker-beating reliability and throughput for the marker-application step when the workpiece is brought to the machine.

sources.title: REA LABEL Robotic Labeler
sources.claim: REA JET markets the REA LABEL Robotic Labeler, a fully automatic robot-arm print-and-apply labeling cell for pallets and products, of the kind installed in guarded industrial cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic application of a visible label to a workpiece presented in a fenced cell. Shows a robot arm, not just a fixed head, can place a marker on varied faces of a presented object — the manipulation analogue of attaching a ribbon to a stem.

sources.system: FROMM automatic strapping systems for wood & timber
sources.title: automatic strapping machines for wood and timber
sources.claim: FROMM supplies automatic strapping machines and wrappers ..., banding lumber bundles hands-free as they move through mill conveyor lines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatically passing a band completely around presented wood and securing it. This is the closest machine analogue to tying a ribbon around a stem — same material, same wrap-and-fasten action, done unattended in a purpose-built line.

sources.developer: Fly4Future / CTU FEE Multi-Robot Systems group
sources.title: Drones In Forest Inspection - Fly4Future
sources.claim: In the Czech KOLDRO project, Fly4Future and the CTU Multi-Robot Systems group built a pair of collaborating drones in which a detection drone finds bark-beetle-infested spruce from above and a second drone flies under canopy, inspects the bark, and sprays paint on the tree to mark it; it is a research/prototype system marking a pest criterion, not structural hazard, and no deployment record was found.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous aerial identification and visible marking of standing trees in a forest. It is the nearest in-forest analogue, but it classifies beetle entry holes rather than structural hazard, applies paint rather than flagging, and is a prototype without evidence of worker-quality coverage of a harvest unit.

sources.title: Kodama Systems uses robotics to mitigate wildfire risk - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Kodama Systems' autopilot kits for forestry machines automate skid-trail travel but hand the dexterous parts of the operation to a human teleoperator on site, indicating that field forestry robotics has not yet reached autonomous fine manipulation in the woods.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous operation of machinery inside working harvest units. It bounds what is achievable in the same environment as this task: navigation is automated, but per-tree dexterous work still requires a human operator.

tasks.label: Determine position, direction, and depth of cuts to be made, and placement of wedges or jacks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial timber harvest in a Pacific Northwest / Inland West conifer stand: the faller sizes up a large second-growth Douglas-fir or hemlock on sloped ground, reads lean, crown weight, limb distribution, wind, and the intended lay, then decides face-cut type and direction, undercut depth (roughly a quarter to a third of diameter), hinge width and holding wood, back-cut height, and whether/where wedges will be needed to lift the stem.

Smaller-diameter second-growth, pulpwood, thinning, or fuels-reduction trees on flat to moderate terrain with the tree leaning toward an open lay: a quick determination of notch direction and depth, hinge, and back-cut, with a single wedge behind the saw or none at all; repeated dozens of times a day.

Hazard/danger tree work (dead, fire-killed, rotten, broken-top, insect-killed snag): the faller must judge how much sound wood remains, whether the shell will hold a hinge, whether to bore-cut or use a modified face, whether the tree can be safely fallen by hand at all, and where wedges or a jack can be set without collapsing punky wood.

Heavy leaner, back-leaner, wind-thrown, or hung-up tree: the faller determines a cut sequence to avoid barber-chairing or fiber pull (bore cut with strap, Humboldt vs. conventional face, stepped cuts), and specifies where jacks, wedges, or a pull line must be placed to shift the tree against its lean or release stored tension.

Right-of-way, roadside, or structure-adjacent felling (powerline corridor, landing edge, near equipment, campground or trail): a tight, mandated lay that is not the tree's natural lean, so the faller determines notch direction and depth plus the specific wedge or jack placement and lifting sequence needed to drive the tree into the narrow target zone.

tasks.label: Maintain and repair chainsaws and other equipment, cleaning, oiling, and greasing equipment, and sharpening equipment properly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid-shift chain touch-up on the cutting strip: the faller shuts the saw down, sets it on a stump or log, and hand-files every cutter with a round file and guide, then checks/lowers the depth gauges. Done on uneven ground, in dust, rain or cold, with gloves and no bench.

Mid-shift fluid and adjustment service in the woods: refill the gas/oil mix and bar-oil tanks from a combi-can, wipe grit from around the caps, re-tension the chain, clear packed chips from the clutch cover and sprocket, and confirm the bar oiler is throwing oil.

Bench grinding of the day's dull chains at the shop or on a truck-mounted grinder: each chain is clamped in the grinder vise, angles and depth set, cutters ground on both sides, depth gauges filed, and the chain returned to the kit ready to hang on a saw.

End-of-shift cleaning and lubrication of the saw at the shop or yard: pull the clutch cover, brush out packed chips and oil sludge, clean the bar groove and oiler holes, dress the rails and flip the bar, grease the bar-nose sprocket, clean or replace the air filter, and check the plug and drive sprocket for wear.

Diagnosing and repairing a saw fault in the shop or at the truck: saw won't start, won't hold idle, or cuts crooked — carburetor adjustment, fuel filter/line and impulse hose replacement, starter rope and recoil spring, clutch and drive sprocket, chain brake band, or a worn bar swapped out; then test-run the saw.

Maintaining the rest of the falling kit: grinding and honing axe and hatchet bits, dressing burred falling wedges, servicing and bleeding hydraulic falling jacks and line pulls, cleaning and refilling fuel/oil cans, and checking wedges, files, scrench and PPE — done at a shop bench, tailgate or landing.

sources.system: Oregon 720-120 Auto Chain Grinder, All In One
sources.title: Auto Chain Grinder, All In One | Oregon Products
sources.claim: Commercially sold all-in-one automatic chain grinder that, once a saw chain is loaded and set up, auto-feeds the chain and grinds the cutters while also setting the depth gauge and cleaning the gullet — the full sharpening job done by machine control on a bench.

sources.title: T-Rex Automatic Chainsaw Chain Sharpener – DinaSaw
sources.claim: Commercial fully automatic chainsaw chain sharpener sold to sawmills, arborists and forestry operators; sensors index the chain and detect tooth position, grinding up to 30 teeth per minute without hand filing.

sources.title: Automatic Chain Grinder – Logosol
sources.claim: Marketed 'chain sharpening robot' for chainsaw users, developed with Markusson Development, that grinds a loaded saw chain automatically (about 1.5 minutes per side, ten teeth per minute), with the operator only changing the head angle between sides.

sources.system: SCOTT Robofuel autonomous refuelling system (and Universal Field Robots AutoFuel)
sources.date: 2020-06 (Robofuel described as in use at a number of sites)
sources.title: Autonomous refuelling solution for mining trucks from Universal Field Robots | International Mining
sources.claim: Autonomous refuelling robots for mining haul trucks are in service at mine sites, filling truck fuel tanks without an operator at a dedicated roadside refuelling installation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated filling of a fuel tank. It does NOT transfer to servicing a chainsaw in the field — the receptacle is a haul-truck fill point in a purpose-built bay, not a 0.5 L screw-cap chainsaw tank plus bar-oil tank, and it covers none of the chain tensioning, chip clearing or oiler checks in that instance.

tasks.label: Trim off the tops and limbs of trees, using chainsaws, delimbers, or axes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steep-ground large-conifer falling (Pacific NW, N. California, SE Alaska): after felling a 20–48 in DBH Douglas-fir/hemlock on a 40–70% slope, the faller limbs the whole stem with a chainsaw and bucks off the top at merchantable diameter; limbs are under compression, the stem lies on a sidehill in brush and slash, footing is poor.

Moderate-terrain conifer/mixed-stand falling: 10–24 in trees felled into a jackstraw of tops, brush and previously felled stems; faller limbs the stem flush and cuts the top off for tree-length skidding or cut-to-length bucking, working around leaners and pinned limbs.

Hardwood, storm-damaged or land-clearing work: irregular heavy crowns, forked tops, blowdown and spring poles under tension, occasional hung-up trees; limbing and topping requires reading tension and repositioning around the crown.

Landing/roadside processing: whole trees are skidded or yarded to a temporary landing where the faller/bucker limbs and tops them with a chainsaw before loading; churned ground, slash piles, machines and other workers moving nearby.
Right-of-way, danger-tree and campground/roadside work: a felled or dropped hazard tree must be limbed and topped in place and the limbs piled, near roads, traffic control, fences or structures.
Small-diameter thinning / pulpwood / fuels-reduction: limbing and topping small stems (4–10 in) felled in plantations or fuel-reduction units, high stem counts, light limbs.

sources.developer: Arbro (Ranssi/Arbro Oy), distributed in North America
sources.title: Harvesting And Processing Heads - Wood Business
sources.claim: Arbro-Stroke 400/1000 stroke harvester heads fell, delimb and cut trees to programmed lengths; once the stem is gripped the head runs an automatic stroke and delimbs the tree with a one-button function, with an integral measuring device for pre-selected lengths (topping cut).
sources.transferJustification: Same task: the head removes limbs from the felled stem and cross-cuts it (including the top) to measured length; only carrier positioning is done by a person.

sources.system: PONSSE cut-to-length harvester with Opti control system (H-series heads)
sources.title: The cut-to-length method - Ponsse
sources.claim: In cut-to-length harvesting the harvester head delimbs and measures the trunk and the control system automatically decides and executes the cross-cuts (automated bucking), i.e. limb removal and topping of a gripped stem run under machine control.

sources.title: Peterson 4800F Chain Flail Debarker - ASTEC
sources.claim: The Peterson 4800F chain flail debarker is a multiple-log delimber/debarker whose upper and lower chain flails continuously strip bark and limbs from stems fed into it, working in tandem with whole-tree chippers in in-woods and yard chipping systems.
sources.transferJustification: Same physical action on the same objects: removal of limbs from felled tree stems; the flail chamber is a purpose-built fixture into which stems are fed.

sources.developer: various (USDA Forest Service equipment catalog listing)
sources.title: Forest Operations Equipment Catalog: Delimbers - USDA Forest Service
sources.claim: Pull-through delimbers are purpose-built stations in which a stem is placed and drawn through wrap-around knives that strip the limbs, and most such delimbers include a topping saw that cuts the top off the stem.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (delimbing and topping felled stems) in a fixtured, purpose-built presentation; cited only for the existence of the fixture, as the stem is pulled through by a human loader operator.

sources.title: Fully Autonomous Drone Harvests Its First Tree in World First | Wood Central
sources.claim: AirForestry's 6.2 m electric drone carries a harvesting tool that grips a ... at the top, delimbs it while descending, cuts it near the ground and flies the trunk out; in May 2026 the company reported a fully autonomous end-to-end harvest in a working production forest for thinning-grade trees of 40–140 kg.

sources.system: Ponsse Bear single-grip harvester with H8 harvesting head
sources.developer: Ponsse Oyj (study: Labelle & Huß, Silva Fennica)
sources.title: Labelle E. R., Huß L. (2018) Creation of value through a harvester on-board bucking optimization system operated in a spruce stand
sources.claim: Study of on-board bucking optimization with a Ponsse Bear harvester and H8 head in spruce: the head's productivity peaked at 50–60 cm dbh stems, with 55 cm corresponding to about 74% of the head's maximum delimbing diameter (i.e. roughly 74 cm / 29 in capacity).
sources.transferJustification: Cited only for the stem-diameter capacity of commercial delimbing/processing heads relevant to large-timber instances, not for autonomy.

tasks.label: Mark logs for identification.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On a steep, brushy cutover, after bucking a felled stem the faller sprays a paint code (sort/species/ownership/timber-sale color) on the cut ends or sides of each log; logs lie at varied angles in slash, mud and snow, ends partly buried, and the faller must climb over debris to reach each end.

Hammer-branding: the faller strikes a registered ownership brand into the end grain of each log with a branding axe/stamp hammer (e.g., state timber-sale rules requiring one end branded and one end painted before removal), working on logs lying on the ground in the cutover or on the skid trail.

Writing identifying information in lumber crayon/keel or marking pen on log ends or bark: faller number, cut/length code, sale or block number, scaling or defect marks, so scalers and buckers can identify the piece; done at the stump in variable weather with wet, dirty log surfaces.

Attaching numbered, barcoded or RFID plastic tags (nailed or hammered into the end grain) to high-value logs — export, veneer or specialty sorts — at the roadside deck or landing, one tag per log, with the number recorded on a tally sheet.

Marking sort colors or grade paint on the exposed ends of logs already decked in a cold deck / landing stack by the loader, where logs are jack-strawed in a pile and only the ends of many pieces are reachable.

sources.system: InfoSight automated marking and tagging systems (InfoTag bar tag nailer, stencil spray marking, dot-peen)
sources.title: Industrial Automated Marking & Tagging Solutions - InfoSight
sources.claim: InfoSight supplies fully automatic, programmable industrial marking and tagging machines that spray-stencil codes, dot-peen permanent marks on rough, curved and irregular surfaces, and nail or weld identification tags onto workpieces moving through steel-mill production lines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: applying identification marks/tags to heavy raw workpieces on a line. It transfers to marking logs because the objects are comparably large, rough-surfaced pieces, the required precision (a legible code or nailed tag on an end face) is no greater than for billets and bars, and the marking is machine-triggered from the line's product data.

sources.system: MARKTEC custom-made printing device for steel pipe (6-axis robot marking cell)
sources.title: Custom-made printing device for steel pipe | MARKTEC Corporation
sources.claim: MARKTEC builds custom marking installations in which a 6-axis industrial robot carries the paint-printing head along the surfaces of steel pipes to apply identification printing in a production cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic paint marking of long cylindrical workpieces presented in a fixed station. A log end presented on a conveyor is a comparable target for a paint-marking end effector, with looser legibility/precision requirements than pipe identification printing.

sources.system: Claussen All-Mark Automated Face Grade Printer
sources.title: Lumber Grade Printers | Claussen Conversion Systems
sources.claim: Claussen All-Mark manufactures automated face grade printers that mount on a lumber mill's driven lug tables and stamp the grade mark on each board as it passes, to a standard accepted for American Lumber Standard Committee accreditation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: stamping identification/grade marks on wood pieces conveyed past the machine. Same substrate (rough sawn wood), same output (a legible ink/stamp mark that downstream parties rely on for identification), differing only in that the piece is carried to the machine.

sources.title: Going Against the Grain: How Lucidyne Is Revolutionizing Lumber Grading with Deep Learning
sources.claim: MiCROTEC/Lucidyne GradeScan scanners with deep-learning software have been deployed in lumber mills since 2017 to grade boards automatically at line speed, supplying the grade decision that drives downstream marking and sorting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatically deciding which identification mark a piece of wood should carry. Marking logs requires the same decision step (which sort/grade/owner code applies); GradeScan shows the decision is machine-made at line speed when the piece is presented to the scanner.

sources.system: BrandNew Industries Nailer Machine Heat Treat Stamps
sources.title: Pallet Branding Irons – BrandNew Industries
sources.claim: Heat-treat branding stamps are built to integrate directly into automated pallet assembly (nailer) machines so that the compliance/identification brand is burned into the wood as part of the machine cycle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-applied branding of wood for regulatory identification. It is the same physical act as hammer-branding a log end (pressing a raised die into wood to leave a registered mark), performed automatically once the wood is presented in the machine.

sources.system: Waratah HTH622B Series-III / HX-series harvester heads with integrated color marking system
sources.title: Harvester Head: HTH622B Series-III - Waratah
sources.claim: Commercial cut-to-length harvester heads are offered with integrated colour-marking systems that spray paint on processed logs while the stem is gripped in the head, showing that paint-marking hardware for log ends exists on forestry equipment; the carrier machine is, however, run continuously by a human operator.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (marking logs with paint for identification/assortment), but performed only when a human operator has gripped and fed the stem into the head, so it is treated as operator-dependent and used only as corroboration that log-end paint marking hardware is mature.

tasks.label: Place supporting limbs or poles under felled trees to avoid splitting undersides, and to prevent logs from rolling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steep-slope Pacific Northwest harvest unit: after felling a large conifer (30"+ DBH) across the slope onto rough, slash-covered ground, the faller bucks limbs from the top and wedges them under the bole at chosen points, and blocks the downhill side, so the log neither splits on the underside when bucked nor rolls downhill.

Rolling to moderate terrain industrial clearcut/commercial thinning in medium second-growth conifer: faller cuts several limbs into short bolsters and lays them under the stem at intervals judged from the stem's bearing points and tension before bucking to length.

Flat or gently sloping ground, small-to-medium trees (fuels reduction, thinning, right-of-way): a single limb or short pole is quickly shoved under the bole where it spans a low spot, plus a chock to keep the log from rolling on the landing side.

Hardwood selective harvest in the eastern US: high-value sawlog stems on uneven, leafy ground; supports carefully placed under the butt log to avoid underside split-out and degrade of veneer-quality wood during bucking.

Storm blowdown, fire-salvage, or hazard-tree work: tangled tops, stems under bind or suspended over other debris; poles and cut limbs placed to support the stem and stop movement before releasing tension with the saw.

sources.date: 2024 (product line in commercial sale for years)
sources.title: USNR - Magazine Stick/Lath Placer
sources.claim: Commercial sawmill stacking lines include magazine stick placers that automatically lay a wooden stick onto each successive tier of lumber so the wood above rests on those supports — the purpose-built-line analogue of laying a support member under a wood workpiece.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic placement of wooden spacer sticks that bear the load of the wood above them. It transfers to the E1 counterfactual of this task, where the stem arrives fixtured on a deck and support poles are presented in a magazine, reducing the work to positioned insertion of a wooden support beneath a wood load.

sources.system: Mill Tech Industries automatic stick placer
sources.title: Stick Placer System - Mill Tech Industries
sources.claim: Automatic stick placers that position wooden supports under/between wood loads are not one-off demos but are deployed and reliable in many operating mills.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repeated accurate placement of wooden support members under wood loads in a fixtured production line; establishes worker-quality reliability for the E1 counterfactual of placing a support under a presented stem.

sources.system: Itipack robotic dunnage / bunk placement system (ABB robot with three vacuum bars)
sources.title: Everything You Need to Know About Wood Panel Strapping / Robotics & Custom - Itipack Systems
sources.claim: A commercial wood-packaging line uses an ABB robot to place bunks (wooden support timbers) automatically beneath heavy wood panel packages, keeping the load supported and undamaged.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic placement of support timbers underneath a heavy wood load so it is held off the deck and does not shift or get damaged — the same functional act as putting a pole under a log, performed in a fenced, fixtured cell.

sources.title: Log Singulator - Timber Automation - Woodyard Manufacturer
sources.claim: Purpose-built woodyard machinery reliably singulates and positions irregular round natural logs and stems across the full commercial size range, showing that the E1 presentation of a felled stem in a known position is realistic equipment practice.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated handling and positioning of the exact objects at issue (felled stems and logs, irregular and heavy) inside a purpose-built line; supports the E1 counterfactual that the workpiece can be presented and held for a support-placing machine.

sources.developer: Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU) and Lulea University of Technology (La Hera et al., Journal of Field Robotics)
sources.title: Researchers develop and test the first unmanned forestry machine
sources.claim: The frontier of autonomous in-woods manipulation is an experimental unmanned machine that picks loose logs off the ground and drives across forest terrain; it does not cut bolsters or place supports under felled stems.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound what autonomous machines actually achieve in the E3 forest setting (grasping loose logs), not to substantiate completion of this task.

sources.title: Automated forestry loader developed by FPInnovations
sources.claim: An automated forestry loader can autonomously detect and grapple logs lying on the ground, but the demonstrated capability is log pickup in a yard, not selecting, cutting and inserting supports beneath a felled stem.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound autonomous log-handling capability in an institution-controlled yard (E2), showing no support-placement capability there.

tasks.label: Secure steel cables or chains to logs for dragging by tractors or for pulling by cable yarding systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cable/skyline yarding on a steep clearcut face: worker pulls choker cables out from the carriage or butt rigging downhill through slash, passes the ball under and around felled stems lying on broken ground, cinches the bell to form a noose, hooks chokers to the butt rigging, signals the yarder operator and moves to a safe clear position.

Ground-based skidding in a cutover: worker pulls the winch line off a cable skidder or crawler tractor, wraps chokers around one or more tree-length stems lying among stumps, brush, mud or snow, attaches them to the butt hook/arch, and clears before the turn is winched in.

Small woodlot, farm or selective-cut work: faller working alone or with one helper wraps a chain or cable choker around a single felled stem and hooks it to a tractor three-point winch, ATV winch or pickup, on uneven ground with standing residual timber to protect.

At the landing or roadside deck: chaining or cabling logs to drag them out of a pile, reposition or deck them, or to pull a stuck log free, working around log piles, loaders and skidder traffic on rough, muddy ground.

During felling: attaching a cable or chain (sometimes well up the stem) to a hung-up, leaning or lodged tree so a tractor or winch can pull it over or free it, with the stem under tension and unpredictable release.

sources.system: Radio/computer-controlled yarders (cable yarding automation, e.g. remote-controlled yarder drums)
sources.developer: Various forest machinery manufacturers (reviewed by Visser & Obi, Croatian Journal of Forest Engineering)
sources.title: Automation and Robotics in Forest Harvesting Operations: Identifying Near-Term Opportunities
sources.claim: A 2021 review of automation and robotics in forest harvesting finds that in computer/radio-controlled yarding systems the travel phases have been automated, but the load-accumulation (hooking) phase is still managed by a human choker-setter with a radio remote control; no autonomous choker-setting machine is reported.
sources.transferJustification: Directly about the task's operation (attaching the turn in cable yarding); it establishes that the hooking step remains a manual human step even in the most automated yarding systems.

sources.title: Falcon Grapple Claw | Nors Equipment
sources.claim: The main mechanized alternative to human choker setting in steep-slope logging is the motorized grapple carriage, which is fully remote controlled by the yarder operator via joystick; it grips stems with hydraulic jaws rather than securing cables or chains to logs.
sources.transferJustification: Closest deployed machine that substitutes for the rigging crew in cable yarding; it is continuously joystick-operated by the yarder operator and never attaches a cable or chain to a log, so it cannot substantiate autonomous completion of this task.

sources.system: Experimental unmanned forwarder (autonomous forestry machine test platform)
sources.developer: Umeå University / Luleå University of Technology (La Hera et al., Journal of Field Robotics)
sources.title: Exploring the feasibility of autonomous forestry operations: Results from the first experimental unmanned machine
sources.claim: The first experimental unmanned forwarder demonstrated autonomous driving and crane log handling in a simplified outdoor forest setting in Sweden, while noting that fully autonomous manipulation of logs remains an open research challenge.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous machine handling of logs in the forest. It shows the frontier is experimental grapple grasping of prepared single logs, not threading and cinching a steel choker around a stem and hooking it to a yarding line.

sources.system: Automated log grasping system on a forwarder (single stereo camera, boom-tip control)
sources.developer: Skogforsk / Semberg, Nilsson et al. (Silva Fennica)
sources.title: Real-time target point identification and automated log grasping by a forwarder, using a single stereo camera for both object detection and boom-tip control
sources.claim: A full-scale, real-time experiment demonstrated automated grapple positioning and log grasping on a forwarder using a single stereo camera for detection and boom-tip control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-vision-guided engagement of a log by a forestry crane. Automation reaches grapple closure on a log, but the demonstrated act is grasping with jaws, not passing a steel choker under a log and securing it for winching, so it does not transfer to this task.

sources.title: Automatic Lifting Hooks Application Videos | Elebia
sources.claim: The most automated industrial rigging hardware (automatic crane hooks) closes on a pre-installed ring or sling master link at the push of an operator's button; a human must still rig the sling to the load.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: making a load-bearing cable/chain connection without a rigger at the load. It only engages a ring that a human has already placed around the load and is operator-triggered, so it does not substantiate securing a cable or chain to a log, even in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Signode automatic steel strapping systems (BPX lumber compression strapping, BRP heavy-duty steel strapping)
sources.title: Application-Specific Strapping Machines | Signode
sources.claim: Fully automatic steel strapping machines pass and tension steel strap around wood loads presented on a purpose-built mill line without an operator.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatically encircling a wood load with steel in a fixtured, purpose-built line. It does not transfer: the strap bundles a compressed pack for transport and is not a load-bearing noose coupled to a winch line or butt rigging that must survive dragging a stem, so it does not complete this task even at E1.

tasks.label: Work as a member of a team, rotating between chain saw operation and skidder operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hardwood harvest on rolling ground (Appalachian/Northeast private woodlot or industrial timberland): crew member hand-fells 100+ merchantable stems a day with a chainsaw (face notch, back cut, wedges, directional control around leave trees), limbs and tops them, then rotates onto a cable/grapple skidder to choke, winch and drag stems along skid trails to the landing.

Steep-slope conifer felling in the West/Northwest: large-diameter timber on slopes over 35%, heavy lean, brush and blowdown underfoot, undercut and back cut placed to control fall and avoid breakage; then rotating onto a skidder/tractor to pull turns down trails to the landing.

Thinning or fuel-reduction work in dense small-diameter stands (state/federal contract or private thinning): fell marked stems with a chainsaw among tightly spaced leave trees, bunch the stems, then rotate onto the skidder to drag bunches to the deck without damaging residual trees.

Salvage of storm-damaged, insect-killed or fire-killed timber: leaning, broken, hung-up and spring-loaded stems with unpredictable rot and tension, debris and stobs on the ground; chainsaw felling plus skidding stems out through the damaged stand.

Clearing/right-of-way and landing-side work: felling trees near roads, fences, structures or powerlines with tight fall paths, plus skidding stems to the deck and bucking/decking at the landing while coordinating with other crew and truck traffic.

sources.title: RBR50 Spotlight: Kodama Systems uses robotics to prevent wildfires
sources.claim: Kodama Systems fielded a skidder retrofit on a forest-thinning project in Stanislaus National Forest; the machine autonomously dragged tree bundles along skid trails, but the platform as deployed is a teleoperation system with a remote human operator.
sources.transferJustification: Covers only the skidder half of the task (dragging stems on skid trails in a working US thinning unit); it does not fell trees, and the deployed cycle is run by a remote operator.

sources.title: Tech Startups Innovate to Snuff Out Wildfires
sources.claim: Contemporary press coverage of the same Kodama deployment describes the skidder as remotely controlled by a human worker while transporting logs in the Stanislaus National ....
sources.transferJustification: Same skidding sub-task; establishes that the fielded control mode is continuous remote operation rather than autonomy.

sources.developer: Luleå University of Technology and Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences
sources.title: Exploring the feasibility of autonomous forestry operations: Results from the first experimental unmanned machine (Journal of Field Robotics)
sources.claim: A Swedish research team demonstrated the first unmanned forestry machine performing autonomous navigation, log detection and crane grasping to extract logs on a clear-cut, i.e. autonomous forwarding rather than felling.
sources.transferJustification: Log extraction (forwarding) is the closest analogue to the skidder half of this task: same forest terrain and log-sized objects. It does not fell trees and is an experimental prototype, so it cannot substantiate the whole task.

sources.developer: ETH Zurich Robotic Systems Lab / DigiForest consortium
sources.title: SAHA: Supervised Autonomous HArvester for selective forest thinning (arXiv 2601.01282)
sources.claim: An ETH-led project demonstrated a 4.5-tonne robotic harvester with supervised autonomy that navigates real forests and positions its boom to targeted trees for selective thinning during kilometre-long field missions; autonomous execution of the fell-and-extract cycle at production rates is not established.
sources.transferJustification: Selective thinning with a harvester head is the mechanized analogue of chainsaw felling plus extraction; the demonstrated autonomy covers navigation and boom reaching under human supervision, not a full crew-rate felling-and-skidding shift.

sources.title: Fully Autonomous Drone Harvests Its First Tree in World First
sources.claim: AirForestry reported the first fully autonomous aerial tree harvest in a Swedish production forest: a 6.2 m electric drone identified a tree, delimbed, felled it and flew the trunk to roadside without ground machinery, at a scale of one to two consecutive trees.

sources.title: AirForestry – Efficient, Electric, and Sustainable Forestry from the Air
sources.claim: AirForestry's own milestone log confirms the autonomous harvest sequence (navigate, identify tree, delimb, fell, lift to roadside) was first completed in 2026 and that the first full-cycle harvest was of two consecutive trees; the drone is sized for thinning stems of roughly 40-140 kg.

sources.system: Xt28 concept forwarder with AI control
sources.developer: Umeå University / Skogforsk Troëdsson Forestry Teleoperation Lab
sources.title: The world's first AI-controlled forest machine trained in Umeå
sources.claim: An AI controller drove a 16-tonne concept forwarder over an obstacle course at a forestry teleoperation test lab, showing autonomous rough-terrain locomotion of a heavy forest machine on a prepared course with remote safety stops.
sources.transferJustification: Machine mobility over forest-like obstacles is a prerequisite for skidder operation, but the trials involved no felling, no log handling and took place on a prepared test course with remote kill switches.

roles.title: Logging Equipment Operators
roles.description: Drive logging tractor or wheeled vehicle equipped with one or more accessories, such as bulldozer blade, frontal shear, grapple, logging arch, cable winches, hoisting rack, or crane boom, to fell tree; to skid, load, unload, or stack logs; or to pull stumps or clear brush. Includes operating stand-alone logging machines, such as log chippers.

tasks.label: Inspect equipment for safety prior to use, and perform necessary basic maintenance tasks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-shift walk-around safety inspection of a tracked feller-buncher, harvester or grapple skidder at the logging site (landing/skid trail, mud, slash, uneven ground, often before daylight): circle and climb the machine, look for hydraulic leaks, chafed hoses, cracked welds and loose pins, check track/tire condition, cab guarding, windows, ROPS/FOPS, lights, backup alarm, fire extinguisher, seat belt, check oil/coolant/hydraulic levels at sight glasses and dipsticks, function-test controls and brakes, and correct the small defects found (tighten a fitting, top off a fluid, replace a bulb) before the machine is put to work.

End-of-shift or mid-day fueling and fluid service at the landing: pull the machine alongside the fuel/service truck or a portable slip tank, ground it, open the fill, pump 50-150 gallons of diesel, add DEF, top off hydraulic oil and coolant from bulk containers, and wipe up spills.

Routine lubrication cycle on a late-model machine equipped with automatic central lubrication and automatic harvester-head saw-chain greasing: the machine doses grease to boom, slew and head bearings and to the cutting chain on programmed intervals while working in the stand; the operator monitors the system and confirms points are receiving grease.

Hand lubrication and cutting-system maintenance in the field: grease-gun work on older machines and on points off the auto-lube circuit, plus replacing or sharpening the harvester-head saw chain and bar, adjusting chain tension, swapping worn teeth on a disc-saw felling head, checking delimbing knives and feed-roller condition — done with hand tools beside the machine on the forest floor.

Fire-prevention cleaning: blowing bark, sawdust and needles out of radiator/cooler cores, the engine compartment, belly pan and around the exhaust with compressed air, and cleaning cab glass, mirrors and lights, typically at the landing at day's end during dry season.

Scheduled service at the contractor's shop or equipment yard on a level concrete floor: engine oil and filter change, fuel/hydraulic filter replacement, replacing a blown hydraulic hose, tensioning tracks or torquing wheel nuts, battery and belt checks, with the machine parked and locked out.

sources.title: Autonomous refuelling solution for mining trucks from Universal Field Robots — International Mining
sources.claim: SCOTT Automation's ROBOFUEL robotic arm refuels large mining haul trucks autonomously at purpose-built refuelling stations and was in use at multiple mine sites, including with an autonomous Komatsu 930E ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: refuelling heavy off-road diesel machinery. It is the fueling element of the logging operator's daily service routine — coupling a nozzle to a large machine's fill point and dispensing a metered volume — with comparable objects and precision.

sources.title: SCOTT making ROBOFUEL refuelling system progress with AHS mining truck fleets - International Mining
sources.claim: ROBOFUEL uses a robotic arm with vision and sensing to locate the fill point and refuel mine trucks without an attendant present.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above: machine-controlled connection and fluid transfer to a heavy machine, substituting for the operator's manual fueling step.

sources.system: PONSSE Greasing System (harvester head chain lubrication)
sources.title: Ponsse Greasing System – new solutions for forest machines chain lubrication - Ponsse Oyj
